Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he’s unfazed by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie

Unknown Publisher

Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.
As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.
In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023.
“If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.”
Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.)
So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life?
“The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman said. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.”
Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted.
Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.”
“It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.”
Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him.
Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir.
Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays.
“I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”

Read, watch, and nothing else. Reading mode keeps the article and its pictures, set to be read. Leave a video's tab and it follows you in a small window, above every app.

10.8 MB on disk. No engine of its own to carry.

The GTA Flu

Grand Theft Auto VI is arriving tomorrow, and it’s going to be a big deal. It’s the most preordered video game ever, with millions of units sold for billions of dollars. Given that popularity, it also has the potential to put a real dent in office productivity. USA Today noted this, but they may have oversold the issue.
That article tosses around a whole bunch of numbers, though, and they don’t really seem to add up. For instance, USA Today’s subhead states “In a survey of 1,000 respondents, nearly 36% said they plan to call out of work ‘sick’ on Nov. 19 to play GTA 6”. That does not seem to match what’s found in the GameSquare press release to which it seemingly refers. Most importantly, the subhead fails to specify who those 1,000 respondents were. The survey in question was of about the general working public, just those employees who “identify as gamers”.
The results, which came from a scientific representative sample of 1,000 full time US employees who identified as gamers (with a margin of error of 3%) looked to identify the potential impact Game Theft Auto VI’s launch will have on the workplace, culture (i.e. Hollywood and sports), and consumer spending.
I don’t know what percentage of workers that actually is, but it’s certainly not 100%. As well:
Furthermore 10% have said they plan to skip work on launch day, with another 30% of US employees considering taking time off. Of those who were considering, 36% said if they did, they would call in “sick.”
I believe that means 10% of workers who identify as gamers have already taken time off (or are simply going to no-show), while another 10.8% are considering calling out sick tomorrow. That’s a much lower number than 36%.
I’ll be curious to see if there’s actually an impact from workers staying home to play a video game tomorrow. I doubt we’ll get good numbers, but I’ll certainly keep an eye out.

Sexp Matrix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
20:01:50 UTC
05:01:50 KST

Here is a simple idea. Could each row in a spreadsheet be represented as a self-contained S-expression? Could we evaluate these expressions remotely and asynchronously, then chain the rows together into a processing pipeline?
What if we designed a new kind of spreadsheet where each row is a rich, editable S-expression?
Let’s explore this idea by formally representing a spreadsheet as a Matrix.
Consider matrix S where the first element in a row is
always a function. The values in the remaining cells are either symbols,
values or s-expressions.
Given a row with n elements, the row function C0 can be applied as C0:C1 → Cn. Cn+1 contains the output of C0:C1 → Cn. The matrix can be sparse or transposable.
Matrix S can then be represented as a list of
s-expressions. This is the core idea.
'((+ 1 2 3)
  (max 10 10 (+ 20 10))
  (avg 10 (compute-discount 100) (/ 10 2)))
This list is eval’d by an external or remote s-expression evaluator. That evaluator has a rich library of functions to do sophisticated, asynchronous tasks.
(apply (symbol (first row)) (map eval (rest row))
S-Matrix has other interesting properties which is beyond the scope of this discussion. Let’s quickly dive into some examples, to demonstrate the core idea.
Our first example is a matrix that computes the shipping fees for each cart total and other parameters.
This is equivalent to the following on the server.
(find-fees 1000 :gold (verify 12345))
find-fees is a remote function that could be a
pre-defined function, AWS Lambda, a microkernel or a LLM agent.
find-fees can actually be a sophisticated function that
takes a lot more parameters into consideration. It could have fees
waived for certain zip codes. It could take into account the current
datetime and so forth. It could be using LLMs to determine the shipping
fees.
If you do not want find-fees to be pre-defined remote function you could inline the function. Something like the following in the function column.
(fn [args]
  (cond
    (= (nth args 1) :gold) 30
    (= (nth args 1) :silver) 50
    (> 4000) 10))
Another example, as shown below, is to compute the account balance by having functions that fetch the actual balance for different financial buckets. Now, this table or matrix is not a static one. It actually is a representation of the actual balance. The functions are remote, asynchronous and arguably secure.
Let’s try another example: Verifying documents - you could think of it as Truthy matrix:
Recall that the last column is the output of the row function. In the first row, driver-license is a function that looks at the field values and verifies if the document is valid.
(driver-license "Bob Smith" "CA" "10-20") -> No
This matrix — a list of S-expressions — was probably generated by a document-extraction process. The idea that code is data applies only to S-expressions.
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of what matrices with remotely evaluated S-expressions could be used for. Now let’s apply the concept to something more familiar: spreadsheets.
Grids and matrices are often easiest to visualize as spreadsheets. But modern spreadsheets are highly GUI-centric with a zillion buttons, and most of their functions run locally, which may not be adequate if they are computationally expensive. What if we reimagined spreadsheets around remote functions, with each row containing a list of S-expressions?
Instead of treating cells as containers for values, we’d treat them as slots for S-expressions. The spreadsheet could include an editor for writing complex expressions, or let users reference code through a URI—such as a Git or HTTP link. The expressions would be evaluated dynamically.
Entangle is a prototype showcasing this concept. It’s a tiny application written in Clojure.
git clone https://git.sr.ht/~icylisper/entangle
cd entangle
clojure -Srepro -M -m entangle.main
;=> Listen HTTP on port 8000
We can test that the API works using csv data.
sample.csv
+,1,2,3
*,4,5,6
+,(+ 2 3),2,(- 5 1)curl -X PUT http://localhost:8000/csv -H 'Content-Type: text/csv' --data-binary @sample.csv
+,1,2,3,6
*,4,5,6,120
+,(+ 2 3),2,(- 5 1),11
We could also capture the output of any row and use it in subsequent
rows kind of creating a pipeline or as mathematicians call it
Transient Matrix.
+,1,2,3
*,$0
+,$0,$1
Where $N specifies the nth row.
We could also do map-reduce kinda computation using the simple reduce function and $* macro/notation.
+,1,2,3
*,$0
+,$0,$1
reduce,$*
Additionally, the row function could point to an LLM agent that computes a value from a collection of expressions, text, or other data. It could just as easily invoke a remote serverless function or call a REST endpoint.
Yo enough talk. Let’s see something in action. Below is a screencast
showing basic usage of the spreadsheet UI. It’s a single page HTML -
just do open index.html
When we hit compute button, it sends the list of
s-expressions to the Entangle REST API. The backend evals the
s-expressions and returns the output asynchronously (via websocket). The
receiving client filled the last column in each row with the
corresponding result. Notice in the screencast that we can edit the
s-expression in an editor (Yes, you can open it in emacs too!). The
first cell’s s-expression is either a symbol or an anonymous function.
The anonymous function always takes the rest of the row as an arg.
Each s-expression evaluation takes it’s own time. The server can decide to parallelize the processing of these expressions.
The goal of entangle is to showcase a new way to think
about spreadsheets - as a matrix of s-expressions that are remotely
evaluated.
Scribbled on 11-06-2026. No LLMs used.

'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64 (calif.io) 2
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here.
The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure.

Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
19:56:39 UTC
04:56:39 KST

Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.
The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.
The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.
Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.
Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.
With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.
AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says.
The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.
Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
19:40:36 UTC
04:40:36 KST

President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.
Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.
Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.
Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.
Peace and prosperity for whom?
“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.
Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.
At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.
“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”
“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.
The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”
The agency says the project will be located on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here
The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.
He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.
Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.
At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.
Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.
“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.
And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

DaisyRose-27B: 1,200-task RL took Qwen3.8 from 5.6% to 12% on Terminal-Bench 4.1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
19:39:16 UTC
04:39:16 KST

All posts
DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.
We are releasing BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.
DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above1. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.
High-quality Training Data
We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria.
- Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from.
- Every task is a long job with several problems chained together. Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens.
- There is no room for reward hacking. We reviewed every task along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training.
Efficient training backend
RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.
57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.
2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.
Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.
Robust sandbox service
During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.
Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.
80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.
Try DaisyRose-27B, or train your own
You can download DaisyRose-27B from Hugging Face, and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework Miles.
DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at contact@radixark.ai.
We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.
- How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run. ↩

What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
19:29:43 UTC
04:29:43 KST

If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
I want you to understand just how much money this company rakes in.
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
I want you to understand just how much money this company rakes in.
It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?
But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.
It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.
If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.
TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.
Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.
Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.
Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?
But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.
And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.
Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.
But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.
In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.
Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”
Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

The leaked Lenovo Legion Go Beam could be the affordable handheld we need

Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
19:07:29 UTC
04:07:29 KST

With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.
Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.
On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against users who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.
“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a new bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.
“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”
Roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that users were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the company’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”
Roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”
Congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.
Litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake issue through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a new wave of legal challenges.
“You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”
In addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”
The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she said she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”
Hilton said over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”
Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who said a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how quickly technology advances.”

My Thanksgiving Butter-Swim Biscuits Are So Easy, You Don’t Even Need to Roll Out the Dough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

My Thanksgiving Butter-Swim Biscuits Are So Easy, You Don’t Even Need to Roll Out the Dough
Thanksgiving dinner always has a lot going on, but I’m a firm believer that there’s always room for one more carb. These Thanksgiving butter-swim biscuits are my favorite alternative to bread or dinner rolls. If you haven’t made butter-swim biscuits before, the dough gets pressed into a pan of melted butter, which means crisp, golden edges and a seriously tender middle. For this twist, I added Thanksgiving butter packed with garlic and fresh herbs. These biscuits pair well with everything on the table, from roast turkey and gravy to mashed potatoes and green bean casserole.
Why You Should Make Thanksgiving Butter-Swim Biscuits
These biscuits are about as low-stress as holiday baking gets. The dough comes together quickly in one bowl, and there’s no rolling or cutting out. I just stir everything together, press it into a pan, and let the butter work its magic. The Thanksgiving butter is what makes these biscuits extra-special, as garlic, parsley, sage, thyme, and rosemary taste like the whole holiday in one bite. I melt the butter right in the pan while the oven preheats, which means the dough sizzles in butter the second it goes in, giving the biscuits their golden, crisp edges. It’s totally optional, but I also like to make a little extra butter to brush on top, because it gives the biscuits an extra hit of herb flavor.
How to Make Thanksgiving Butter-Swim Biscuits
- Make the Thanksgiving butter. Arrange a rack in the middle of the oven and heat the oven to 400°F. Place 1 stick unsalted butter in an 8×8-inch baking dish and set it in the oven while it preheats until the butter is fully melted. Carefully remove the dish and stir in 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 tablespoon chopped fresh parsley, 1 teaspoon chopped fresh sage, 1 teaspoon chopped fresh thyme, 1 teaspoon chopped fresh rosemary, and 3/4 teaspoon kosher salt. Swirl the butter around so it coats the sides.
- Mix the dough. Whisk 2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 tablespoon baking powder, 4 teaspoons granulated sugar, 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, and 1 teaspoon baking soda in a large bowl. Add 1 1/2 cups cold buttermilk and stir with a flexible spatula until a shaggy, sticky dough forms and there are no pockets of dry flour left.
- Bake the biscuits. Transfer the dough into the baking pan. Using the spatula, press the dough evenly into the pan until it touches all the sides (the dough will be swimming in the herb butter). Cut the dough with a knife all the way down to the bottom of the pan in a 3×3 grid to make 9 squares (the squares will still be touching each other). Bake until the biscuits are golden-brown and have puffed up significantly, and a tester inserted into the center biscuit comes out clean, 25 to 27 minutes. Immediately cut along the scores again to separate the biscuits, then let cool for 15 minutes in the pan before serving.
- Make extra butter to brush on top (optional). While the biscuits bake, make another half batch of the Thanksgiving butter in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Brush it over the tops of the hot biscuits right after cutting them.
Tips for Making Thanksgiving Butter-Swim Biscuits
- Keep the dough shaggy. The dough should look sticky and a little messy, and that’s exactly what you want. Stir just until there are no dry pockets of flour left, and the biscuits will stay soft and tender.
- Stir in the herbs after the butter melts. Wait until the butter is fully melted and the pan is out of the oven before adding the garlic and herbs.
- Use the butter on everything. This herb butter is delicious well beyond biscuits. I love it melted over mashed potatoes, brushed on warm dinner rolls, and tossed with roasted vegetables. It would also be great for drizzling on roast turkey or stirred into your bread stuffing before baking for an extra boost of flavor.

Genie 4 is now available
Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie, an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them.
So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds.
Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser.
Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie
With Genie 4, our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue.
Discover new Genie 3 capabilities
While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include:
- Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys.
- 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images.
- Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore.
Create new interactive experiences
The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood.
You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds.
Explore the new gallery
When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.”
The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism.
Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix.
Learn how we are building responsibly
We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings.
Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview.
Try Project Genie today
Eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers can try the new Project Genie experience starting today, and Google AI Pro members can join the waitlist on the same page.

The 6 Best Cutting Boards for Anyone Avoiding Plastics
I didn’t think a sturdy, large cutting board was essential until I put up with a small, flimsy, plastic one for months. When my roommate finally decided enough was enough and grabbed us a huge wooden one, I noticed the difference immediately. I quickly became a member of the “I’m obsessed with my cutting board” club, and discovered that my grandmother is, too: She recently splurged on a titanium cutting board, and says it has completely changed the way she cooks.
These days many people are trying to steer away from plastic cutting boards (shoutout to Quinn Fish for explaining the potentially harmful effects of microplastics in the kitchen). So I decided to poll our team to find out their favorites. Here are some picks that have also transformed everyone’s time chopping, dicing, and slicing in the kitchen.
This titanium cutting board is the exact one my grandmother raves about. The material not only keeps the board hygienic when she uses it for raw meat, but it also makes the board itself super-lightweight (which means it’s easier for her to manage). It’s designed specifically with home cooks in mind, featuring a knife sharpener, handle, and grinding area.
Something to keep in mind is that Titanium (or any metal) can actually dull your knives faster than wood or plastic. If sharpening your knives more frequently is something you’re worried about, then you might want to consider another material.
Gorilla Grip’s stainless steel cutting board has quickly become Deputy Food Editor Kristina Razon’s go-to when cooking. She loves how the rubber edges keep it from slipping while she’s chopping, and the stainless steel material makes it odor- and stain-resistant “which is ideal for prepping raw or cooked meat, fish, or really anything that tends to leave residue,” she explains. Just note: The same disclaimer about sharpening knives from the board above rings true here as well.
Jill Waldbieser has been using these boards for five years and says they still look brand-new. “They are self-healing, dishwasher-safe, and roll up so you can slice and chop on them, then curl them up and dump the contents into a hot pot or pan with zero issues,” she says.
This 100% plant-based cutting board is a recent favorite of Shopping Writer Micki Wagner. She had high hopes when testing the board, and it did not disappoint. It’s large enough to chop multiple things at once, super durable so there aren’t knife marks, and dishwasher-safe for easy cleanup.
Micki also loves this small cutting board, which quickly became her go-to for pretty much everything except major jobs (read: when a ton of chopping is required). It may look made of wood, but it’s actually paper composite, and its non-slip grips make it dependable for whatever she’s slicing.
Social Media Manager Andrea Kaufman had been wanting to upgrade from her plastic cutting boards for a while, but was worried a wooden one might have the same intimidating maintenance requirements as a cast iron skillet. Her new Hexclad board hasn’t been hard to maintain (so far). It’s super-sturdy, and the built-in handles and grooves on the sides are nice touches, so it’s easy to carry and can tackle cutting meat (actually the first thing she used it for). “I haven’t used it for entertaining yet,” she says, “but I definitely plan to!”
Do you have a favorite plastic-free cutting board? Tell us about it in the comments!

When Free Software Isn't Free Enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
18:39:28 UTC
03:39:28 KST

When Free Software Isn't Free Enough
Published on 2026/11/13
If you’ve previously read my blog, it should come as no surprise that I’ve been a champion of free software for a very long time. The idea that you should be able to run, study, change, and share the programs that run your life is something I truly believe in, maybe even to an annoying degree. This past week though, a mailing list thread made me wonder whether the movement built around that idea is aiming high enough.
What happened
The thread is called “Human Emacs”, and it ran on the emacs-devel mailing list. It asks a question many projects are facing: should GNU Emacs accept LLM-generated contributions?
Brian Cully, who argued against, posed a hypothetical to find out where the maintainers draw their line:
if I live in a territory that permits slavery, and by law i am granted sole ownership of the products of that forced labor, and then i use that to create contributions to gnu emacs, complete with copyright assignment, and it is technically correct, and, above all, you, the emacs maintainers are aware of how this was produced, would it be ethical to accept those contributions?
As part of their response, Eli Zaretskii said: “Our answer must be YES.”
Their reasoning was that weighing contributors’ politics, ethics, or origins would split the community along ideological lines, and that the Free Software movement addresses only problems that directly affect software freedoms. They also rejected the idea that GNU pursues liberty for all humanity, saying its goals are narrower than that.
The internet did what it did, and the story became “GNU supports slavery”, which is not a fair summary, and I want to say so plainly. Eli later clarified that they personally don’t tolerate slavery. Their argument was that in the context of Emacs development, the only thing that matters is the quality of the code being contributed, and that bringing personal values into those decisions would hurt the project. Another maintainer pointed to GNU’s stated position: the project endorses only two political positions, that users should control their own computing and that basic human rights in computing should be supported. Everything else, they said, is off-topic.
Now, I don’t think anyone in that thread is a villain. I think their answers were consistent with the question they were asked, but that consistency is exactly what bothers me.
As an aside, if you’re an Emacs user, do consider checking out the Human Emacs website.
The case for their answer
Let’s consider the strongest version of the maintainers’ position, because I don’t think it’s foolish.
A project that tries to enforce a moral purity test on every contribution has to decide whose morality counts. Once “is this code ethically sourced?” becomes a gate, maintainers become the judges of every contributor’s life, labor, and country. That is unworkable, and it invites exactly the kind of factional fights that kill volunteer projects. There is also a fair point that rejecting the patch frees no one. The people in the hypothetical are no better off if Emacs says no.
I take that seriously, but I don’t think that it settles the question.
Where it falls short
Someone on the thread put the problem better than I can:
there is no such thing as justice for only one group of people
They went on to say that narrowly focusing on one arena is fine, as long as the work exists in the context of a larger, universal struggle. Otherwise it’s hollow.
That’s really the heart of this whole thing for me. The free software movement has a rich vocabulary of freedom and liberty, and almost all of it is about one relationship: that of the person running the software and the code they run.
To be fair, free software has never been neutral about ethics. Its founding claim is that proprietary software is an ethical wrong, and the FSF campaigns on issues like surveillance and DRM. So my complaint isn’t that the movement has no ethics. It’s where those ethics stop. They stop at one relationship: that between a person and the software on their own computer. Anything outside of that line, such as how the code was made, who was paid what, or what the finished software does to other people, gets declared off-topic. That’s the edge this thread ran into.
When “the only thing that matters is the code” is the rule, the movement has decided pre-emptively that it cannot see the labor behind the code, the data behind the models, the people who are surveilled, scored, or sorted by software they never chose and can’t inspect, or the people who can’t use any of it because they lack a computer, a language, an accessible interface, or time. A freedom that only reaches people who already have the privilege of reading source code is a narrow freedom.
I’ll note that GNU’s own stated principles include supporting basic human rights in computing. That is a real commitment, and it suggests the door is open further than the thread made it look. But a commitment that appears only when it’s convenient, and disappears when someone asks it to carry weight, doesn’t amount to much.
About the LLM question
The full case against LLMs — how they’re built on unconsented labor, sold through hype, and coercively pushed onto workers — deserves its own post, which I’ll link here once I publish it.
For now, the short version is simple: a movement built around user freedom has to ask what those freedoms are for when the tools being pushed into its codebase rely on mass extraction and coercion.
To be clear, I don’t judge people who are forced to use them at work. Most people have no say over the tools their job requires, and if the choice is between using the tool and keeping your livelihood, I don’t blame anyone for choosing their livelihood.
A volunteer contributing on their own time, or a maintainer setting a project’s rules, has a choice that an employee under a mandate doesn’t. That’s why I hold FOSS projects and their leadership to a higher standard here. My criticism is for how projects use that choice, not for people who don’t have one.
What I’d like to see
I’m not suggesting that we throw out the four freedoms. They’re foundational, and I’m not interested in burning everything to the ground to replace it with something more vague. I want to start from them and add something. Here’s where I’d start, with the small and concrete.
- Projects should decide how they treat LLM contributions, in the open, instead of defaulting to “only the code matters.” That could mean a policy that rejects them, or one that allows them with disclosure. Either way, it should be written down, argued over in public, and owned by the maintainers. Not deciding is also a decision, and it’s the one that favors whoever is pushing the hardest.
- Judge the process, not the person. I’m not asking maintainers to audit a contributor’s politics or country. That’s the unworkable version, and I think Eli is correct to fear it. A contribution policy that asks whether the code was written by a consenting human who understands and stands behind the change — rather than extracted from coerced labor or generated by a model trained on unconsented work — sets an ethical boundary without putting anyone’s personal beliefs on trial.
From there, the larger principles follow:
- Freedom for users, not just programmers. Source code access means little if you can’t read it. Real software freedom has to include usability, accessibility, documentation, and support in the languages people actually speak.
- Software has a supply chain, and it’s made up of people. Who wrote this, under what conditions, and who profits? These questions belong in the conversation, even when the answers are inconvenient.
- Software has effects beyond the machine. Systems that decide who gets a loan, a job, or bail are freedom issues, whether or not the license is permissive.
- Neutrality has costs. Declining to take a position is itself a position, and it tends to favor whoever already has power.
- Solidarity over purity. The goal isn’t a perfect test for every patch. It’s a movement that sees itself as part of a larger struggle, and shows that in how it conducts itself.
None of these are particularly new ideas. People have been arguing for a long time that struggles for justice are linked. I’m only asking that the people who build the tools of the future treat that as part of the job.
The obvious objections
- “Who decides whose morality counts?” The maintainers do, the same way they already decide everything else about a project: openly, and accountably. Setting a contribution policy isn’t a moral purity test. Every project already has standards for what it will accept.
- “Doesn’t this violate freedom zero?” I don’t think so, and I want to be careful here. Freedom zero is about what you can do with the software once you have it. A project declining a patch doesn’t stop anyone from running, changing, or sharing the code. If the policy is unpopular, anyone can fork, and that’s the system working as designed. I’m not proposing licenses that restrict who can use the software or for what. That’s a whole other thing. At the same time, we shouldn’t pretend “just fork it” solves anything. Legally, anyone can fork any free software project. Practically though, that’s only true up to a certain point. You might be able to fork a smaller tool, but nobody is going to feasibly fork something like the Linux kernel, for example — not when it’s backed by billions of dollars in corporate hardware support and engineering resources. When foundational projects refuse to draw ethical lines, the rest of us don’t actually have a realistic exit option.
- “Rejecting the patch frees no one.” Yes, but I’d rather say so than pretend otherwise. Also, accepting a contribution isn’t neutral either. It rewards how the work was done and signals to everyone watching what the project will take. A project can’t be indifferent to its inputs and also claim to care about freedom.
Where I’m landing
I’ll be honest, it’s hard not to feel a little disillusioned with the free software movement at the moment. I’m not angry at the maintainers and I’m still going to use and appreciate the software they’ve built, but I can’t keep treating “freedom” as a word that means so much to some people and so little to everyone else.
If you feel the same way, I’d like to hear from you. What would a movement like this look like to you? What should it commit to, and what should it refuse?
And remember, nobody is free until we’re all free. That includes people who write the code, and the people who live with what it does.

If the glorious AI revolution rests entirely on the well-being of one man, AI is perhaps not as robust a technology as I had previously been led to believe. Nonetheless, chunks of Silicon Valley are now insisting he is indispensable. For instance, if Elon Musk is telling the truth, then Jensen Huang (the former CEO of Nvidia, a company with a market cap of about $3 trillion) has been making deals that were “a handshake with Jensen” with suppliers — “not a written contract,” Musk wrote.
What is Nvidia without AI’s sugar daddy in charge?
Collette Kress’ first earnings call gives us some clues.
What is Nvidia without AI’s sugar daddy in charge?
Collette Kress’ first earnings call gives us some clues.
Fascinating stuff to tell shareholders. But after listening to Nvidia’s first earnings call with its new CEO, Colette Kress, I do think something may have shifted. In her former role as CFO, Kress generally told Huang to stop spending so much money on financing its customers, because telling the CEO to stop spending so much goddamn money is the CFO’s job. Apparently he belittled her about this, but that’s the CEO–CFO relationship, baby! Anyway she’s the boss now, at least temporarily. I think it’s reasonable to assume that though Nvidia has for years been the AI industry’s sugar daddy, without Huang and his handshakes in the picture, it may be less liberal with its cash.
Kress shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia
Kress’ job was never going to be easy. Even without tantrums from the likes of Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Musk, both of whom seem to have a lot of free time for guys who are ostensibly running multibillion-dollar companies, having to steer a company after an event on the scale of Huang’s meltdown is a miserable task. But this woman also is now having to deal with a bunch of guys publicly insisting that Huang was the only reason Nvidia succeeded. It amused me on the call that she did the thing I often do when men decide they can bully me, which is to tap in another man who is theoretically or actually in charge of me — and so on the call, Nvidia board Chair Harvey C. Jones politely told these losers to get bent. The board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company won’t be taking questions about him.
On the call, Kress pointedly noted that Nvidia’s agreements with suppliers last through the end of the decade, so I suppose we must entertain the possibility that when it comes to the handshake deals, Musk is, once again, lying. This is an important thing, though — as SemiAnalysis noted in its bizarrely conspiratorial post on the situation, Nvidia is successful because it has choked off the supply chain.
Do you have information about Nvidia? Contact Elizabeth Lopatto securely on Signal at lopatto.46
Kress also shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia, or the kind of open internal revolt that got Sam Altman reinstated at OpenAI during “the blip” in 2023. She told investors that “our employees, we believe, are committed. They are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.” Nvidia’s employees have “been working seamlessly on what they need to complete,” she added. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” I’m sure we’ll hear more about this in the coming days, but unlike with Altman, Huang resigned, and we all know why. And while some employees support reinstating Huang, I notice that there’s a real dearth of “we’ll quit with him” in those sentiments.
I don’t think this is going to shut the Branch Nvidians up, but I do think the board doesn’t have another choice here. Hilariously, we learned this weekend that Nvidia did not buy complete directors’ and officers’ insurance. While the individual executives’ and board members’ personal assets are shielded from lawsuits that stem from its executives’ behavior, the company is not. So if someone, or perhaps several someones, were to file a suit because of, say, Huang’s personal life and its damaging effects on the stock price, Nvidia itself is on the hook.
The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them
This is to say nothing of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s investigation — which, given how cliqued up Huang was with President Donald Trump, may be investigating on his behalf rather than investigating him — or the California attorney general going on Bloomberg TV to say that he was going to start kicking the tires on an investigation, or Huang and general counsel Tim Teter’s upcoming congressional testimony. The three actual lawyers left at the Department of Justice may be doing their own investigation, too. Elizabeth Warren seems mad. A reminder: The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them. It is about Nvidia customers allegedly circumventing a ban on selling chips to China. The scandal is already big enough that US policy has been altered; the Department of Commerce informed us all on November 16th that there were new restrictions on selling chips to countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. Also, data centers around the world need licenses from the US to lease compute to companies headquartered in China.

The company also addressed this, though somewhat obliquely: It raised its forecast, saying that revenue will grow by 75 percent next year. Still, given that Singapore alone was responsible for $104 billion of revenue in 2025, I am curious about the number; at the time, it was the second-biggest geographic area by revenue, dwarfed only by the US. I can’t tell you how much Singaporean sales matter to Nvidia now, because around the time that Singaporean sales reportedly started to represent half the company’s revenue, Nvidia switched its reporting methodology. The company had previously noted that “most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.” Notably, Megaspeed had a Singapore address — and was the subject of a truncated Commerce Department investigation into whether its chips were being diverted to China. Fun stuff!
You know what else is fun? Jensen Huang’s children are still at the company, at least as far as anyone knows. His daughter Madison, described as Huang’s “chief of staff” by The New York Times, even helped direct Nvidia’s response to inquiries about Megaspeed, which have been mounting now for a year, the Financial Times reported. Her husband, Nico Caprez, “was promoted to a role that covered international deals with cloud computing clients in Asia” around the time those inquiries were getting started. “They had a lot of power and influence and were allowed to operate unchecked,” an anonymous source told the FT. “No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”
His kids — one of them, Spencer, ran a bar before his role at Nvidia — likely haven’t endeared themselves to their colleagues, based on some of the reporting now trickling out about them. What was Spencer doing at Nvidia? Unknown. “Some executives said they had never encountered Spencer Huang in the course of business,” The Wall Street Journal wrote.
As a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming
Employing the CEO’s relatives was already a governance risk. If the outside agitation continues to reinstate Jensen Huang, there are three key lambs that Nvidia can slaughter, and all of them are his relatives. I suppose the thing I find most astonishing is that Huang doesn’t see the writing on the wall; he has posted that if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” The post was met with, among other things, Altman posting a green heart in response.
Now, as a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming. I mean, Huang can nominate two people to the board of directors before the company’s shareholder meeting next year. Let’s have a stupid proxy fight and see what else leaks about Huang’s leadership and children! Of course, that will be difficult for Kress to manage — but that’s I guess what she’s getting paid for.

According to the Journal’s story, Huang noted that the vaunted deals he’d made with suppliers “were coming at him like an ‘avalanche,’” while “major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia.” This does explain Nvidia’s role as the sugar daddy for the neocloud industry. Kress reportedly pushed back on some of its agreements, apparently significantly downsizing a financial commitment to OpenAI among other things. Now, while she’ll be spending plenty of her time managing the fallout from Huang’s departure, she won’t be directly fighting with him over Nvidia’s finances.
It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support
On the earnings call, analyst Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein Research asked about a new paragraph he’d noticed in the earnings release about neoclouds. Nvidia had been supplying guarantees to some neoclouds by saying it would purchase compute if no one else would. The new paragraph reads, in part, “Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us.” Kress clarified that this meant that if neoclouds’ buildout was delayed — or they otherwise had a challenge in building the warehouse to stick the chips in — Nvidia’s guarantee “doesn’t exist anymore,” she said. “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said.
I have no way of knowing if this language had been ready to go in the press release before Huang resigned, but it does seem notable all the same. It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support. And knowing Kress wanted Huang to spend less on this stuff, I think it tees us up for an interesting period. Passing under the radar last week were some indications that the Federal Reserve may be about to do an interest rate hike, which is trouble for a number of companies, such as CoreWeave, that rely on debt for their data center buildouts. If we are entering a period where financing is more expensive or more difficult to get, we may see some neoclouds falter. The new paragraph in the earnings release suggests that Nvidia wants us all to know that it’s not going to bail them out forever. Bring Huang back if you want, I guess, but even he can’t control the Fed — or the increasingly odd outlook for data center financing. In the coming months, Nvidia may be better off with a woman who wants to keep the costs down.
You know who is getting money under Kress, though? Nvidia staff. They can expect raises and equity in December.
