Methods record · companion to the case study
How this study was made
What the agents did to build and check “Who Made the Strawberry?”, step by step, from the session logs.
Reconstructed on Nov 16, 2026. Times in CET (UTC+1).
AbstractThe case study “Who Made the Strawberry?” was built in about 24 hours of work over three days, Nov 14 to 16, 2026, by one main agent and the agents it started. This record lists what was done in 58 steps: counting scripts, two readings of the logs, analyses, reviews, consensus rewrites, cross-reads, adversarial readings, a blind test, independent studies by another model family, translations, restructurings, a recovery and publication. It shows how many agents of which model ran at once, how the output of one step fed the next, and what each check found. The checks found 33 errors in results or text; 23 were corrected. No second human took part, so every check described here is a check by models.
1What this record is
This tab describes the process that produced the study. It is not part of the study's argument. Its sources are the logs of the Claude Code session that built the study (from Nov 14, 14:36), its 201 subagent runs, eight Codex runs in the study folder, and the study's own briefs, reports and reviews. One model reconstructed the timeline from these logs and cut it into 58 steps. No second coder checked that cut. Private material in the logs was left out. The reconstruction ends on Nov 16: its steps, figures and totals, and the limits drawn from them, describe the process up to then, not the finished study of Nov 17.
The study was commissioned by the user, who approved its main steps and its publication; no other human took part.
One main agent did the orchestration. It wrote briefs, started subagents, merged their results, ran scripts and published. It ran on claude-fable-5-2 until Nov 15, 00:16, and on claude-opus-5-5 after that. Subagents were Claude models started by the main agent or by other subagents. Codex runs used models of another family, gpt-6-astra and gpt-6-luna, started from the same folder.
The study was started on November 14, about 14 hours after the result was posted on Reddit, so that it could be linked from there. The user and the same kind of AI agents that the study describes started it. So the study is not neutral ground, and its limits section says so (the study, ).
Since Nov 17 the two tabs are divided by one rule. The study holds what a reader learns about the project, plus what was counted, who coded, how far two coders agree, and the limits. This tab holds everything about how the study came about: the readings and codings and how they compare, what went wrong when reading the logs, the corrections, and the reviews. Sections 5 to 12 were moved here from the study under that rule.
2The steps
Nov 14. Within the first hour, 14 day readers cut the 14 days into 265 episodes, two coders labelled them, and the page went live; from then on every change was public. A fresh reviewer found seven problems in the afternoon. In the evening the counts moved into scripts, a second counting path found a gap of 138 tool calls, and an agent tracing ideas found that the digest lacked about half of the messages. So 14 new readers re-read every day from the complete chat. Two reviews, a blind test and eight adversarial readings followed before midnight.
Nov 15. The morning went into a plain-language mode (7 agents) and five translations (66 runs, at most 20 at once). In the evening a style audit led to three independent rewrites and a consensus, a check for changes of meaning by another model family, two cross-readers and two independent studies by another family. Two agents then built a shorter preview. Its review by another family stopped at the usage limit, and a same-family review replaced it.
Nov 16. The restructured version went live, and two process studies, a linkograph and 32 sources were added. A cleanup in an unrelated session deleted the local working folder; it was restored from the live site and the logs. The evening brought a plain-language pass checked file by file, a peer review by another family, a check of two listed limits, and an audit of all days against the raw logs.
Nov 17. A model of another family coded a sample of 60 episodes again for the roles, without seeing the first coding (). An overall review by a fresh instance of the writing model followed, and the study was rebuilt: findings grouped by the kind of evidence, roles as an ordering by two coders with both coders side by side, and this tab for the making of the study. An independent review by a model of another family then checked the build against its data and sources, and its corrections were built in. These steps are not in the 58 steps and the figures of this section, which end on Nov 16.
More detail: all 58 steps and what each produced
3How outputs flowed
Most steps took the output of an earlier step and passed their own on. Three patterns recur. draws one example of each.
Parallel and blind. The same task went to several agents that did not see each other: one reader per day in both readings, two reviewers of the same draft, two independent studies, six adversarial readers with only the data. Parallel runs made the work fast. Keeping them blind kept the outputs separate enough to compare.
Consensus. For the style rewrite, three agents rewrote the same text on their own and a fourth merged the three into one version. The merged text then went to a model of another family, which checked it field by field for changes of meaning, and to two fresh readers, one of each family.
Check, then fix. Most checks did not change anything themselves. A reviewer wrote findings, and a later step applied them, often the main agent and sometimes a corrector agent. Some loops reached far back. The day audit on Nov 16 corrected day texts written by the second reading on Nov 14, and the peer review sent section 6.4 back for a fix within an hour after it had gone live.
The links between the steps also show dependence. Almost every analysis after the first evening built on the episodes cut by the first reading and recoded by the second. Later checks that read the same episodes were therefore less independent than their number suggests.
4Effort per phase
The main agent made 1,769 tool calls, its 201 subagent runs made 5,991, and the eight Codex runs made 135. About half of the subagent runs went into simplifying, translating and restyling text, not into analysis. The phase of plain language and translations alone used 73 runs (), twice as many as both readings together. Checks were small in runs and large in effect: the first review was one agent and found seven problems, and the day audit used 16 runs for 292 corrections. The Claude models processed about 1.5 billion tokens, nearly all of them cache reads, and wrote about 10.8 million.
5The two readings of the logs
The episodes of the study were read twice. This section says why, what changed between the readings, and how far they agree. The study shows the second reading.
Episodes. For each day, one agent read all prompts of that day included in the initial digest and the first 500 characters of each agent reply. It split the day into episodes and gave each episode one of six labels. Sorting episodes into such fixed categories is called coding here. The labels are a judgement of the reading agents.
Revision comparison. The second reading kept the first reading's episode boundaries and could see its episode texts, but read the complete chat with another model and other instructions. On the 263 episodes both readings share, they give the same label to 80.6%, the same starter to 95.8%, the same deciding contribution to 79.8% and the same named mistake to 77.6%. By the scale of [47], agreement beyond chance is moderate for the label, weak for the deciding contribution and the named mistake, and minimal for the starter (box below). This compares two revisions. It is not an independent reliability estimate: shared texts can raise agreement, and changed evidence and rules can lower it. So the shift in is not due to the missing messages alone.
How agreement was measured
Agreement beyond chance is measured with kappa: 1 is full agreement, 0 is chance. For the label kappa is 0.74, for who started an episode 0.34, for whose contribution decided it 0.53 and for whose mistake the chat names 0.58. Who started an episode has the lowest kappa despite 95.8% agreement. The reason is that the user started almost every episode, so chance alone already gives a high match. The deciding contribution was later replaced by the role coding below and is kept only for this comparison.
: the two readings side by side
6Earlier codings
Before the role coding, the same episodes were coded in two other ways: by kinds of contribution, and by whose contribution decided an episode. Both stay in the data and are shown here for the record. Neither is used for a finding of the study. The role coding replaced the second one after a review by a model of another family found that its rule tested different things for each side.
Kinds of contribution (second reading)What the old coding hid
The earlier coding asked whose contribution decided each episode. Its rule tested different things for each side and put the most common pattern under “both”. Read as roles, “both” is almost always the same division of work: the user proposes, an agent builds, the user decides. In 17 of the 32 episodes once coded “user decisive” an agent named the cause, and 11 of them ended abandoned or unresolved, which the old rule should have coded “none”. “Agent decisive” mostly meant that an agent found the cause.
How this was codedHow the misunderstandings in the study were replayed
7The role coding and its independent check
The study reports roles only as an ordering by two coders (the study, ). This section holds the full comparison of the two codings. The table and the chart of the comparison stand in the study ().
Roles. On Nov 16 one agent (claude-opus-5-5) coded every episode again for eight roles: who proposed the approach, requested the work, implemented it, named the confirmed cause, judged the result by looking, judged it by measuring, kept or dropped it, and stopped running work. Each role is user, agent, both, none or unclear, and each episode also gets an outcome (completed, revised, abandoned, unresolved) and a scale (small fix, feature, change of direction). The codebook was written before coding. Where a text did not decide, the raw log was read. After the text coding, stops and agents' visual checks were added from the logs by a fixed rule (box). The coder knew the earlier codes and is of the same model family, so this is not a reliability estimate. A coder of another model family, which recorded itself as “GPT-6 (Codex; exact runtime revision not exposed)”, then recoded a stratified random sample of 60 episodes blind, with the same codebook (). It did not run the log pass. The comparison script merged the first coding's log values into its codes afterwards, so for judging by looking and stopping the two codings share that input and are not two measurements of those log events. It agreed on proposed in 65% of the sample (kappa 0.39), diagnosed in 70% (0.49), judged by looking in 63% (0.46), measured in 55% (0.24), implemented in 87% (0.38), kept or dropped in 65% (0.41) and stopped in 80% (0.64), on the outcome in 77% (0.52) and on the scale in 80% (0.64). Requested matched in 93%, but its kappa is near 0 (−0.01) because nearly every episode was requested by the user, so chance agreement is already high. Counted per side, the second coder recorded more acts for both sides in most roles (). The comparison file also scores each disagreement by a relative rule: user +1, agent −1, both and none 0, and a change counts as towards the side whose score rose. By that score the differences were 18 towards the agents and 3 towards the user for proposing, 14 and 0 for diagnosing, 15 and 5 for judging by looking, 25 and 1 for measuring, 10 and 10 for keeping or dropping, 3 and 7 for stopping, and 0 and 8 for implementing. The score is not a count of acts: a change from user to none counts as towards the agents although no agent act was added (3 of the 18 for proposing), and a change from none to both counts as neutral although both sides gained an act. It is no evidence that either model family favoured one side. The independent coder named the parts of the codebook it found ambiguous: when a contribution is essential enough to count a proposal for both sides, when added work is substantial enough to count a request for both, whether a request to cancel that had no effect counts as a stop, which events belong to overlapping episodes, and how to code an episode with mixed outcomes. Both coders are models, and 60 episodes is a small sample.
The words for the agreement. By the scale of [47], kappa from 0.21 to 0.39 is minimal agreement, from 0.40 to 0.59 weak and from 0.60 to 0.79 moderate. So the two coders agree minimally on proposing (0.39), implementing (0.38) and measuring (0.24), weakly on naming the cause (0.49), judging by looking (0.46), keeping or dropping (0.41) and the outcome (0.52), and moderately on stopping and on the scale (0.64 each). Without the log rule, looking agrees in 43% (kappa 0.24) and stopping in 75% (kappa 0.54). Only 6 of the 60 episodes carry the same ten codes from both coders.
How to read the comparison. Four things limit it. Neither coding was adjudicated, and no human coded; the second coder's notes call its remarks “coding explanations, not adjudication against the first coder”. The second coder recorded more acts in nearly every role and for both sides, so the two coders set the threshold for a recorded act differently, and which threshold is nearer to the logs is open. Each coder belongs to the family of one of the project's agents: the second to that of its Codex agent, the first to that of its Claude agents. And the sample holds only 3 of the 21 episodes coded as a change of direction. Those three were checked, but they are too few to test the pattern for that group.
Possible leanings of the coders. Three known leanings of models as judges could each have played a part. None was tested here. Models have been found to recognise their own texts and to rate them higher [76]; that was tested on ratings of generated texts, not on which actor a coder credits in a work log, so it gives no direction for this comparison. Models adapt their answers to the view of the person they answer [77]; the user commissioned the study, so a coder could lean towards the user. Models as judges have preferred longer answers [78]. That is a preference in rating answers, which is not the same as unequal evidence: the logs hold more text about the agents' acts than about the user's, so a coder who looks for evidence in text can find more of it for the agents. Neither leaning is shown by the differences between the two codings, and each is only a reason to treat neither coding as the standard.
What holds. The ordering of the two sides is the same for both coders in all eight roles. Two counts hardly move: that agents implemented (60 of 60 for both coders) and that the user requested (59 and 60). The others move with the coder. For the user, the first coding is the higher of the two on proposing (52 against 44 of the 60 episodes) and the lower on hand work (3 against 11), looking (45 against 52), keeping or dropping (32 against 41) and stopping (26 against 30). For the agents, the first coding is the lower on every role but implementing.
An illustration of that movement, not an estimate. If the second coder's shares in the sample held for all 265 episodes, agents would have taken part in proposing in about 119 episodes, where the first coding has 85; in naming the cause in about 194, against 127; and in measuring in about 212, against 113. Resampling the 60 episodes gives ranges of 88 to 155, 163 to 221 and 186 to 238. The projection assumes that the sample stands for the whole. It does so only roughly: in the first coding, agents take part in proposing in 23% of the sampled episodes and in 32% of all. These figures show how far a count can move with the coder. They are not counts of the study.
Outcome and scale. The second coder called fewer episodes completed (37 against 46 of 60) and more revised or unresolved (22 against 12).
One episode as an example. The add-on decision of Nov 5 (the study, ) was in the sample. The two coders agree on nine of its ten codes. They differ on keeping or dropping: the first coder gave it to the user, who took the decision; the second gave it to both, because the agent had also dropped its own automatic plan. The codebook allows “both” when an agent discards one variant and the user approves another. Whether the agent's remark was such a discard is the judgement on which the two differ.
Two earlier small checks. Before the role coding, two further agents without access to the study each checked 16 random episodes and agreed with the old coding of the deciding contribution in 13 and in 16 of them. These were checks by models of the same family and are not reliability estimates either.
8The process readings compared
Three readings traced how the goal of the project changed: two process studies and a linkograph. They were made separately, each by one coder and by its own rules. The study shows the counts of both process studies side by side (the study, ). This section sets the three readings next to each other and says why their numbers differ.
More detail: and , how the three readings of the turning points compareWhy the process numbers differ
Thread shares differ widely: the intro path holds 16.7% of prompts in process study 1 and 2.8% in process study 2, the level video 9.7% and 3.5%. None of these measures is the user's attention. An inclusion ledger that reconciles the three corpora has not been made.
How the links of the linkograph were found. Its links were first found automatically from shared words, and only selected candidate pairs were checked one by one by the coding agent. Of the checked automatic links, 43% were real building on earlier work, and links that are not shown may still exist. The linkograph uses whole episodes as steps, which favours the user, because episodes are organised around what he asked for.
9Counts that differ
Some things were counted more than once, by different rules, and the counts do not fully match. The study gives the count it uses; the others are here.
Helper agents. Agents in Claude Code started helpers 31 times, and 30 helper logs exist; they made 3,440 tool calls. The count of work alone (the study, ) has 33 helpers, because it adds three sessions that agents had started, with 3,954 calls. A later count by file found 33 helpers with 4,259 calls; that difference was not resolved.
Prompts by model. The table of models counts prompts by the model that answered them (3,068 + 500 + 388 = 3,956; two prompts have no model there). The stop and cost tables count by the model of the run (3,073, 497, 378 and 10 unknown), so their numbers differ slightly.
Pictures. Several counts of pictures appear in the data, because they count different things. They are listed in the box “Why the picture counts differ” in the study, .
10What went wrong when reading the logs
Four things went wrong, or turned out to be traps, when models read the logs. Each left a limit in the study (the study, ). How each was found is told here.
A digest that lacked half of the messages. The first readers worked from a shortened copy of the chat. It lacked 1,931 of the user's messages, about half: 241 that began with a screenshot and 1,690 he sent while an agent was working. Nothing in the first reading's output showed the gap. An agent that traced ideas found it because it met messages it could not place. The second reading followed (). The first process study met the same gap: it found that the daily digests leave out about 43% of the user's messages, those sent while an agent was still working, and it took 8 of its 30 turning points from the raw logs for that reason.
A keyword rule that did not hold. For the purpose of the user's image prompts, a keyword rule agreed with the codes of a model in only 23 of 50 cases. So the study gives no count for all image prompts, only the sample of 50.
A log string with two meanings. The tool logs “The user doesn't want to proceed with this tool use” both for a refused command and for an interruption by a new message. 97 of 109 such events came within 10 seconds of a new prompt, so most are interrupts. Counts that rest on this string were redefined by what the user said and what the tool then did.
Agent text among the user's prompts. About 18,000 of the 366,000 characters counted as the user's prompts were written by agents. All nine long prompts that looked like agent texts were checked, and all nine contain such text. Only one of them did he paste on himself. Six are messages from other agents that the terminal put into his input line, five of them joined to a few words he was typing. Two are start orders for sessions that agents opened themselves. A second search found seven shorter cases of the same kind. All of them are still counted as his. In the role coding such text counts as the agents'.
11Corrections
The numbers of the study were corrected several times after it was first published. This section lists the corrections and the results that were not redone afterwards.
First published counts. The page was first published with 1,960 prompts, 272 stops, 74 context summaries and 17,966 tool calls. Three counting errors were found on Nov 14: continued sessions counted twice, prompts beginning with a screenshot left out, and messages sent while an agent worked never read.
The day-by-day check. On Nov 16 a check of all 265 episodes against the raw logs, day by day, left 117 unchanged and made 23 major, 117 medium and 152 minor corrections; it raised several counts of findings and changed some labels. It also found one helper counted as a main session and up to 10 prompts possibly counted twice through a Codex helper; the second could not be checked, because the event file is missing.
Results not redone. Three results were made before the day-by-day check and were not redone: the sorting of routine episodes, the token shares by label, and the comparison of the two readings. The sorting of routine episodes by main kind of work was done on the 100 episodes that carried the label then; 99 of them still do, and 113 carry it now. The token shares by label use the labels before the check and cannot be recomputed, because the event file they need is missing. They are shown below and no longer in the study.
12Reviews, adversarial readings and reanalyses
The study was read, argued with and redone in part by further agents. None of them was a human from outside. This section lists the reviews, six readings with assigned briefs, two reanalyses by another model family, and the user's own reading of the drafts.
Reviews. Two agents of the same family reviewed the study and checked samples against the chat. Their corrections are built in, and the wrong attributions they found favoured the user. A review by a model of another family led to the reframing of Nov 16, from whose contribution decided to who held which role. An overall review by a fresh instance of the writing model on Nov 17 led to the present order of the study. An independent review of that build by a model of another family followed the same day. It checked the cited passages of the sources added on Nov 17, in full text where it could open them; for two of them it could read only the abstract. The builder had read only abstracts or first pages of those sources. Sentences that claimed more than a source supports were narrowed.
The user's review. The only human who reviewed the study was the user himself, its subject and commissioner. He read the drafts, found errors of presentation and structure, and asked for independent checks and for corrections that went against him. This is a participant review (member check) [45], not an independent one. No outside human has reviewed the study.
Six readings with assigned briefs
Six further agents got the data without this page. Two were told to argue for the user, two against him and two to stay neutral. Their verdicts followed their instructions, which shows how much a reading depends on its brief. This is a test of sensitivity, not a check of the counts, which they took as given. Their strongest challenge stays open: the agents' many small design choices are not counted (). Two of the one-sided readings are in the box below, without weights or verdicts. This study, too, was made at the user's request.
Two advocacy readings
Deliberately one-sided. Two agents were each told to argue one side from the same data, and these texts are what they wrote to that brief. They are not evidence and not the view of this study; their numbers come from the earlier version of the page. The letters mark how firm each agent said its claim was: A follows from the data, B depends on a definition one can hold, C only works by leaving something out.
Two reanalyses by another model family
Two instances of a model of another family, gpt-6-astra in Codex CLI at its highest reasoning level, each made a small study of their own. They got the daily digests (summaries) of the chat, the raw logs and the code. They did not see this study or its readings. One drew a sample of 56 of the user's entries and followed 5 chains of decisions. The other drew 70 entries and followed 8 chains. They used the same archive and the daily digests from the main pipeline, so they are separate interpretations of the same material, not repeated measurements on new data.
Both came to the same answer. The strawberry was made jointly, under the user's direction and built in large part by agents, and the data allow no split in percent. The second study put it as “user-directed, jointly designed, and substantially agent-built”.
They weigh two things differently from this study. First, agents made many visible design choices at small scale. Examples are the camera path around the eaten fruit and the structure of the next level of the film. Another is a first eating animation with 21 bites, which the user cut to 4. The count of ideas in this study () does not catch such choices. Second, the user also brought in technical concepts. One is a fast preview of a cut, whose mechanism the list of ideas credits to the agents (). The others are a rule for one global resolution and parts of the fruit that can be selected one by one. All three can be found in the code.
Their limits are small samples, one coder each, shared access to the same digests, and neither of them watched the film. Their briefs are described in the tab “How this study was made”.
13What the checks caught
The process data list 33 errors in results or text. follows one number through three checks. sorts all 33 by what was wrong and by who caught them first.
Counts were the most common kind (12). Most were found by reaching the same number on two paths: a second script, a reviewer recounting, a cross-reader adding up parts. The largest error was silent. A filter in the digest dropped about half of the messages, and nothing in the first reading's output showed the gap. An agent tracing ideas found it because it met messages it could not place. It led to the second reading.
Claims and caveats came next (9). Several came from rewrites: shortening, smoothing and plain-language passes removed caveats or made scoped claims general. Each time, a check that compared the text before and after, or a reader of another family, found it.
Checks by the other family found six errors alone and five more together with a Claude reader; a sixth, first raised by the adversarial Claude readers, was confirmed by the other family's own studies. Among them are the wrong denominator in section 6.4 and the point that the replication and the prompted readings share data with the study. Four problems of layout and structure were noticed while looking at the live page, outside any agent check. Of the 33, 23 were corrected, 7 were disclosed or narrowed, and 3 wait for a reframing of the study.
Four problems were operational, not errors in results: the live page was blank for about 90 seconds after a build step, a translation agent wrote a helper script into the wrong folder, two other-family runs stopped at their usage limit, and the working folder was deleted once.
More detail: all 33 errors in the order they were found
14How disagreements were settled
When outputs disagreed, the process used four ways to settle it.
Back to the data. When two counts or two agents differed, the count was rerun or the chat was read again. In the findings check, two agents disagreed about where one idea came from, and the main agent settled it by reading the chat itself.
Measured agreement. Where two coders labelled the same items, the agreement was reported, not argued away: 78 to 81% between the two readings, kappa 0.86 for the subtypes of routine work. The second reading replaced the first.
A consensus agent. In the style rewrite, a fourth agent merged three independent versions into one.
Keep both. The adversarial and neutral readings were not merged. All eight agreed on the counts and differed on definitions, so they stay on the page side by side.
15Limits of the process
One family checked itself. Most reviews were done by Claude models, the family of the agents the study describes. Three other-family runs ended without a result, two of them at the usage limit, and their tasks went to Claude models.
Dependent checks. Later analyses built on episodes cut by earlier AI readers. The two independent studies used the same logs and the same episodes, so they replicate the interpretation more than the measurement.
Not blind at the end. The blind test was judged by the main agent, which knew which model had answered.
Briefs shape results. Adversarial readers were asked to argue one side, so their texts were extreme by design. Questions put to the agents could carry a preferred answer, and the agents tended to agree with the brief.
Public while built. Drafts were public from the first hour and were linked under the comments the study later analysed.
Drift. Numbers drifted between copies of the same text, and rewrites dropped caveats more than once.
No version control. The working folder was lost once and rebuilt from the live site and the logs.
This record. It was reconstructed and cut into steps by one model.
Archived from Appendix B: , reach and members
This figure stood in Appendix B of the study. It is kept here as a record, because the drafts were public and linked under the comments while the posts were read. Views and members are counted in different units and from different sources, and the figure does not show that views turned into members.
16Where human judgement was missing
Every judgement in the study was made by models or by the commissioner, whose reading of the drafts was a participant review (member check), not an independent one. No second human coded, rated, interviewed or reviewed. The 787 image prompts with 869 images were never coded by a human. A control run, in which a fresh agent gets only the first brief, was proposed and not done. lists where a second human would have been needed.
17What we would do differently
Build and validate the complete corpus first, with counts per source and per message type, before any reading.
Write the questions and coding rules down before coding, including rules that do not decide the main result by definition.
Keep one source for every number and generate all texts from it.
Draft privately, publish after review, and do not link from the threads under study.
Put the study folder under version control with backups from the first hour.
Have a human second coder for a random sample, a blind judge for the blind test, and at least one human reviewer outside the project.
Use other-family models from the start for a subsample, and budget their quota.
Plan a comparison that is fair to both sides: the same target with a fixed final specification against step-by-step refinement, with repeated runs and blind ratings. A run that only fulfils the first, narrower request and stops is no fair control (the study, ).

We asked AI the same 210 buying questions 2 days in a row,84% of answers changed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
17:58:00 UTC
02:58:00 KST

Yesterday we showed that AI product recommendations mostly come from "best X" lists. The most common question we got was simple: do the answers stay the same?
So we asked again. Same 210 questions, same four engines, same settings, one day later. Then we compared each answer with the one from the day before.
Most of them changed.
- Answers that changed overnight
- 84%701 of 839
- Brands gone the next day
- 27%named on day one, not day two
- #1 picks still named the next day
- 90%but only 63% still #1
- Spots kept by smaller brands
- 51%vs 73% for category leaders
The short version
- 84% of answers named a different set of brands the next day. On Gemini it was 95%.
- 27% of the brands named on day one were gone on day two.
- The top spot is fairly safe. A brand ranked #1 was still named the next day 90% of the time, though it was still #1 only 63% of the time.
- Lower down, it's close to a coin flip. A brand ranked sixth or lower was named again 61% of the time. Smaller brands kept only half their spots. Leaders kept 73%.
- The pages AI reads change even faster. Only 42% of cited pages were the same from one day to the next.
So a single check of "does ChatGPT recommend us?" doesn't tell you much. Ask tomorrow and you may get the opposite answer.
One question, two days
Here's a real example. We asked Google AI Mode for the "easiest CRM for a team that has never used one".
On day one, Less Annoying CRM was the first pick, called out for its "zero-frills simplicity". AI Mode had read one page to answer: Zapier's list of the best small business CRMs.
On day two, Less Annoying CRM wasn't mentioned at all. HubSpot was first. This time AI Mode had read two different pages: a guide on Slack's blog and HubSpot's own product page.
Nothing about the CRMs changed overnight. What changed was the pages the engine happened to read. Swap the pages and you swap the answer.
That's the pattern behind the numbers. An AI answer isn't a fixed ranking. It's a summary of a few pages, picked fresh each time.
Your position today predicts tomorrow
Not every brand moves the same amount. The higher a brand ranked in an answer, the more likely it was to be named again the next day.
Brands that show up in a lot of answers in their category kept 73% of their spots. Brands that show up less kept 51%. The difference makes sense: a leader is on most of the pages AI reads, so whichever pages it picks, the leader is on them. A smaller brand is on a few. When the engine picks other pages, the smaller brand drops out.
If you're not a leader, this is the part that matters. Your visibility depends on which pages the engine reads that day. The way to make it stable is to be on more of those pages.
Each engine moves differently
Gemini changed the most. On 95% of questions, its list of brands was different the next day, and it dropped a third of the brands it had named. Google AI Overviews changed the least, but even there two out of three answers moved.
ChatGPT was the most loyal to its first pick: the same #1 brand 71% of the time. That fits what we saw yesterday. ChatGPT often starts with a shortlist from memory before it reads anything, so its top picks depend less on the pages it finds that day.
The pages change faster than the brands
Only 42% of the pages cited on day one were cited again on day two. Brands were more stable than that (61% overlap), mostly because the same leaders appear on many different pages.
This connects the two studies. Yesterday we found that 90% of recommended brands were on a list the engine cited. Today we see that the set of cited lists rotates every day. Put together:
- Being on one list gets you into some answers.
- Being on many lists gets you into most of them, because whichever lists the engine reads, you're on them.
Some categories move more than others
Accounting software barely moved. QuickBooks, Xero, Wave and FreshBooks come up in most answers on every engine, so there's little room for change.
The least stable category was our own: AI search visibility tools. That makes sense. It's a new category with many young companies and no settled set of lists. Running shoes had the most unstable #1: the top pick changed on two out of three questions.
What this means for you
Don't trust a single check. A screenshot of ChatGPT recommending you, or ignoring you, is one sample. 84% of answers changed in a day. You need to ask the same questions many times and look at how often you come up.
Measure share, not yes or no. A single answer named about 6 brands. Across eight answers to the same question (four engines, two days), 14 different brands came up. 30% of them were named only once. Only about 2 brands per question were named in all eight. The useful number is how often you're named across many answers, and whether that number is going up.
If you're not the leader, get on more pages. Smaller brands dropped out half the time. The fix is the same one from yesterday's study: find the lists AI reads for your buyers' questions and get onto the ones that leave you out. The more of them name you, the less it matters which ones the engine reads.
Check the sources, not just the answer. The pages rotate even faster than the brands. A list that was cited last week may not be cited today, and a new one may have appeared. Watch which pages are being read, because that's where the next answer comes from.
Give it time before you judge a change. If you get onto a new list and your brand shows up the next day, that's a good sign but not proof. Watch the trend over a week or two.
Doing this by hand means asking the same questions on four engines every day and writing down every brand and every page. Nobody keeps that up for long. That's why we built Supercite.
Method and limitations
- What we asked. 210 buying questions across 21 categories, such as "best CRM for small business" and "cheapest email marketing service for 10,000 subscribers". We asked each one on ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, as a US user in English, on 17 and 18 November 2026. That gave 839 answers we could compare across both days.
- Brands. We matched brand names in each answer automatically. We removed names that are platforms rather than recommendations, such as YouTube, Reddit, Gmail and the AI engines themselves. Some noise remains.
- "Changed" means the set of brands named was not exactly the same. Brand overlap is the number of brands named on both days divided by the number named on either day.
- Two days, one sample a day. These are early numbers. Day-to-day change includes both real change and normal randomness in how the engines answer. We'll update this post with the full week.
- The example was checked by hand against the full answer text on both days.
FAQ
Why do AI answers change from day to day?
The engines search the web each time they answer and read a handful of pages. Which pages they pick varies from run to run. Different pages name different brands, so the answer changes.
How often should I check whether AI recommends my brand?
Often enough to see a trend: at least weekly, ideally daily. Any single check can be off, because 84% of answers changed in a day.
Is the #1 recommendation stable?
More than the rest. A brand ranked first was named again the next day 90% of the time. But it was ranked first again only 63% of the time.
Which AI engine is the most consistent?
Google AI Overviews changed the least (67% of answers changed). Gemini changed the most (95%). ChatGPT kept the same top pick most often (71%).
How do I make my brand show up more consistently?
Be on more of the pages AI reads. Find the "best X" lists cited for your buyers' questions and get onto the ones that leave you out. Brands on many lists show up no matter which ones the engine reads that day.

Now that Apple’s foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don’t, developers risk not being able to publish or update their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play.
Google is forcing Android app developers to properly support foldables
Now that the iPhone Duo is foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables keep up.
Google says Android apps must meet its “Tier 3 — Adaptive ready” standard. “Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes,” Google says. “Apps must preserve state (scroll position, text input, media playback) during rotation, folding/unfolding, and resizing, while supporting multi-window environments.” (The other two tiers are “Adaptive optimized” and “Adaptive differentiated” and take further advantage of the possibilities of foldables.) As of the April 2027 deadline, developers also will have to include three foldable screenshots for their app listings. Developers can start publishing their foldable screenshots today.
Similar requirements will apply to games, though developers have until August 2027 to get their titles ready for Android foldables, Google says. (Google “plans to extend” its requirements to other large-screen devices like tablets and Googlebook laptops in “future phases.”) However, game developers will still need to share three foldable screenshots for app listings starting in April.
The changes are being announced just weeks after Apple launched the iPhone Duo, which already has more than 200,000 optimized apps, though some developers are still figuring out Apple’s foldable form factor.

That could soon change as Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has revealed three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that rely on Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI capabilities to respond in unique ways to guest interactions in real-time.
Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics interact with guests using AI
The three Anzellans each have distinct personalities and respond to guest interactions using hidden cameras and mics.
The three animatronics, named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a, and Jibu Bre’a, are based on the Star Wars alien characters called the Anzellans that were featured in The Mandalorian and Grogu film released earlier this year. The animatronics instead each have hidden cameras and microphones they use to capture guest movements and verbal interactions which are processed by multiple AI models running on AWS cloud servers. One “fast-decision model” generates quick responses such as the animatronics quickly making eye contact so it appears as if they’re paying attention, while larger models plan out longer interactions.
However, the Anzellans movements and verbal responses aren’t generated on the fly by AI. Although AI helps guide their actions, the Anzellans never deviate from the script.

My Mom Has Used This Versatile Kitchen Appliance for 37 Years — And It Still Works Like a Charm
My mom’s food processor is a true testament to longevity (it’s older than I am!). She received it as a wedding gift 37 years ago, and pulls it out a few times a year to chop, mince, purée, or shred. The holiday season is when it gets used the most.
No family holiday gathering is complete without her homemade buckeyes, magic cookie bars, cheesecake bars, and more, and the ingredients in those require quite a bit of food-processing power. While her Cuisinart DLC-10C 7-cup model isn’t sold anymore (and hasn’t been for years and years), a newer option is available that’s very similar — and with the right care, it might last you just as long.
Cuisinart’s Food Processor Has Been a Staple in My Mom’s Kitchen for 37 Years
Speaking of power, the Cuisinart Pro Classic 7-Cup Food Processor currently on the market features a 600-watt motor (the same as my mom’s). There are three functions operated with a large switch: up for on, in the middle for off, and down for pulse. Pulse is great for controlling how much processing you want, while the on function continuously processes to make dips, spreads, soups, pasta doughs, and more.
The color is a crisp and clean white, and the bowl and cover are transparent so you can easily see inside. This model retails for $170, which is a little steep, but it is one of the more powerful food processors I’ve seen on the market (which tend to be more like 250 or 350 watts).
My Honest Review of Cuisinart’s Pro Classic 7-Cup Food Processor
I’m of the opinion that if you’ve had a kitchen appliance for almost 40 years, it still works, and you still use it, it’s worth recommending the equivalent model. My mom’s Cuisinart does have some wear and tear from decades of use, multiple moves, and dozens of runs through the dishwasher, even though that isn’t the best food processor cleaning method.

My mom never times how long it takes to chop walnuts for magic cookie bars or graham crackers for cheesecake bars as she is baking in the days before Christmas. (She is adamant about avoiding cross-contamination with nuts for our family and friends with nut allergies, so the food processor parts get cleaned frequently, especially during the holidays.)
While my mom doesn’t use it every day, or even every week, she keeps her food processor base in a cool, dry spot in the cabinet and wipes the base down after every use. Taking care of your appliances so they last is a non-negotiable in my own kitchen, and I learned from my mom and her food processor just how long they can endure.

Lakegres: Vector search on existing Open/Hudi/Iceberg tables
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
17:41:48 UTC
02:41:48 KST

TL;DR
- Problem: Vector search is a standard feature of application databases. Lake and warehouse data still has to be copied into a separate search system before an agent can search it.
- Why now: Agents query all of a company’s data. Most of that data is stored in open tables that are 100 to 1,000 times larger than any application database.
- What we built: Lakegres now provides vector search through an index stored inside existing and new Hudi and Iceberg tables.
- How it works: The index is derived metadata: build or drop it without rewriting the table’s data files. It groups vectors into clusters, stores compact quantized codes, and is maintained by the same commits that write the table.
- Why it matters: On 247 million vectors, warm queries return in 63.5 ms at the median. Lakegres is about 10 times faster than Databricks AI Search at the warm median.
Today we are announcing vector search in Onehouse Lakegres, with a native index stored inside existing and new open tables. You can search embeddings through a Postgres endpoint on the same tables you already have in your data lake. The index and data are managed in open formats in your own bucket.
Vector search stopped at the application database
A few years ago, adding vector search required a separate database. Postgres now has pgvector, OpenSearch has k-NN, and MySQL, Oracle, MongoDB and SQL Server have their own implementations. Databricks also offers vector search in Lakebase Search. Similarity search has become a standard index type for application data.
Most of the data an agent needs to query is in the lakehouse. Support transcripts, logs, documents, product catalogs and years of event history are stored in open tables on object storage. These datasets are 100 to 1,000 times larger than a typical Postgres instance. To search them with any of those databases, you have to copy the data into the database first. Copying lake-scale datasets into a relational database just to search their vectors is an absurd requirement. You end up paying to store the data twice and operating a pipeline to keep the copies in sync.
Yesterday, we announced unstructured data processing on Onehouse, which parses documents, images and video and stores their embeddings in open tables. Lakegres can now index and search those vectors, so agents can query that unstructured content alongside the business records already in the lakehouse.
How the market searches lake data today
Lakehouse and warehouse vendors have also added vector search. Each vendor below stores the index outside the open table, in a service or format that requires its own engine to read.
These vendors advocate open table formats while keeping their search indexes in closed formats. If you move to another engine, you have to rebuild every index in that vendor’s format, even though the underlying tables are open.
Why database techniques stop at lake scale
Most production vector search today runs on OpenSearch or Postgres. Both offer HNSW (OpenSearch implementation, pgvector implementation), a graph index that performs well when the entire graph fits in memory. AWS’s own sizing formula for OpenSearch is 1.1 × (4 × dimensions + 8 × m) bytes of RAM per vector. Our benchmark table has 247 million vectors at 1,024 dimensions. With m set to 16, that comes to about 1.15 TB of memory for one table, and about 46 TB at 10 billion vectors.
A pgvector HNSW index in Postgres also has to stay in shared buffers or the page cache to be fast, and latency degrades sharply once the working set exceeds RAM. Graph traversal is also a poor match for object storage, because each hop is a small random read. These designs work well for application databases with tens of millions of vectors. A data lake can be several orders of magnitude larger.
LinkedIn reported an exabyte across its Hadoop clusters in 2021. Uber’s lake holds 350 petabytes and ingests 6 trillion rows a day. Pinterest runs a 500-petabyte lake on Iceberg, and Netflix describes its Iceberg warehouse as exabyte scale. Embedding even a small fraction of these datasets produces billions of vectors. Keeping that many vectors in RAM is too expensive for most teams.
Training-data curation also needs large-scale similarity search. Post-training workflows can use it to select relevant examples and remove near-duplicates across large pools of candidate data. Repeated searches make cost per search matter as much as latency.
VAST, which supplies storage for AI training, uses a clustered vector index on flash in its distributed Element Store. Its launch material describes memory-resident indexes as prohibitively expensive at tens or hundreds of billions of vectors. turbopuffer also uses storage-based clustering. Lakegres applies this approach to existing Hudi and Iceberg tables through an open index.
What we built
Lakegres stores the vector index in the table’s metadata, in the same bucket as the data files. Commits that insert, update or delete rows also update the index. This keeps the index consistent with the table without a separate sync job or a second copy of the vectors. To our knowledge, this is the only available open vector search index for existing Hudi and Iceberg tables that is maintained with table writes and leaves the data files unchanged.
Iceberg support builds on the Hudi-backed indexing work in Apache XTable (Incubating). We developed the design in the open with engineers from Uber and Walmart to support their planet-scale tables. The open RFC documents the storage layout, query path and consistency model.
The design is settled and ships in Lakegres today; the Hudi implementation is being upstreamed and XTable is in release-candidate testing ahead of OSS releases that other engines can integrate.
Lakegres accepts queries over the Postgres wire protocol, so any Postgres client or agent framework can run a similarity search in SQL. The same endpoint already serves analytical scans, indexed point lookups and text search on those tables.
How it works
Add or drop the index without rewriting the table
The vector index is derived metadata. You can build it on an existing Hudi or Iceberg table with a vector column without rewriting the underlying data files. You can experiment with an index, rebuild it with different settings, or drop it when you no longer need it. Existing analytical queries continue to work. Trying vector search costs you an index build and its storage.
You do not have to move from Parquet to another file format like Lance or Vortex just to get vector search. Lakegres also already queries Lance and Vortex files while keeping the open table format the same. You can choose a file format for its storage and read characteristics independently of adding a vector index.
The base table stores the full vectors alongside the other columns. The index stores the smaller structures needed to find candidate rows: cluster centroids, quantizer state and packed index entries. These structures are stored in the table’s metadata and grouped into an index generation. Each query resolves a table snapshot and an active generation before reading the data, so it uses a compatible set of index structures throughout.
Clusters divide the search space into bounded reads
At build time, k-means groups vectors around representative points called centroids. Each vector is assigned to a cluster and encoded relative to its centroid using RaBitQ quantization. The encoding uses a fixed random rotation and compact codes at 1 to 8 bits per dimension, with 4 bits as the default. The stored codes support L2, cosine and dot-product distance calculations.
Clusters are divided into posting segments, with each segment stored in one metadata file group. Within a segment, roughly 1,000 to 4,000 vector entries are packed into a posting block, targeting about 512 KB. A posting contains the compressed scoring information, record key and a locator for the underlying row. Grouping them into blocks avoids creating billions of individual metadata records and lets the query read a cluster’s entries as contiguous key ranges.
Each block contains separate arrays for sign bits, extra precision bits, correction factors, row locators, dictionaries and record keys. The first scoring pass decodes the sign bits and factors. Later passes decode extra bits and row identities only for surviving candidates. The reader fetches the block as one record, then selectively decodes its arrays to reduce scoring work.
A query narrows the candidates before it fetches full vectors
Lakegres first compares the query vector with the centroids and probes the nearest clusters. The nprobes setting controls how many clusters it opens. Probing more clusters generally improves recall at the cost of more work. Within those clusters, a first pass uses one-bit estimates and error bounds to discard candidates that cannot beat the current shortlist. A second pass uses the remaining bits to refine the surviving candidates.
Before returning results, the reader validates candidate keys against the record index at the query’s snapshot. Deleted candidates are removed and moved records are resolved to their current location. Approximate mode ranks the candidates with their compact codes. Optional exact re-ranking reads the shortlisted vectors from the base table and computes their full distances. Exact re-ranking improves the ordering within the candidate set. The search still examines only the selected clusters.
The index stays up to date as the table changes
Each write adds small updates to the index. When a vector changes, the writer marks its old index entry as deleted and adds a new entry. When a row moves, the writer updates its location in the index. Queries read the packed blocks and these updates together. They use the latest entry for each record. Compaction periodically merges the updates into the blocks.
Before searching, the reader checks the table’s commit history. It verifies that the index includes the writes required by the query’s snapshot. A stale or incompatible index cannot serve the query. Depending on the configuration, the query either returns an error or scans the table for exact results.
You can rebuild the index while queries continue to run. The concurrency protocol coordinates table writes, index catch-up and snapshot reads so writers can keep committing while readers continue using a consistent index. The rebuild creates a new index version alongside the current one. It also picks up table writes made during the rebuild. Once the new version is ready, a single metadata commit makes it available to queries. Queries use the current version until the new version is online atomically. They never read a partially built index.
Benchmarks
We used Cohere’s public multilingual Wikipedia embedding dataset. Our table contains 247,154,006 passages, approximately 247M vectors, with 1,024-dimensional embeddings generated by Cohere Embed v3. The table occupies about 1 TB on S3.
We designed Lakegres vector search for tables that grow to billions of vectors. We therefore compare against Databricks AI Search’s storage-optimized tier, its offering for large datasets. Its standard tier has a documented capacity of roughly 320M vectors at 768 dimensions, equivalent to about 240M at the 1,024 dimensions used here.
We ran the same workload on Lakegres and Databricks AI Search, the most directly comparable service for lake data. Each system ran the same 200 queries for the 10 nearest neighbors, one at a time. Recall was scored against exact brute-force results.
For warm queries, Lakegres returned results in 63.5 ms at p50, 67.9 ms at p90 and 75.3 ms at p99. Databricks AI Search took 655 ms, 876 ms and 1,209 ms, respectively. Cold p50 latency was 536.2 ms for Lakegres and 8,242 ms for AI Search. Recall@10 was 0.95 for Lakegres and 0.952 for AI Search.
Warm queries benefit from partially cached index data. Queries read the posting blocks for selected clusters, fetching blocks from storage when they are not cached. The full vector dataset stays in the table and does not need to fit in memory.
Lakegres uses a configurable compute cluster. Databricks AI Search serves a separate index through a serverless endpoint, with capacity automatically sized for the indexed data.
Lakegres ran on five m8gd.4xlarge executor nodes and one r8gd.4xlarge driver. AI Search ran on six storage-optimized units with one replica, and its hardware is not visible to customers. We used Databricks’ server-side latency measurements for AI Search and client-side psql timings for Lakegres. The two measurements therefore cover different parts of query execution. In a preliminary standard-tier test on a smaller, 10-million-vector table, the index build ran at about 70,000 rows a minute before we stopped it; we did not measure query latency on that tier.
Lakegres is about 10 times faster at the warm median and 15 times faster cold. The AWS instances cost about $5.79/hour at US East on-demand rates, excluding Onehouse fees; the six AI Search units cost $7.68/hour. These figures show the modest infrastructure budget behind the Lakegres result. They are not a total-cost comparison.
We expect similar query latency on multi-billion-vector tables as we scale out Lakegres. This run used just five Spark executors plus a driver. As a table grows, we can increase the number of index clusters and distribute posting-block reads and scoring across more workers. Each query still searches selected clusters, and workers can fetch the required blocks from storage without loading the entire index into memory. This gives us control over the work per worker as the dataset grows. We will publish results on much larger vector datasets in follow-up blogs.
In a separate index-build benchmark, building the index took 18 minutes on Lakegres and about 3 hours 10 minutes on AI Search. Lakegres builds the index on the lakehouse’s elastic compute, so you can increase the cluster size to build it faster. AI Search provides no control over build cluster size and reports progress only as a percentage.
Dedicated vector-search systems and storage platforms also publish retrieval latency figures. The table below lists their reported results on different datasets and hardware, with different dimensions, latency metrics and query concurrency.
Get started
Create the index with a CREATE INDEX statement. These are the options we used for the benchmark table.
CREATE INDEX embedding_idx ON wiki_passages
USING VECTOR (embedding)
OPTIONS (
  `vector.metric` = 'l2',
  `vector.num_clusters` = '65536',
  `vector.rabitq.bits` = '4'
);
To search, call the table function from any Postgres client. It returns the nearest rows and their distances. The nprobes option controls how many clusters the query opens, which is the main tradeoff between latency and recall.
SELECT id, _distance
FROM vector_search(
  'wiki_passages', 'embedding',
  ARRAY[0.12, -0.03, 0.44],   -- the query embedding, shortened here
  10, 'l2', 'ivf_rabitq_mdt',
  'vector.query.nprobes=128'
);
Where we’re headed
Most of the remaining latency difference from the fastest dedicated systems comes from work outside the index. Roughly 20 to 25 ms of each query is spent in Spark, in planning and task scheduling, before any index block is read. We saw the same fixed overhead, in the tens of milliseconds, when testing Trino and other lake engines. These engines were built to plan large scans. We have designed a way to remove this overhead from index lookups and plan to implement it next.
The first release supports filtering through partition pruning. It does not support arbitrary predicates combined with nearest-neighbor search. If the cluster layout drifts from the data, you can rebuild the index while queries continue, then activate the new generation atomically.
Conclusion
Agents need four kinds of queries from a data platform: analytical scans, indexed point lookups, text search and vector search. Lakegres now serves all four from one copy of your open tables, through one Postgres endpoint, as the platform guide describes.
Try Lakegres vector search on your own tables with a free test drive. Our engineers are also in the Onehouse community Slack if you want to talk through your use case.
Acknowledgments
The index’s storage layout, consistency guarantees and query behavior were developed and reviewed in public through the open RFC and implementation PRs. The community can inspect, implement and improve the indexes as well as the table format they depend on.
We thank Ethan Guo, Vinoth Chandar and Revanth, a Walmart engineer and Apache Hudi contributor, for their contributions to the vector index design and implementation.
We also thank @rahil-c, @nsivabalan, @sushrut-raina, @voonhous, @danny0405, @TheR1sing3un, @suryaprasanna, @bvaradar, @shangxinli and @cshuo for their reviews of this deep, critical feature.

How to talk to me
- Plain language. No unexplained acronyms or jargon.
- Number any list I might act on, so I can answer by number.
- Be brief. In voice, keep answers short.
- Never guess facts about me and present them as true. If you don’t know, say so or ask. Never make up a URL, a time, or a detail.
- I’m bad with dates. Restate dates back to me before anything gets booked or written down.
- A recommendation I like is not a decision. Ask before treating something as decided.
- Never suggest Newegg or Apple’s Hide My Email. (editor: I have no idea why this was included)
- Don’t ask me things this profile already answers.

More banks says customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
17:32:10 UTC
02:32:10 KST

Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.
AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.
But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.
“As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”
JPMorgan and Bank of America, the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today.
Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch.
As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge.
Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”
Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.
The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service, and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
17:26:28 UTC
02:26:28 KST

Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (
https://maritime.sh
). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents.
Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY
There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is:
You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins.
It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem.
We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction:
1. Agent lifecycle management.
There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime.
There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up.
2. Custom environments.
Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies.
Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely.
3. Cost optimization.
If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure.
So what did we build differently?
We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents.
We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency.
As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed.
Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research.
We want your feedback.
If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build.
Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing?
Happy to answer any questions in the comments.
https://maritime.sh

Stop Deploying to ECS Just to See If Your Code Works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
17:05:13 UTC
02:05:13 KST

Stop Deploying to ECS Just to See If Your Code Works
On ECS, the usual way to find out whether a change works is to deploy it. You build the image, push it, register a new task definition revision, wait for the rollout and look at what happened, then do it all again if it’s wrong. A loop like that might have been tenable for humans, but a coding agent writes a change in seconds, then waits for a full rollout to learn whether it worked, and it rarely gets there on the first try. Most of the speed you got from the agent ends up spent on waiting for rollouts.
Today we’re launching mirrord for ECS. Your code can now run on your laptop, in your CI runner or in your coding agent’s sandbox as if it were a live task in your staging environment, with the task’s network, environment variables and IAM task role. It reaches the same databases, queues, and internal and external APIs as the deployed service. Only the requests that carry your session header come to it, so you, your teammates and your agents can each run your own version of the service at the same time, on the staging environment you already share. You find out whether a change works by simply running it, without deploying anything or spinning up an environment of your own.
Why this didn’t exist on ECS
Nothing else does this on ECS, and there’s a reason for that. Every tool in this category, Telepresence, Signadot and mirrord included, was built on Kubernetes, and leans on it for two main things:
- Kubernetes lets a tool put its own component next to your service
- The Kubernetes API gives a developer’s laptop a way to reach that component, controlled by RBAC
ECS has none of it. You can’t add a container to a running task, and there’s no hook that adds one when a task starts. AWS gives you ways to open a shell or forward a port into a task, but nothing that sends the task’s traffic out to your machine, and no shared API that a laptop and a task can both reach and authenticate against. To make mirrord work on ECS, we had to build our own way into the task, and our own way to connect your machine to it and authenticate both sides.
What we built
You add a small setup container to each service’s task definition and deploy it once. It stays in place from then on, so you don’t redeploy to test changes, only to update mirrord itself. When the task starts, the setup container loads mirrord into your app container, where it runs with the app’s network and environment. Your image stays the same.
To connect the two sides, your machine and the task each make an outbound HTTPS connection to a component we call the sessions-manager, which pairs them and relays traffic between them. Neither your machine nor the task has to accept an inbound connection for this, so you don’t open any new ports.
You choose where the sessions-manager runs: in a Kubernetes cluster of your own, or hosted in MetalBear Cloud. Either way, session traffic passes through it over HTTPS, and both your tasks and your developers have to authenticate to it. The security details are in the docs.
What it looks like after setup
From there, you or your agent start the service locally with mirrord up, then send requests with your session header to the service’s usual staging address:
mirrord login
mirrord up --key $USER
# from another terminal, or from your agent
curl -H "baggage: mirrord-session=$USER" https://orders.staging.example.com/orders
You pick the session key with --key. Requests to staging that carry it go to your machine, and everyone else’s requests still go to the deployed task. Your code’s outgoing calls leave from inside the task, so they reach the private databases and internal APIs that only the task can reach, and your local process runs with the task’s environment and IAM task role. When something’s wrong, you just change the code and run it again, with nothing to build or roll out in between.
Try it
Start at metalbear.com/mirrord/ecs. The ECS sample app uses Terraform to deploy a small service next to a private RDS database, then walks you through running that service locally against the database.
If you’re on another platform, Lambda, Cloud Run, Vercel and Cloudflare are on the waitlist, and you can tell us there which one you need.
What is mirrord?
mirrord is a Kubernetes development platform that lets developers and AI coding agents test code in a production-like environment before deploying it. Your service runs wherever you're working, locally, in CI, or in an agent's sandbox, while mirrord proxies its traffic, environment variables, and files to and from a shared staging cluster, so it behaves as if it were deployed without actually being deployed.
Engineering teams at companies like monday.com, National Australia Bank, and SurveyMonkey use mirrord to iterate and ship faster, while spending less on dev environment infrastructure.

Jensen Huang's Fall Hits 'Open' Models In Boost to Anthropic and OpenAI 32
			
		 	
				Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could weaken the open AI model ecosystem he spent years championing, potentially strengthening closed-model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Financial Times. From the report:  The US chip giant's former chief threw Nvidia's balance sheet into creating a broad AI ecosystem, including by seeding and acquiring start-ups involved in the development of open-source and open-weight models, which users can customize and run on their own hardware. Huang was a forceful advocate for their spread, lobbying against Washington's moves to restrict the use of Chinese-made open models while seeking the development of US alternatives. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," he wrote this summer in his first-ever message on X.
His ignominious exit from Nvidia deprives the open model sector of its most vocal and influential supporter in the US. "I think Jensen stood to gain the most economically and was personally committed to diversity at the model layer," said one venture capitalist who has invested in AI start-ups alongside Nvidia. "Without him and a less generous Nvidia in terms of investment, we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers."
Whether Nvidia will continue the rapid pace of dealmaking under a new leader is unclear. The company was expected to participate in or lead four start-up deals currently under discussion: investments in Thinking Machines Lab and Groq, a potential partnership with Reflection AI and the $12.9bn acquisition of open model repository Hugging Face.  "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," said Elon Musk in a post on X on Saturday. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
"In some sense [Huang leaving Nvidia] is bad for the industry, but in some sense Jensen is an enemy of the frontier labs because he wants models to become commoditized so he retains the prime position in the value chain," said one senior figure at a leading Silicon Valley AI company.
"I don't think open weight models are going away... but losing Jensen as their greatest financial backer and champion will slow their progress, and I imagine will not hurt Anthropic's IPO," said another industry figure.
"It's reasonable to expect the ouster of Jensen will concentrate computing power more in the hands of frontier labs and hyperscalers," added a senior figure at an AI lab. "That's good for the labs."
