Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:59:00 UTC
01:59:00 KST

OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.
“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman.
The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.
Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.
“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said.
Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done.
“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new … technology,” he said.
Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.
“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.
OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face. In Wednesday’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.
But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.
“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now … in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said.

Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:53:42 UTC
01:53:42 KST

Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.
Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.
Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.
At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.
There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.
Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).
When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.
We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.
You can get started with `npm create factory`.
It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!
https://factory.mastra.ai
https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory

The Only Water Filters Worth Buying (and Why), According to Experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:45:00 UTC
01:45:00 KST

The Only Water Filters Worth Buying (and Why), According to Experts
Our home came with a water filtration system that was built right into the kitchen sink. It was nice not having to worry about the tap water every time we opened the faucet or to constantly fill a Brita pitcher. But not everyone has the luxury of a built-in water filtration system — and, to be honest, my husband and I weren’t even entirely sure why we needed one in the first place. I mean, does it even really work? And what is it actually doing, anyway?
It turns out, there are tons of different types of water filters, and the one your home needs depends on where you live and your local contaminants. I spoke to experts about the different types of filters, how they work, when and why you might need one, and most importantly, the very best water filters you can buy on any budget, from pitchers to faucet attachments to under-sink systems. Here’s what they had to say.
Do I Need a Water Filter?
Yes, according to the CDC, you need a good water filter no matter where you live or how your water is supplied. Water filters offer several health benefits. By removing impurities, they provide cleaner and safer drinking water, reducing the risk of consuming harmful substances. Filtered water also has improved taste and odor, making it more appealing and encourages people to drink more of it (a need!). 
Additionally, lots of filters are designed to retain essential minerals, like calcium and magnesium, which are beneficial for overall health. But first, you need to know which contaminants are likely in your tap water.
What Type of Water Filter Do I Need?
You can search by your zip code in the Environmental Working Group’s Tap Water Database to find out which of the EPA’s biggest contaminants may be in your water, and for recommendations on which type of filter is best.
According to Logan Cox, assistant general manager of John The Plumber Niagara Falls, an essential aspect to look for in a water filter is its ability to target specific contaminants that may be found in your water. “Different filters employ various technologies, such as activated carbon, reverse osmosis, or distillation, to remove contaminants like chlorine, lead, bacteria, pesticides, and other harmful substances.”
Cox also recommends checking if the filter you choose is certified by independent organizations like NSF International, which can speak to its effectiveness in removing specific contaminants.
6 Types of Water Filters You Should Know
Once you’ve figured out what contaminants are likely in your tap water, there are still lots of considerations when it comes to different types of water filters. Here’s a breakdown of the type of filters Cox says to look for.
- Activated Carbon Filters: These water filters use activated carbon, which has a large surface area with tiny pores to trap and absorb contaminants. Activated carbon filters are effective in removing chlorine, volatile organic compounds, some pesticides, and chemicals that affect taste and odor.
- Reverse Osmosis (RO) Filters: RO water filters use a semi-permeable membrane to remove a wide range of contaminants, including dissolved solids, heavy metals like lead and mercury, fluoride, nitrates, and certain chemicals. The membrane allows water molecules to pass through while blocking larger particles and impurities.
- Ceramic Filters: Ceramic water filters typically consist of small pores that physically trap contaminants like bacteria, protozoa, sediment, and larger particles. They can effectively remove harmful microorganisms and improve water clarity.
- UV Filters: Ultraviolet (UV) water filters use UV light to disinfect water by inactivating bacteria, viruses, and other microorganisms. They are particularly effective in destroying pathogens and ensuring microbiologically safe water.
- Ion Exchange Filters: Ion exchange water filters use resin beads that exchange ions to remove specific contaminants like heavy metals (like lead and copper), calcium, and magnesium. They work by replacing unwanted ions with more desirable ones, typically sodium or potassium.
- Distillation Filters: Distillation water filters involve heating water to create steam, which is then condensed to produce purified water. This process effectively removes impurities, including minerals, heavy metals, bacteria, and some chemicals.

Software Factory builds 30 complex open source libraries in a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:26:42 UTC
01:26:42 KST

My software factory builds the kind of software I’d expect a specialist team to spend a long time on, and it keeps that software maintained after it ships. So far that’s a SQLite-compatible database engine, a game engine on deterministic physics, a GPU stack with its own shader compiler, and readers and writers for Word, Excel and PowerPoint files. I run it by myself.
There are 30 libraries in all. 28 reached 1.0 between early October and mid-November, and together they’re nearly 1.9 million lines of handwritten library code. They’ve had 241 releases so far, and 183 of those were on libraries already past 1.0. They’re C# on NuGet, and oneyaml also ships in Rust and Go.
What it built
Documents and the web
OnePdf Complexity Innovation
Read, repair, edit, sign and fill PDFs, and write PDF/A and accessible PDF/UA.
OneDocument Complexity Innovation
Read, edit, recalculate and write Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, and render them to PDF.
OneHtml Complexity Innovation
Parse and edit HTML like a browser, and check pages for accessibility without one.
OneRender Complexity Innovation
Lay out and render HTML and CSS to pixels or tagged PDF, without a browser.
OneFont Complexity Innovation
Load fonts and shape text in any script, with bidi and line breaking.
OneImage Complexity Innovation
Decode, edit, convert and resize images, from PNG and JPEG to layered PSD.
Data and formats
OneLite Complexity Innovation
Embed a SQLite-compatible database that reads and writes the same files as sqlite3.
OneIndex (preview) Complexity Innovation
Run full-text, vector and hybrid search in-process, or in the browser.
OneArchive Complexity Innovation
Compress and unpack zip, 7z, tar and other archives, with the same bytes everywhere.
OneMail Complexity Innovation
Read, write and convert mail stores, Outlook PST included, and send and fetch mail.
OneCrypto (preview) Complexity Innovation
Load keys and certificates, validate certificate paths, and sign and encrypt with OpenPGP.
oneyaml Complexity Innovation
Load, dump and edit YAML in place in Rust, Go and C#, keeping comments.
OneContact Complexity Innovation
Parse and normalize phone numbers, emails, URLs, addresses and names, and find them in pages.
OneDiff Complexity Innovation
Diff and merge text like git, and redline changes between PDFs, digital or scanned.
AI and ML
OneModel Complexity Innovation
Run and train ONNX models in pure C#, on CPU, GPU or in the browser.
OneNlp Complexity Innovation
Tokenize, tag, parse and extract entities from text, and train the models in C#.
OneSpeech Complexity Innovation
Transcribe, time and diarize speech with Whisper and other open models, in .NET.
OneOcr Complexity Innovation
Read text, tables and invoice fields from scans and PDFs.
OneLlm Complexity Innovation
Call Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini models through one API, and run agents as files.
OneModelContext Complexity Innovation
Serve tools to AI agents over MCP, or connect to MCP servers, with OAuth.
Languages, GPU and media
OneEcma Complexity Innovation
Run JavaScript inside .NET under limits, with error reports that explain the failure.
OneShader Complexity Innovation
Compile HLSL to Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU shaders as part of dotnet build.
OneGpu Complexity Innovation
Run compute and ML kernels on Vulkan, Metal or WebGPU from pure C#.
OneAudio Complexity Innovation
Decode, encode, mix and resample audio, measure loudness, and play it on devices.
OneMedia Complexity Innovation
Remux, trim, tag, repair and package video and audio files without re-encoding.
Games and simulation
OneGame Complexity Innovation
Let AI agents build, run, test, inspect and change games through commands, with no editor.
OneMath Complexity Innovation
Compute sin, exp, pow and more correctly rounded, the same bits on every machine.
OnePath Complexity Innovation
Find paths on grids, graphs and navmeshes, build the navmeshes, and steer crowds.
OnePhysics Complexity Innovation
Simulate 2D and 3D rigid bodies, cloth, soft bodies, fluids and vehicles, bit-identical everywhere.
OneScope Complexity Innovation
Scrub, fork and compare runs of a deterministic simulation, recorded or live.
OnePdf implements ISO 32000 for reading, three-step repair of damaged files, the security handler’s revisions 2 through 6, signing, and writing PDF/A, PDF/UA-1 and PDF/UA-2. An outside validator decides whether the output is right: of veraPDF’s own 2,906-file corpus, 2,694 converted to PDF/A-2b and every one of those passed veraPDF. A sweep over GovDocs1, a 5,000-file SafeDocs sample and the veraPDF corpus opened each file and interpreted every page with 0 crashes and 0 hangs. It’s about 120,000 lines of C#.
OnePdf is a from-scratch implementation of ISO 32000 and its PDF/A and PDF/UA profiles. The value is having reading, repair, editing, signing and compliant writing exact in one managed library.
OneDocument covers OOXML, the old binary DOC, XLS and PPT, RTF and ODF, and the Word 6/95 and early Excel layouts come from observed files because there’s no spec for them. A save has to keep every part of the package exactly, including parts the library never touches: over a public corpus of 4,900 files, 111,239 of 111,239 parts came back byte-identical. Real Office judges what it writes, and 718 generated files open in Word, Excel and PowerPoint with no repair prompt. It’s about 285,000 lines of handwritten C#, and it renders through OneRender and the libraries under it.
The formats are existing standards. What it adds is a document model that’s a view over the file’s own markup, so untouched parts go back out as the original zip entries and edits keep unknown elements and extensions in order. The same library renders documents, workbooks and decks to tagged, accessible PDF.
OneHtml implements the WHATWG parser with every insertion mode, Selectors Level 4, the CSS cascade, and the ARIA, AccName and HTML-AAM specs that define the accessibility tree. It’s checked against Chrome itself: across 2,095 pages it matched 1,779,203 of Chrome’s 1,840,086 accessibility nodes. A no-edit round trip is byte-identical on all 18,330 corpus pages and stylesheets. It’s about 85,000 lines of C# on the .NET base library alone.
Edits go through a byte-level source map, so an edit changes only the bytes it touches and old snapshots of the DOM stay valid. It computes the accessibility tree Chromium exposes and runs accessibility checks with no browser, with Chromium’s choices written down as a profile.
OneRender implements CSS from the specs: computed values, the box tree, layout, fragmentation and paged media, painting, DOM events, transitions and animations. Its geometry is checked against Chrome on the same fonts, and its six templates match 3,051 of 3,052 elements at both 1280×800 and 390×844. It’s built on four other factory libraries, OneHtml, OneFont, OneImage and OnePdf, and it’s about 89,000 lines of C#.
It’s a browser-class layout engine packaged as a library, with no JavaScript, networking or clock of its own; the host passes the time. One engine serves both a 200-page report and a game UI that updates every frame, and incremental relayout gives the same result as a full rebuild. Output goes to pixels, a versioned display list a game engine can draw, or tagged PDF/UA.
OneFont implements TrueType, CFF, every GSUB and GPOS lookup type, and the script shapers for Arabic, Indic, the Universal Shaping Engine and Thai/Lao. Indic alone means syllable cutting, reph movement and pre-base matras in Microsoft’s documented feature order. The Unicode 17 conformance files for line, grapheme, word and sentence breaking and bidi pass in full, read unmodified. It’s about 11,500 lines of C# with no dependencies.
OneFont is a from-scratch implementation of OpenType layout and the Unicode text algorithms. The value is having shaping, bidi and segmentation exact in one dependency-free library.
OneImage has its own codecs for PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, TIFF, BMP and ICO, plus ICC v2/v4 color, JPEG 2000 and JBIG2 for PDF images, PSD/PSB layers, metafiles and SVG. On 2,327 JBIG2 streams from government PDFs, 1,925 decode bit-identical to poppler’s pdfimages and the other 402 are its exact inverse, because pdfimages applies the PDF’s decode polarity and OneImage leaves that to the caller. Lossless JPEG 2000 is bit-exact on the T.803 conformance set. It’s about 145,000 lines of C#.
These are existing codecs and formats, written from scratch. The value is having them exact in one managed library, with pixels computed lazily, tile by tile, only when you save.
OneLite reimplements SQLite 3.53.4’s file format, rollback journal, WAL, SQL semantics, result codes and error messages, plus FTS3/4/5, R*Tree and SQLCipher 4 pages. Compatible means it can share a live database with sqlite3: 10,000 interleaved WAL commits stay consistent from both sides. It was written from SQLite’s public docs with sqlite3 as a black box, and differential testing against sqlite3 found 0 unexplained differences in about 12,000 cases. It’s about 115,000 lines of C#.
OneLite is a from-scratch reimplementation of SQLite, and compatibility is the point. The value is a SQLite engine in pure managed code, NativeAOT and the browser included, that reads and writes standard SQLite files.
OneIndex implements known search algorithms: BM25F with block-max WAND, HNSW, rank fusion, UAX #29 segmentation and Snowball stemmers for 34 languages. The stemmers reproduce the published Snowball vocabularies exactly, 11,481,578 of 11,481,578 words. Durability testing ran about 890,000 fault-injection schedules and more than 7,000 process kills with no lost commit. It’s about 70,000 lines of C#.
The algorithms are known ones, implemented from scratch. The value is text, vector and hybrid search exact in one in-process library, which can also serve the same index to a browser as static files.
OneArchive has its own codecs for Zstandard, LZ4, Deflate, Brotli, LZMA and xz, bzip2 and PPMd, and its own readers and writers for zip, tar, 7z, ISO 9660, cab and more. Its compressed output is part of the contract: each codec and level writes the same bytes on every OS, CPU, runtime and thread count, in every 1.x release. PPMd output is byte-identical to what 7-Zip writes. It’s about 95,000 lines of C#.
These are existing codecs and containers, written from scratch. The value is having them in one managed library whose 1.x contract is that each codec and level writes the same bytes on every platform, so the output can serve as a content address.
OneMail implements MIME and Outlook’s formats from Microsoft’s Open Specifications, MSG and PST among them, plus mbox, Maildir, calendars, contacts and SMTP, IMAP and POP3. Untouched MIME writes back byte-identical, 523,424 of 523,424 messages including the Enron maildir. PSTs it writes, including edits made in place to an existing store, open in Outlook. It’s about 112,000 lines of C#.
The formats and protocols are existing ones. What’s uncommon is writing Unicode PST from managed code, as a new file or in place in an existing store, with in-place writes committed by MS-PST’s two-root protocol and the results opened in Outlook. Its forensic recovery got back more items than Outlook’s own repair tool in all 12 damaged stores compared.
OneCrypto implements ASN.1, X.509 and path validation, CMS, PKCS#8 and #12, OpenSSH keys, OpenPGP RFC 9580 with post-quantum algorithms, and the modern curves, all on the .NET base library. OpenPGP messages written by GnuPG, Sequoia, RNP, OpenPGP.js and gosop parse and write back byte for byte, and two-way interop runs against each of them with 0 failures. Path validation passes all 9,572 BetterTLS cases. It’s about 82,000 lines of C#.
OneCrypto is a clean-room implementation of published crypto standards. The value is having them in one managed library that also runs in the browser, with every secret-handling primitive under a timing test.
oneyaml implements one spec, YAML 1.2.2, three times: natively in Rust, Go and C#, at about 87,000, 34,000 and 46,000 lines. The Rust parser scores 402 of 402 on the yaml-test-suite under a strict criterion that also checks its lossless events and exact diagnostics. Every YAML 1.1 behavior is a named setting, off by default.
YAML is an existing standard, and byte-preserving round trips exist elsewhere. What’s uncommon is that typed reads and in-place edits share one parser and one resolver, so they can’t disagree about what a file means, and one shared conformance kit holds the Go and C# libraries to the same cases through their public APIs.
OneContact reproduces libphonenumber 9.0.43’s behavior and implements RFC 5322 email, WHATWG URL, the Public Suffix List and UTS #46. The phone side has 0 mismatches against libphonenumber in 2,819,630 results, and the URL side passes all 896 of WPT’s URL tests. It’s about 50,000 lines of C#.
Each piece reproduces an existing standard or reference library. The value is phones, email, URLs, addresses, names and page extraction exact in one library that never touches the network.
The text core is Myers, patience and histogram diff, held to outside tools: edit lengths equal GNU diff --minimal on 9,483 of 9,483 cases, and three-way merges equal git merge-file byte for byte in all three conflict styles. The document layer marks changes on the PDF pages and re-reads its own marks to confirm they match the change list. It’s about 39,000 lines of C#.
The diff algorithms are known. What it adds is document redlines where every comparison is checked to be invertible: old plus the changes gives new, and new minus the changes gives old. Changes come back typed with resolved values, like “30 days → 60 days”, and a renumbering counts as one change.
OneModel reads ONNX with its own protobuf reader, any opset from 7, and runs it on its own kernels for AVX2, AVX-512, NEON and portable SIMD, with graph optimization, quantization and training. On the ONNX 1.22.0 backend suite it passes 1,580 cases in fast mode with 0 failures. Exact mode has to give the same output hash on every x64 and arm64 path, NativeAOT and the browser, which rules out fused multiply-add and fixes the order of every addition. It’s about 73,000 lines of C#, and its GPU sessions run on OneGpu.
ONNX runtimes exist; OneModel adds an exact mode that gives the same bits on every CPU path and in the browser, at any thread count. The rules are written down, one accumulator per output in a stated order, no fused multiply-add and its own fixed polynomials for exp and tanh, so a port can reproduce the bits. It also trains, in the same managed library.
OneNlp implements five tokenizer families, UAX #29 segmentation, and a full neural pipeline: tagger, lemmatizer, biaffine dependency parser, entity recognizer and classifiers. Its tokenizers match Hugging Face tokenizers and tiktoken with 0 mismatches across 12 families, down to ids, offsets and special-token masks. It’s about 52,000 lines of C#, built on OneModel for inference and training.
The components are established NLP techniques. The value is running and training the whole stack in managed .NET, with models shipped as NuGet packages.
OneSpeech runs existing models: Whisper, Qwen3-ASR, Moonshine and Parakeet for recognition, plus alignment, voice activity detection, diarization and speaker embeddings. It reads PyTorch checkpoints, safetensors and NumPy files itself, and Whisper large-v3-turbo’s word error rate on LibriSpeech is within noise of openai-whisper’s. It’s about 17,000 lines of C#, with the heavy lifting in OneModel and OneAudio.
OneSpeech implements existing published models and decoding methods. The value is running them in managed .NET on OneModel, with no native inference runtime.
OneOcr has its own models, a page detector, line recognizers for Latin, Greek and Cyrillic, and a document extractor, defined by 20 written specs, and it trains them with its own backward passes. Output is bit-identical across AVX-512, AVX2, SSE/NEON and scalar paths at any thread count, which takes a fixed 16-lane accumulation order and its own polynomial exp and tanh. It’s about 43,000 lines of C# on its own SIMD kernels, not OneModel.
When you add an LLM pass, OneOcr sends the page along with its own word list, and the model has to cite the word ids each value came from. Every value is then checked against those words, the rest of the page, or arithmetic over cited amounts, and a value that doesn’t match is marked as a possible hallucination and asked for once more. The check is deterministic, and its spec says a port must reproduce it exactly.
OneLlm puts Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini, first-party and through Bedrock, Vertex and Azure OpenAI, plus any OpenAI-compatible server, behind one message model with streaming, tools, structured output and reasoning replay. Each provider is checked by replaying recorded fixtures that compare request bytes and parsed results. It also has its own prompt template language, diff-tested against Go’s text/template on 12,858,638 generated templates. It’s about 62,000 lines of C#.
The provider layer implements existing vendor APIs. The value is one message model over all of them, with agents, scripts and deciders as files you can persist, fork and resume.
OneModelContext implements every Model Context Protocol revision from 2024-11-05 to 2026-07-28, as client and server, over stdio and Streamable HTTP, with OAuth 2.1 and an embedded authorization server. Run as a black box, it passes the official conformance suite’s server scenarios at every revision. Its JSON-RPC, SSE, HTTP, OAuth and JOSE layers are its own code on the base library, about 43,000 lines of C# in all.
It’s a clean-room implementation of a published protocol. The value is both protocol eras behind one API, so application code is written once against the modern semantics.
OneEcma implements ES2026 in strict and sloppy mode, with its own RegExp engine, ECMA-426 source maps and Intl for six locales. On test262 it passes 22,973 language tests and 18,337 built-ins tests. Error messages and stack traces use V8’s exact wording, and lodash, preact and react SSR output must equal Node’s byte for byte. It’s about 78,000 lines of C#.
The engine is a from-scratch implementation of ECMA-262, 402 and 426. The value is a sandboxed JavaScript runtime in pure .NET whose error reports, built by replaying the failed run with tracing on, say where the failing value came from and how to fix it.
OneShader compiles Shader Model 6 HLSL to three targets, SPIR-V, Metal Shading Language and WGSL, including wave intrinsics, 16- and 64-bit types, bindless resources and cooperative matrices. Every target is checked by outside tools: spirv-val and a GPU run beside DXC’s compile for SPIR-V, naga and browser WebGPU for WGSL, and Apple’s compiler and Metal for MSL. Buffer offsets and strides must equal DXC’s. It’s about 58,000 lines of C#.
It’s an HLSL compiler in C# that runs inside dotnet build: shader mistakes become MSBuild errors on the HLSL line, and the generated C# structs match the compiled layout, so a CPU/GPU layout mismatch fails the build. It also compiles cooperative matrices with bfloat16_t, which the repo states DXC cannot compile.
OneGpu drives Vulkan 1.3, Metal through the Objective-C runtime and browser WebGPU from C#, with no native binaries of its own. Its ML kernels include FlashAttention-style attention that never writes the score matrix to memory and a GEMM that picks cooperative-matrix variants from the device’s capabilities. It’s about 24,000 lines of C# plus HLSL kernels compiled by OneShader.
The kernel algorithms are published ones. What’s uncommon is ONNX-class ML kernels on Vulkan, Metal and browser WebGPU from pure C#, with no CUDA. 41 of its 62 kernel files are written once in HLSL and compile to all three APIs; the rest are vendor fast paths with portable fallbacks.
OneAudio implements Opus, Vorbis, FLAC, MP3, AAC including HE-AAC, and AMR and AMR-WB from the specs, plus BS.1770 loudness. Several have to be bit-exact against the reference: the Opus encoder’s packets match the RFC 6716 reference encoder byte for byte in 269 of 269 configurations, and AMR decoding is bit-exact on all 573 3GPP test sequences. It’s about 57,000 lines of C#.
These are published codecs and loudness standards, written from scratch. The value is having them exact in one managed library, with a mixer that allocates nothing while it renders.
OneMedia reads MP4, Matroska, MPEG-TS, ASF, AVI and a long list of other containers, writes MP4, Matroska, MPEG-TS and WAV, and reads subtitles from SRT to CEA-608 and PGS bitmaps, all without decoding a sample. Tags and facts agree with ExifTool and MediaInfo on 116 files, and 445 untouched tag-edit round trips come back byte-identical. It’s about 134,000 lines of C#.
The container formats are existing standards, implemented from scratch. The value is reading, editing and repairing nearly every common container in one managed library with no dependency beyond the base library.
OneGame is a whole engine: 2D and 3D renderers, client/server sync, its own Noise-protocol encryption, Wayland, X11 and Win32 platform layers, glTF import, and Roslyn generators and analyzers. It’s built on 13 packages from eight other factory libraries plus oneyaml, including physics, GPU, shaders, rendering and audio. Sample games must give the same state hashes on Linux and Windows in CI. It’s about 122,000 lines of handwritten C#.
A game is plain C# and text assets, and every operation is a command that returns JSON: build, run headless, test YAML scenarios, capture frames, record and replay, poke live state over MCP, and hot-reload code into the running game. Determinism rules are compile errors, and the analyzer follows every call out of simulation code to any depth. It’s built so an AI agent can make a game from a terminal.
Correctly rounded means returning the IEEE 754 nearest value of the exact mathematical result, for 21 functions in float and double. OneMath does it with Ziv’s method: a fast table stage settles most inputs, and when the rounding is in doubt a double-double stage and then an exact 500-bit stage run. All 232 float inputs were checked for the 17 unary functions, with 0 not correctly rounded. It’s about 8,500 lines of C#.
Correctly rounded results are the same bits on every machine, which ordinary Math.Sin doesn’t promise: Microsoft’s docs say its result may differ between operating systems or architectures. OneMath never calls Math.Sin or fused multiply-add, an analyzer enforces that, and no 1.x release changes any bit. OnePhysics and OnePath build their determinism on it.
OnePath implements A*, JPS, JPS+, Theta*, HPA*, D* Lite, flow fields, a Recast-class navmesh pipeline and ORCA crowds. Grid path costs equal the Moving AI benchmark’s published optimal lengths, and 3D navmesh coverage is within 0.35% of Recast 1.6.0 on the same settings. Results are bit-identical on x64, arm64 and WebAssembly. It’s about 49,000 lines of C#, built on OneMath.
Results and saved state are bit-identical on x64, arm64 and WebAssembly, so searches, flow fields, navmeshes and crowds restore to the same bytes on every machine in a lockstep or rollback game. The algorithms underneath are known ones, which the repo names, implemented from scratch for grids, graphs, navmeshes and crowds in one package.
OnePhysics covers rigid bodies, joints, ropes, cloth, soft bodies, fracture, particle fluids, shallow water, granular matter, characters, vehicles and ragdolls, in 2D and 3D. All of it has to stay bit-identical, so it uses only exact + - * / and sqrt plus OneMath’s functions, fixed-order reductions and a graph-colored solver. CI hashes every step: 165 of 165 scenarios match on Linux x64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64, on eight threads, under NativeAOT and in the browser. It’s about 137,000 lines of C#.
The physics methods are published. What’s uncommon is the guarantee: the same world state, bit for bit, on every OS, CPU, vector width, WebAssembly mode and thread count. That’s what lockstep and rollback multiplayer need, and the tools for it are built in: byte-exact snapshots, per-step hashes, replay checks and a desync finder that reports the first difference.
OneScope’s scope is bounded: its own probe, session and cache formats, and no outside spec. The work is in seek and attach: a seek restores the nearest keyframe and re-simulates to land on the same hash as straight play, and a live attach re-simulates the stream so the viewer’s hash matches the host’s at every step. It’s about 15,000 lines of C#, and the window is built on OneGame.
It treats a deterministic run as a pure function of its recording, so you can seek to any step, fork from it, poke state and see the step where the fork diverges. It attaches to a running program without changing or slowing it, and every window action is also a CLI command and an MCP tool, so an agent can debug with it the same way.
A few up close
OneGame
OneGame is a C# game engine with no editor. A game is plain C# plus text assets. Roslyn source generators write each entity’s change tracking, codecs, deltas and snapshots, and analyzers turn the engine’s rules into compile errors: synced state is fixed-point and only changes through commands, and view code never writes it.
Clients and servers run the same stack, so state syncs between processes with prediction, authority transfer and drift detection. It runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS and the web, and a CLI and an MCP control protocol let an agent build, run, inspect and replay a game from a terminal. It sits directly on nine of the factory’s other libraries.
The repo carries sample games, and CI runs them on Linux and Windows. Solitaire and Lanterns come out with the same state hash on both in every scenario.
OnePhysics
OneGame’s physics comes from OnePhysics, deterministic 2D and 3D physics written from first principles: rigid bodies and joints, ropes, cloth, soft bodies, fracture, particle fluids, shallow water, vehicles and ragdolls, with byte-exact snapshot and restore for rollback netcode.
Determinism is the hard part. Ordinary Math.Sin can return different bits on different platforms, and in a simulation one different bit compounds until the two worlds diverge. So OnePhysics does its math through OneMath, which is correctly rounded and checked against an exact stage on all four billion float inputs. CI hashes the world every step: 165 of 165 scenarios give identical hashes on Linux x64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64, under JIT, on eight threads and NativeAOT, and in the browser. In 2D it’s also at or ahead of Box2D.NET on every scene at every thread count.
The GPU stack
OneShader is an HLSL compiler written in C#. It emits SPIR-V for Vulkan, Metal Shading Language and WGSL for WebGPU, and generates the C# bindings for each shader; DXC, spirv-val and naga validate its output in CI.
OneGpu is a pure C# GPU layer over Vulkan 1.3, Metal and browser WebGPU. It used to be part of OneGame. When OneModel, the ONNX runtime, needed the GPU too, I said “Fine, move it to onegpu,” and it became its own library, with ML kernels for GEMM, flash-style attention, convolution and RNNs.
OneModel now runs seven ONNX models on it on an RTX 4070, every row within 1.5× of ONNX Runtime’s WebGPU provider, with the same results on llvmpipe, RADV and an Apple M2 under Metal. OneGpu 1.0, OneModel 1.3 and OneGame 2.0 then shipped in dependency order within about 15 hours.
OneLite
OneLite is a SQLite 3.53.4-compatible database engine in managed C#: the database file format, the rollback journal and WAL, SQL semantics, FTS3/4/5, R*Tree and SQLCipher 4 pages, with an ADO.NET provider and an EF Core adapter.
Compatible here means the files, in both directions. A database the sqlite3 shell wrote reads identically in OneLite, and files OneLite writes pass sqlite3’s integrity_check. The WAL test runs 10,000 interleaved commits between OneLite and live sqlite3 processes on the same database, and it stays consistent from both sides. sqlite3 is a black box to the team; nobody reads SQLite’s source.
SQLite’s own sqllogictest passes all but one of nearly six million records, and on that one SQLite 3.53.4 raises the same integer overflow.
OneDocument
OneDocument reads and writes Word, Excel and PowerPoint in the OOXML formats from a 6,730-page standard, plus RTF and ODF. It also reads the old binary DOC, XLS and PPT, and it comes with a formula engine and rendering to tagged PDF.
The hard part is losing nothing. An OOXML file is a package of parts, and a save has to keep every part exactly, including the ones the library has no reason to touch. OneDocument opened and saved 4,900 real-world files without changes, and all 111,239 of their parts came out byte-identical.
Then real Office judges the output. Desktop Word, Excel and PowerPoint on my laptop open what it writes, all 104 of the authoring and revision documents included, and the formula engine runs against Excel’s own recalculation.
They’re built on each other
21 of the 30 depend on others in the set. The documents side shows it best: OneDocument renders through OneRender, and OneRender is built on four more of the factory’s libraries.
OneDocument’s 1.0 day, Friday, November 6, shows what that means in practice. Three libraries under it shipped what it needed first. OneRender added the tagged-PDF roles OneDocument needed, OnePdf fixed a PDF/UA failure OneDocument found two layers down, and OneImage fixed a crash OneDocument’s fuzzer found.
Anything the agents need from me goes on a projects board on my phone. A request to release is a Ship card: the evidence for the release and a Ship button. All three fixes were on NuGet before OneDocument’s Ship card reached me, and I tapped Ship about ten minutes after it arrived. No team edits another team’s repo; a team that needs something from a library below it asks that library’s team through the project manager.
How the factory runs
Each library starts with a planner agent that designs it through multiple-choice questions, one at a time. A project manager agent answers them for me unless only I can, and every design decision records who made it.
A build lead agent for each library splits the work into units and gives each one to an engineer agent in its own git worktree. Engineers can’t push, tag or publish; the lead checks their work with its own commands and merges it. Every run starts with no memory, so state lives in files. Each library’s PLAN.md is its lead’s memory, and the project manager role has passed through 12 agent instances since November 4, each handing off by note.
Each library’s release is gated on whatever evidence fits it. Where a standard has its own conformance suite, that suite is the gate. Where there’s a reference tool, it runs as a black box from its published release, and where real applications exist, they have to open what the library writes. Where nothing outside exists, as with the game engine and the physics, the gates are hash matrices across platforms and sample games. No agent can relax a gate.
When a release candidate passes CI on four operating systems, the project manager posts its Ship card. When I tap Ship, the release workflow tags it and publishes it to NuGet, and the project manager checks that every package is listed.
My part is the rules and the Ship taps. In those two weeks, every one of the 16 releases went out on a single tap.
Three issues from strangers
OnePdf reached 1.0 on October 23 and is on 1.23.0 now, 30 releases in under four weeks. 1.23.0 came from three GitHub issues filed by people I don’t know. The first came in on Tuesday, November 10, from a team moving off a commercial PDF library: they needed to rename form fields nested under parents while keeping their widgets linked, and to set a field’s appearance with the appearance streams rebuilt. The other two came in on Monday afternoon, November 16: about 6 KB allocated per short text in table-heavy layouts, and exact “N/M” page totals without a second layout pass.
That Monday evening I told the project manager to start monitoring GitHub issues on every open-source project and handling them, with the same care as email, since issues are untrusted input. It replied on all three itself within minutes; the automated issue poller went live later that night and handled none of them. The OnePdf lead read the issues once, as data, and wrote briefs, so the engineers never saw the issue text.
I tapped Ship on Tuesday morning and asked whether the documentation was updated, and the project manager pointed me to docs/forms.md, docs/layout.md and the changelog. The allocation fix, as posted on the issue: one-word cells went from about 6.6 KB to about 2.2 KB, about 3× faster, with the PDF bytes unchanged. I wrote no code, reviewed no diff and wrote none of the replies.
The libraries are on the libraries page, and the source is at github.com/recursive-ai-oss.

RFC 2675: IPv6 Jumbograms
- D. Borman,
- S. Deering,
- R. Hinden
Proposed Standard
- 10 subscribed
Network Working Group                                          D. Borman
Request for Comments: 2675                      Berkeley Software Design
Obsoletes: 2147                                               S. Deering
Category: Standards Track                                          Cisco
                                                               R. Hinden
                                                                   Nokia
                                                             August 1999
                            IPv6 Jumbograms
Status of this Memo
   This document specifies an Internet standards track protocol for the
   Internet community, and requests discussion and suggestions for
   improvements.  Please refer to the current edition of the "Internet
   Official Protocol Standards" (STD 1) for the standardization state
   and status of this protocol.  Distribution of this memo is unlimited.
Copyright Notice
   Copyright (C) The Internet Society (1999).  All Rights Reserved.
Abstract
   A "jumbogram" is an IPv6 packet containing a payload longer than
   65,535 octets.  This document describes the IPv6 Jumbo Payload
   option, which provides the means of specifying such large payload
   lengths.  It also describes the changes needed to TCP and UDP to make
   use of jumbograms.
   Jumbograms are relevant only to IPv6 nodes that may be attached to
   links with a link MTU greater than 65,575 octets, and need not be
   implemented or understood by IPv6 nodes that do not support
   attachment to links with such large MTUs.
1. Introduction
      jumbo (jum'bO),
          n., pl. -bos, adj.
          -n.
          1. a person, animal, or thing very large of its kind.
          -adj.
          2. very large: the jumbo box of cereal.
          [1800-10; orig. uncert.; popularized as the name of a large
           elephant purchased and exhibited by P.T. Barnum in 1882]
                                              -- www.infoplease.com
Borman, et al.              Standards Track                     [Page 1]
RFC 2675                    IPv6 Jumbograms                  August 1999
   The IPv6 header [IPv6] has a 16-bit Payload Length field and,
   therefore, supports payloads up to 65,535 octets long.  This document
   specifies an IPv6 hop-by-hop option, called the Jumbo Payload option,
   that carries a 32-bit length field in order to allow transmission of
   IPv6 packets with payloads between 65,536 and 4,294,967,295 octets in
   length.  Packets with such long payloads are referred to as
   "jumbograms".
   The Jumbo Payload option is relevant only for IPv6 nodes that may be
   attached to links with a link MTU greater than 65,575 octets (that
   is, 65,535 + 40, where 40 octets is the size of the IPv6 header).
   The Jumbo Payload option need not be implemented or understood by
   IPv6 nodes that do not support attachment to links with MTU greater
   than 65,575.
   On links with configurable MTUs, the MTU must not be configured to a
   value greater than 65,575 octets if there are nodes attached to that
   link that do not support the Jumbo Payload option and it can not be
   guaranteed that the Jumbo Payload option will not be sent to those
   nodes.
   The UDP header [UDP] has a 16-bit Length field which prevents it from
   making use of jumbograms, and though the TCP header [TCP] does not
   have a Length field, both the TCP MSS option and the TCP Urgent field
   are constrained to 16 bits.  This document specifies some simple
   enhancements to TCP and UDP to enable them to make use of jumbograms.
   An implementation of TCP or UDP on an IPv6 node that supports the
   Jumbo Payload option must include the enhancements specified here.
   Note: The 16 bit checksum used by UDP and TCP becomes less accurate
   as the length of the data being checksummed is increased.
   Application designers may want to take this into consideration.
1.1 Document History
   This document merges and updates material that was previously
   published in two separate documents:
   -  The specification of the Jumbo Payload option previously appeared
      as part of the IPv6 specification in RFC 1883.  RFC 1883 has been
      superseded by RFC 2460, which no longer includes specification of
      the Jumbo Payload option.
   -  The specification of TCP and UDP enhancements to support
      jumbograms previously appeared as RFC 2147.  RFC 2147 is obsoleted
      by this document.
Borman, et al.              Standards Track                     [Page 2]
RFC 2675                    IPv6 Jumbograms                  August 1999
2. Format of the Jumbo Payload Option
   The Jumbo Payload option is carried in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options
   header, immediately following the IPv6 header.  This option has an
   alignment requirement of 4n + 2.  (See [IPv6, Section 4.2] for
   discussion of option alignment.)  The option has the following
   format:
                                   +-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
                                   |  Option Type  |  Opt Data Len |
   +-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
   |                     Jumbo Payload Length                      |
   +-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
   Option Type           8-bit value C2 (hexadecimal).
   Opt Data Len          8-bit value 4.
   Jumbo Payload Length  32-bit unsigned integer.  Length of the IPv6
                         packet in octets, excluding the IPv6 header
                         but including the Hop-by-Hop Options header
                         and any other extension headers present.
                         Must be greater than 65,535.
3. Usage of the Jumbo Payload Option
   The Payload Length field in the IPv6 header must be set to zero in
   every packet that carries the Jumbo Payload option.
   If a node that understands the Jumbo Payload option receives a packet
   whose IPv6 header carries a Payload Length of zero and a Next Header
   value of zero (meaning that a Hop-by-Hop Options header follows), and
   whose link-layer framing indicates the presence of octets beyond the
   IPv6 header, the node must proceed to process the Hop-by-Hop Options
   header in order to determine the actual length of the payload from
   the Jumbo Payload option.
   The Jumbo Payload option must not be used in a packet that carries a
   Fragment header.
   Higher-layer protocols that use the IPv6 Payload Length field to
   compute the value of the Upper-Layer Packet Length field in the
   checksum pseudo-header described in [IPv6, Section 8.1] must instead
   use the Jumbo Payload Length field for that computation, for packets
   that carry the Jumbo Payload option.
Borman, et al.              Standards Track                     [Page 3]
RFC 2675                    IPv6 Jumbograms                  August 1999
   Nodes that understand the Jumbo Payload option are required to detect
   a number of possible format errors, and if the erroneous packet was
   not destined to a multicast address, report the error by sending an
   ICMP Parameter Problem message [ICMPv6] to the packet's source.   The
   following list of errors specifies the values to be used in the Code
   and Pointer fields of the Parameter Problem message:
      error: IPv6 Payload Length = 0 and
             IPv6 Next Header = Hop-by-Hop Options and
             Jumbo Payload option not present
             Code: 0
             Pointer: high-order octet of the IPv6 Payload Length
      error: IPv6 Payload Length != 0 and
             Jumbo Payload option present
             Code: 0
             Pointer: Option Type field of the Jumbo Payload option
      error: Jumbo Payload option present and
             Jumbo Payload Length < 65,536
             Code: 0
             Pointer: high-order octet of the Jumbo Payload Length
      error: Jumbo Payload option present and
             Fragment header present
             Code: 0
             Pointer: high-order octet of the Fragment header.
   A node that does not understand the Jumbo Payload option is expected
   to respond to erroneously-received jumbograms as follows, according
   to the IPv6 specification:
      error: IPv6 Payload Length = 0 and
             IPv6 Next Header = Hop-by-Hop Options
             Code: 0
             Pointer: high-order octet of the IPv6 Payload Length
      error: IPv6 Payload Length != 0 and
             Jumbo Payload option present
             Code: 2
             Pointer: Option Type field of the Jumbo Payload option
Borman, et al.              Standards Track                     [Page 4]
RFC 2675                    IPv6 Jumbograms                  August 1999
4. UDP Jumbograms
   The 16-bit Length field of the UDP header limits the total length of
   a UDP packet (that is, a UDP header plus data) to no greater than
   65,535 octets.  This document specifies the following modification of
   UDP to relax that limit: UDP packets longer than 65,535 octets may be
   sent by setting the UDP Length field to zero, and letting the
   receiver derive the actual UDP packet length from the IPv6 payload
   length.  (Note that, prior to this modification, zero was not a legal
   value for the UDP Length field, because the UDP packet length
   includes the UDP header and therefore has a minimum value of 8.)
   The specific requirements for sending a UDP jumbogram are as follows:
      When sending a UDP packet, if and only if the length of the UDP
      header plus UDP data is greater than 65,535, set the Length field
      in the UDP header to zero.
      The IPv6 packet carrying such a large UDP packet will necessarily
      include a Jumbo Payload option in a Hop-by-Hop Options header; set
      the Jumbo Payload Length field of that option to be the actual
      length of the UDP header plus data, plus the length of all IPv6
      extension headers present between the IPv6 header and the UDP
      header.
      For generating the UDP checksum, use the actual length of the UDP
      header plus data, NOT zero, in the checksum pseudo-header [IPv6,
      Section 8.1].
   The specific requirements for receiving a UDP jumbogram are as
   follows:
      When receiving a UDP packet, if and only if the Length field in
      the UDP header is zero, calculate the actual length of the UDP
      header plus data from the IPv6 Jumbo Payload Length field minus
      the length of all extension headers present between the IPv6
      header and the UDP header.
      In the unexpected case that the UDP Length field is zero but no
      Jumbo Payload option is present (i.e., the IPv6 packet is not a
      jumbogram), use the Payload Length field in the IPv6 header, in
      place of the Jumbo Payload Length field, in the above calculation.
      For verifying the received UDP checksum, use the calculated length
      of the UDP header plus data, NOT zero, in the checksum pseudo-
      header.
Borman, et al.              Standards Track                     [Page 5]
RFC 2675                    IPv6 Jumbograms                  August 1999
5. TCP Jumbograms
   Because there is no length field in the TCP header, there is nothing
   limiting the length of an individual TCP packet.  However, the MSS
   value that is negotiated at the beginning of the connection limits
   the largest TCP packet that can be sent, and the Urgent Pointer
   cannot reference data beyond 65,535 bytes.
5.1 TCP MSS
   When determining what MSS value to send, if the MTU of the directly
   attached interface minus 60 [IPv6, Section 8.3] is greater than or
   equal to 65,535, then set the MSS value to 65,535.
   When an MSS value of 65,535 is received, it is to be treated as
   infinity.  The actual MSS is determined by subtracting 60 from the
   value learned by performing Path MTU Discovery [MTU-DISC] over the
   path to the TCP peer.
5.2 TCP Urgent Pointer
   The Urgent Pointer problem could be fixed by adding a TCP Urgent
   Pointer Option.  However, since it is unlikely that applications
   using jumbograms will also use Urgent Pointers, a less intrusive
   change similar to the MSS change will suffice.
   When a TCP packet is to be sent with an Urgent Pointer (i.e., the URG
   bit set), first calculate the offset from the Sequence Number to the
   Urgent Pointer.  If the offset is less than 65,535, fill in the
   Urgent field and continue with the normal TCP processing.  If the
   offset is greater than 65,535, and the offset is greater than or
   equal to the length of the TCP data, fill in the Urgent Pointer with
   65,535 and continue with the normal TCP processing.  Otherwise, the
   TCP packet must be split into two pieces.  The first piece contains
   data up to, but not including the data pointed to by the Urgent
   Pointer, and the Urgent field is set to 65,535 to indicate that the
   Urgent Pointer is beyond the end of this packet.  The second piece
   can then be sent with the Urgent field set normally.
   Note: The first piece does not have to include all of the data up to
   the Urgent Pointer.  It can be shorter, just as long as it ends
   within 65,534 bytes of the Urgent Pointer, so that the offset to the
   Urgent Pointer in the second piece will be less than 65,535 bytes.
   For TCP input processing, when a TCP packet is received with the URG
   bit set and an Urgent field of 65,535, the Urgent Pointer is
   calculated using an offset equal to the length of the TCP data,
   rather than the offset in the Urgent field.
Borman, et al.              Standards Track                     [Page 6]
RFC 2675                    IPv6 Jumbograms                  August 1999
   It should also be noted that though the TCP window is only 16-bits,
   larger windows can be used through use of the TCP Window Scale option
   [TCP-EXT].
6. Security Considerations
   The Jumbo Payload option and TCP/UDP jumbograms do not introduce any
   known new security concerns.

"Cowboy Stew" is The Cozy Meal I Cook Over and Over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:15:00 UTC
01:15:00 KST

The Cowboy Beef Stew I Make All Winter
Lately the food world seems to be overtaken by recipes that draw inspiration from a surprising source: cowboys. From butter, to casseroles, to “caviar,” there appears to be some mystical draw to these hearty, almost nostalgic recipes. Although it’s hard to say whether any cowboy ever actually ate any of this stuff, we can’t deny the appeal.
The latest cowboy craze? Cowboy stew. Kathleen of Gonna Want Seconds has a version that is rapidly garnering five-star reviews, so we figured it was only natural we gave this Western-inspired recipe a shot. Although it’s quite different from the colorfully named cowboy stew of yore, which featured meat and organs from a calf, it’s still loaded with lots of hearty, stick-to-your-ribs ingredients. 
Get the recipe: Cowboy Stew
How to Make Cowboy Stew
Slice kielbasa sausages into 1/2-inch pieces and chop slices of bacon. Add bacon to a large pot over medium heat. Cook until crispy, then transfer to a plate lined with a paper towel.
Add the sliced sausage to the pot and brown on both sides, then remove to another paper towel-lined plate. Add 80/20 ground beef to the pot, along with diced onion and minced garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is no longer pink. Add all-purpose flour, salt, black pepper, and chili powder, and cook for one minute more. Add canned petite diced tomatoes (with liquid), baked beans, chopped green chilies, canned sweet corn (with liquid), peeled and cubed russet potatoes, and water. Return bacon and sausage to pot, bring mixture up to a simmer, and cover. Cook, stirring occasionally, for an hour.
Serve garnished with chopped parsley. If the stew is too thick, loosen with additional water.
My Honest Review of Cowboy Stew
As someone who eats meat rather infrequently, I found the inclusion of ground beef and two types of pork to be somewhat intimidating. The resulting stew is a bit like chili, but even meatier. Incorporating all of this protein makes for an intensely savory dish, with baked beans and corn bringing some sweetness for balance. The addition of potatoes and flour creates a thick, ultra-rich broth imbued with tons of smoky flavor from the kielbasa. All this to say that this stew is about as hearty as it gets. If you’re a meat-lover, there’s a good chance you’ll be into this recipe, but for me it was a bit too intense.
If you need to feed a lot of hungry people fast, this recipe couldn’t be easier. Although the inclusion of lots of canned ingredients does lighten up prep time considerably, I couldn’t shake the subtle tinny flavor you sometimes taste in canned ingredients. I think swapping in a couple of non-canned ingredients (like fresh or frozen corn or chopped fresh tomatoes) would help mask this unpleasant flavor. Any canning liquid lost in these swaps could easily be replaced by water or broth, as the stew is already plenty thick — even more so after spending a night in the fridge.
3 Tips for Making Cowboy Stew
- Use a really big pot. This recipe makes a lot of stew! I used a 6.75-quart pot, which gave me plenty of room for stirring and simmering.
- Sear off your kielbasa in batches. Even with a large pot, it’s impossible to sear off all your sausage in one go. Add enough sliced kielbasa to lay flat in a single layer to achieve that perfect golden-brown, and adjust the heat as you go to avoid accumulating too many browned bits on the bottom of your pan.
- Stir often while the stew simmers. With two whole cans of baked beans, this recipe actually contains a fair amount of sugar. Stir every few minutes while the stew is simmering to avoid burning those sugars.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it’s ‘hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:14:09 UTC
01:14:09 KST

The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.
Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.
“Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”
OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.
Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”
“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”
Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.
Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”
“I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

SuperEMeans: Making e-means 3× faster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:09:50 UTC
01:09:50 KST

TL;DR: We fused SuperKMeans and e-means, resulting in 3× faster clustering of high-dimensional vectors without quality trade-offs. Available now at https://github.com/cwida/SuperKMeans.
Recently, there has been a lot of buzz around clustering of vector embeddings: EVōC, SuperKMeans, QGKmeans, and just last week, e-means, o-means, and s-means. Among these, e-means is a big deal: it promises the same quality as Lloyd’s with only 2 epochs. Why is this a big deal for vector search?
Well, clustering is a key building block for large-scale vector indexes (e.g., IVF, ScANN), which is precisely the bottleneck that users have to wait on before issuing similarity search queries.
A year ago, we released SuperKMeans. SuperKMeans accelerates Lloyd’s k-means by 2—10× by avoiding scanning vector dimensions while clustering, without trade-offs in clustering quality. SuperKMeans has been rapidly adopted by industry (ParadeDB, Zilliz, FAISS), showing how timely it is to improve clustering performance for high-dimensional vectors. However, e-means is also exciting because it tackles effort by running fewer epochs. Traditionally, clustering for vector embeddings is standardized to 10 epochs. e-means promises the same (or better) clustering quality with just 2 epochs. I would recommend checking out the wonderful website made by e-means’ authors: https://e-means.github.io/
Interestingly, in their paper, the authors suggest that SuperKMeans’ idea of pruning dimensions is orthogonal to e-means. We agree: there is nothing about these two ideas that opposes the other. Naturally, this put us to work!
The Setup
We have extended our clustering library to implement e-means and SuperEMeans (open-sourced at https://github.com/cwida/SuperKMeans) and have measured their benefits.
The datasets: We will be using two datasets: i) 5M 1536-dimensional OpenAI embeddings from the VectorDBBench benchmark: https://huggingface.co/datasets/makneeee/openai_large_5m. (27 GB). ii) The first 10M MS MARCO passages embedded with the Cohere Embed V3 model (1024-dimensional vectors): https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cohere/msmarco-v2.1-embed-english-v3 (40 GB).
The index: We will build an IVF index with a point-per-cluster ratio of 1:256, resulting in approximately 20,000 centroids for OpenAI and 40,000 centroids for the Cohere dataset.
The setup: For this experiment, I will use a single Zen 5 machine with 16 cores and 128 GB of RAM (r8a.4xlarge | $1.278/hr). However, our SuperKMeans library works on any CPU (e.g., Intel, Graviton, Zen).
The Results
The following plot compares the end-to-end clustering runtime of Lloyd’s (10 iterations), SuperKMeans (10 iterations), e-means (2 epochs), and SuperEMeans (2 epochs). SuperEMeans substantially accelerates e-means, up to 1.8× faster.
But… is it a high-quality index?
Let’s compare the centroids obtained by each approach in terms of how well they perform on vector search tasks. For this analysis, we issue 1000 queries to our IVF index. Then, we measure the proportion of top-100 retrieved results that are in the true top-100 results while scanning 1% of the available clusters (recall@100). We have also compared the balance of clusters by counting the number of distance calculations performed when scanning those clusters. The results for OpenAI are summarized in the table below:
Recall@100 is slightly higher in e-means. However, we end up scanning around 10% more vectors during searches. To match the number of vectors scanned, we have to probe slightly fewer clusters in e-means, around 0.90% of the total clusters. This results in recall@100 = 0.964 while scanning 51,962 vectors, resulting in an ultimately better trade-off than traditional k-means.
The story is the same for Cohere:
Again, we have to probe slightly fewer clusters in e-means, around 0.90% of the total clusters. This results in recall@100 = 0.918 while scanning 121,511 vectors. Here, the gap is not favorable for e-means, which scans 8% more vectors for the same recall.
Why does e-means scan more vectors?
In e-means, clusters are more bloated than in Lloyd’s k-means in the regions of the vector space queried most often. Yet e-means reaches a lower WCSS (MSE), since that objective doesn’t reward balanced clusters, while vector search pays for every point it scans. Note that the cost is latency at a fixed number of probed clusters, not retrieval quality (since matching the number of vectors scanned yields roughly the same recall).
As for the algorithmic reason why, the imbalance comes from e-means’ mini-batch updates. A cluster that gains just a few points in the initial batches stays with just a few points for the rest of the clustering.
To counteract this, e-means introduces a revival step that, every five batches, re-seeds clusters whose usage in a batch fell below 0.1× the mean usage across clusters. If this happens, that cluster is eliminated and a large cluster is split into two. We found this threshold too conservative, leaving many small clusters stuck with few points across batches. Raising the revival threshold from 0.1 to 0.3 brings cluster balance and scan cost closer to Lloyd’s level in the Cohere dataset.
More Epochs
At 5 epochs (the author’s default in their implementation), the speedup from SuperEMeans is remarkable: up to 3× faster!
Closing Remarks
e-means is an interesting advancement in clustering algorithms. I would love to see more advancements that pay attention to cluster balance. This is a key factor for vector search performance that doesn’t necessarily align with the WCSS / MSE objective of k-means.
Anyways, I am excited to see where we go from here! As the authors also mention in their paper, approximate assignment can accelerate large-scale clustering (+1B points), where even 1 epoch can cost hours. In our library, we implement hierarchical k-means, which has also seen success on vector-embedding datasets (implemented in NVIDIA’s cuVS library). However, it didn’t work quite well with e-means. I suspect this might also be due to how cluster’s revival works.
Another option is to cluster quantized vectors. For example, quantize 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers, or 1-bit RaBitQ codes before clustering. We have explored this in another research paper with remarkable results.
SuperKMeans and e-means detailed technical reports are available on arXiv.
Reproducibility
The source code to reproduce the results of this blog post are available at: https://github.com/lkuffo/reproducibility-superemeans

Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:09:40 UTC
01:09:40 KST

Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits, the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.
“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”
Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.
Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.
The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”
See more on the artist’s Instagram.

8BitDo’s new gamepad modernizes the Nintendo GameCube’s WaveBird
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:01:23 UTC
01:01:23 KST

The 8BitDo 64 was a loose remake of the Nintendo 64’s unusual triple-grip controller that did away with that gamepad’s centered analog stick. But with its new GC Bluetooth Gamepad, 8BitDo has done a much better job at staying faithful to the design of the Nintendo GameCube’s excellent controllers, including their unique button layout, thumbstick design, and shoulder buttons.
8BitDo’s new gamepad modernizes the Nintendo GameCube’s WaveBird
Diehard GameCube fans can connect the controller to their original console, or use it with the Switch.
The 8BitDo GC Bluetooth Gamepad is available for preorder starting today for $49.99 in orange or purple and is expected to start shipping on December 10th. That’s much cheaper than Nintendo’s $69.99 wireless remake of the GameCube controller, although 8BitDo’s version isn’t an exact copy of the original’s shape and ergonomics. If that’s important to you, and you have your GameCube’s original accessories on hand, you can still buy 8BitDo’s $25.98 upgrade kit, which is a cheaper way to make it compatible with modern consoles and devices.
8BitDo’s GameCube redux carries forward the original’s octagonal gates around the base of each thumbstick, making it well-suited to playing fighting games like Super Smash Bros. Ultimate. And while Nintendo continues to skip modern thumbstick technologies, the 8BitDo GC features both drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks and Hall effect linear triggers.
The controller connects to all versions of the Nintendo Switch over Bluetooth, as well as PCs or handheld consoles running Windows. It also comes with a 2.4GHz wireless USB receiver for players who prefer a connection with lower latency, or you can connect it with a USB-C cable for the best possible performance.

Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now (theverge.com) 37
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?"
I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it."
Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic."

the graffiti wall of the internet
BTC:1PPB5oGiYnujQ3tvSWUSwSQQyGwMbh5oJC
ratwires is an anonymous, javascriptless, single-board textboard. No accounts, no names, no images: just text.
Every post is numbered in order, so the 300th post ever is No.300, and >>300
links to it. Each page of the wall holds 255 posts. When a page fills up, a new one
starts, and the old pages stay up.
Inside a thread, each poster gets an ID like ID:k3Fq9aZx. It's a scrambled code (a hash)
of your IP address, the thread and the date, so it differs between threads and changes every day.
It lets you tell who's who in a conversation.
See something that shouldn't be here? Use the ⚑ next to a post to report it. Reports are anonymous.
The server hands out badges, which show up next to a post's number:
!dice roll in the post uses dice with
6 or more sides and every die lands on its highest number.
This is a revival of ratwires.space as it looked in 2020. The original ran on Ratmachine, an AGPL board written in Crystal with the Amber Framework and inspired by Make Frontend Shit Again and 2channel. This one is a from-scratch rebuild, not run by the original operators, and none of the original posts were carried over.
