The x86 CPU: From 4004 to 486
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
14:47:53 UTC
23:47:53 KST

We already covered the main ideas behind Real Mode & Protected Mode in one of our previous posts. This article will build on those concepts and take a deeper look at the history and evolution of the x86 family of CPUs. But rather than simply looking at the innovations introduced with each new chip, we need to understand how the architecture accumulated over time, from its origins in the early 70s up until the launch of the 486.
Every time a new student starts learning x86 assembler with us, it's not rare to hear them complain that many aspects of the instruction set look arbitrary. An accumulator that some instructions insist on, a base register that is the only one allowed to point at memory, a parity flag nobody seems to use, and an addressing scheme that adds two 16-bit numbers together in a very strange way.
The majority of teaching resources out there will help you write your first lines of x86 code, assemble it, link it, and as proceed as soon as the output matches what you were expecting. I try to always explain the evolution of the x86 family of CPUs, so every aspect of our code makes a little bit more sense.
None of these things are arbitrary, of course. Each one is a decision someone made under pressure, usually to keep old software running on a new chip. If you want to really understand x86 (and especially if you want to program a 486 under DOS), the best place to start is not the 486 manual. It's the story.
Here is the family tree we're going to walk through:
A table like this makes the evolution look neat and planned. It wasn't. Between these rows there are cancelled projects, a customer who walked away from its own chip, a stopgap that was supposed to last a couple of years, a sales campaign, a keyboard controller wired into the address bus, and a lawsuit.
Let's travel back to 1969 and see how it all happened!
A Calculator Chip: The 4004
The story starts with a Japanese calculator company. In 1969, Busicom asked Intel (then a young memory company) to build a set of custom chips for a new printing calculator. Instead of designing many single-purpose chips, Intel's team proposed something more general: a small programmable processor that would run the calculator's logic from ROM.
The result was the 4004, released on November 15, 1971, and designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. It had 2,300 transistors, ran at about 740 kHz, and could address 4 KB of program ROM.
The most important line in the 4004's story is not technical, though. Busicom had paid for the design and owned the rights. When Busicom ran into financial trouble in 1971, Faggin convinced Intel's CEO Bob Noyce to lower the chip's price in exchange for Intel getting out of the exclusivity deal. Intel paid back Busicom's $60,000 development costs and won the right to sell the chip to anyone (outside the calculator market).
That deal is why "a microprocessor" became something Intel could sell, rather than a part buried inside one calculator.
The Terminal That Didn't Want Its CPU: The 8008
At almost the same time, a second customer walked through Intel's door. In late 1969, Computer Terminal Corporation (CTC, later called Datapoint) asked Intel to build a chip for a programmable terminal called the Datapoint 2200.
This detail matters a lot: Intel did not design the instruction set of this chip. CTC's engineers Victor Poor and Harry Pyle did. They had already built the Datapoint 2200's processor out of dozens of discrete TTL chips, and they wanted Intel to squeeze that same design onto one piece of silicon.
Intel was slow. Texas Instruments also tried to build the chip, but its samples were buggy and rejected. Meanwhile, CTC shipped the Datapoint 2200 in 1970 with its TTL processor anyway, and later moved on to a faster design. In the end, CTC voted to walk away from the project and leave the design to Intel instead of paying the $50,000 contract. Intel renamed it the 8008 and released it in April 1972 with 3,500 transistors and 16 KB of addressable memory.
So the ancestor of every x86 chip was designed by a terminal company, for a terminal, and then rejected by that terminal company. And two of the terminal's habits are still inside your PC today.
Why x86 is Little-Endian
The Datapoint 2200 processed numbers one bit at a time (a bit-serial design). If you're adding two numbers one bit at a time, you want to start with the lowest bit, because that's where the carry starts. So it made sense to store the lowest byte first in memory.
The 8008 copied the Datapoint's design, the 8080 kept compatibility with the 8008, and the 8086 kept compatibility with the 8080. Stephen Morse, the architect of the 8086, put it this way in his history of the early Intel processors:
"This inverted storage, which was to haunt all processors evolved from the 8008, was a result of compatibility with the Datapoint bit-serial processor."
That's why, on your 486 (and even in a more modern Core i9), this instruction:
mov DWORD ptr [buffer], 12345678h
...stores the bytes 78 56 34 12 in memory.
Why x86 Has a Parity Flag
The second habit is the parity flag (PF), which tells you if the result of the last operation had an even number of 1 bits. It's one of those flags that beginners look at and wonder who on earth needs it.
The answer is: a terminal does! Morse again: "This permits testing for transmission errors, an obviously useful function for a CRT terminal." Data arriving over a serial line often carried a parity bit, and the Datapoint needed a fast way to check it.
Fifty years later, PF is still bit 2 of the x86 FLAGS register.
The 8080 and the Birth of the PC Hobby
The 8008 was slow and awkward, so Intel designed a much better successor. The 8080 was released in April 1974, with Federico Faggin as its primary architect and Masatoshi Shima on the detailed design. It had about 4,500 transistors, ran at 2 MHz, and could address 64 KB of memory.
The 8080 was not binary compatible with the 8008, but it kept the same register set and the same "flavor." More importantly, it added several things you will recognize as an x86 programmer:
- Register pairs: B and C could be used together as the 16-bit pair BC, and the same for DE and HL
- The HL pair as the main way to point at memory (MOV A, M reads the byte at address HL)
- A real 16-bit stack pointer
- A separate I/O space with 256 ports, accessed with IN and OUT
That separate I/O space is the reason why, many years later, VGA registers live at "port 3C8h" instead of at a memory address.
The 8080 powered the Altair 8800 and became the standard CPU for CP/M, the most popular operating system for small business computers in the late 70s. Suddenly, there was a lot of 8080 software out there.
And then Intel got some serious competition. Faggin and Shima left Intel and went to Zilog, where they built the Z80: a chip that could run 8080 machine code, but was faster, cheaper to build a computer around, and had more instructions. The Z80 started eating Intel's market.
The 8085: A Quiet Hint of What Was Coming
Intel's answer was the 8085, released in March 1976. The "5" in the name refers to its biggest selling point: it needed a single +5 V power supply, while the 8080 needed +5 V, -5 V, and +12 V.
To fit everything into a 40-pin package, the 8085 also multiplexed its bus: the same eight pins carried the low byte of the address first, and then the data. Remember this trick, because the 8086 uses it too.
There's a lovely footnote here: the 8085 had 12 new instructions, but Intel made a last-minute decision to document only 2 of them. The reason? To keep things simple for the next chip, which was already being designed. That chip was the 8086.
The Stopgap That Took Over the World: The 8086
In the mid 70s, Intel's big bet for the future was not the 8086. It was the iAPX 432, a very ambitious processor designed with object-oriented programming and high-level languages in mind. The 432 was late, and with the Z80 taking customers away, Intel needed something to sell in the meantime.
So, in May 1976, Intel started the 8086 project as a temporary product. Stephen Morse was the principal architect, Jim McKevitt and John Bayliss were the lead hardware engineers, and Bill Pohlman managed the project. The 8086 was released on June 8, 1978.
The brief was clear: the new chip had to address more than 64 KB, do 16-bit arithmetic, and (this is the important part) make it easy for existing 8080 software to move over.
Source Compatibility, Not Binary Compatibility
The 8086 cannot run 8080 machine code. Instead, Intel aimed for source compatibility: you could take your 8080 assembly program and translate it, line by line, into 8086 assembly. Intel even shipped a translator called CONV86 (available from 1978) to do this automatically. Morse described the goal like this: "the 8080 register set and instruction set appear as logical subsets of the 8086 registers and instructions."
For that translation to work, every 8080 register needed an obvious home in the 8086. And this is where the 8086's register names come from:
Here's a tiny 8080 routine and its 8086 translation side by side:
; 8080                     ; 8086
LXI  H, buffer             mov  bx, offset buffer   ; HL becomes BX
MOV  A, M                  mov  al, [bx]            ; A becomes AL
INX  H                     inc  bx
ADD  M                     add  al, [bx]
Now some of the "weird" things about x86 suddenly make sense:
- AX is the accumulator because 8080's A became AL. That's why MUL, DIV, IN, and OUT insist on using it, and why many instructions have shorter encodings when they use AL/AX.
- BX is the base register because the 8080's memory pointer HL became BX. That's why, in 16-bit code, BX is the only one of AX, BX, CX, DX that can point at memory.
- CX is the count register (used by LOOP, REP, and shifts) and DX is the data register (used for I/O port numbers and the high half of 32-bit results).
- The 8080's flags byte became the low byte of the 8086's FLAGS register, and the instructions LAHF and SAHF exist just to move that 8080-shaped byte in and out of AH.
Have you ever wondered why the 8086 numbers its registers in the order AX, CX, DX, BX (0, 1, 2, 3) inside instruction encodings, instead of the obvious A, B, C, D? It follows the 8080's order of register pairs: BC, DE, HL. Once A is placed first, BC becomes CX, DE becomes DX, and HL becomes BX.
And what does the "X" mean? According to Morse himself, nothing special. It was simply an arbitrary letter combining the "H" and "L" halves into one 16-bit register (as told to Vladimir Keleshev).
Segmentation: Reaching 1 MB with 16-bit Registers
The second big requirement was memory. Intel wanted 1 MB of address space, and that needs 20 address bits. But the 8086's registers were only 16 bits wide.
Morse's solution was segmentation. The chip has four segment registers (CS, DS, SS, and ES), and every memory access combines a segment with a 16-bit offset:
$$ \text{address} = \text{segment} \times 16 + \text{offset} $$
Multiplying by 16 is just a shift of 4 bits to the left. For example, if we want to write to pixel (160, 100) in VGA mode 13h, which lives at segment A000h:
mov  ax, 0A000h
mov  es, ax                       ; segment = A000h
mov  di, 320*100 + 160            ; offset  = 7DA0h
mov  byte ptr es:[di], 15         ; physical address = A0000h + 7DA0h = A7DA0h
Why 16 and not something bigger, like 256? Morse explained that with 8 bits of shift, "segments would be forced to start on 256-byte boundaries, resulting in excessive memory fragmentation."
Segmentation was cheap (a small adder in the chip) and it worked very well with the source-compatibility goal: an 8080 program expected a 64 KB world, so you could give it one segment and it would run unchanged, wherever in memory that segment happened to be.
But it also created a rule that haunted every DOS programmer for the next 15 years:
That rule is why C compilers for DOS had near, far, and huge pointers, and memory models with names like tiny, small, compact, and large. It's also why mode 13h is so beloved: 320 × 200 = 64,000 bytes, which fits in one segment!
Operation Crush and the 8088
The 8086 was not an instant hit. Motorola's 68000 and Zilog's Z8000 were more elegant 16-bit designs, and many engineers preferred them.
Intel's response was a sales campaign called Operation Crush, launched in a meeting in December 1979. Instead of selling the 8086 on raw specs, Intel sold it as a complete solution: development tools, support chips, documentation, and support. The goal was 2,000 "design wins" (products using the chip) in one year. They got nearly 2,500.
One of them was a small project inside IBM in Boca Raton.
A year after the 8086, Intel had released the 8088 (June 1, 1979). Internally it's the same 16-bit processor, but with an 8-bit external data bus. Every 16-bit memory access takes two bus cycles, so it's slower. But an 8-bit bus meant you could build the computer with cheap, plentiful support chips designed for the 8085. Intel also offered IBM a better price and could supply more units.
The IBM PC was launched on August 12, 1981, with an 8088 running at 4.77 MHz. That odd number comes from television: the PC used a 14.31818 MHz crystal (four times the NTSC color carrier, which the CGA video card needed), divided by 3.
IBM made one more decision that shaped the whole industry: it required a second source for the CPU, so it would never depend on a single supplier. That led to a 10-year technology exchange agreement between Intel and AMD, first signed in October 1981 and formally executed in February 1982. Keep that agreement in mind, because it comes back with the 386.
The famous "640 KB limit" is not a limit of the CPU. The 8088 could address 1 MB. It was IBM who placed video memory at address A0000h (that's 640 KB) and the BIOS ROM at the top of memory, leaving 640 KB of conventional memory for DOS and its programs.
The "temporary" 8086 family was now inside the machine that would define personal computing. From this point on, every new Intel chip had to run software written for the IBM PC. Compatibility was no longer a nice-to-have.
The 286: Protection Nobody Could Use
The 80286 was released on February 1, 1982, with 134,000 transistors. IBM used it in the PC/AT in 1984, running at 6 MHz.
The 286 was designed for multitasking operating systems. Its new protected mode changed what a segment register means: instead of holding a paragraph number, it holds a selector, an index into a table of descriptors. Each descriptor says where a segment starts (anywhere in 16 MB of memory), how big it is, and who is allowed to use it. The chip checks every memory access against those rules, and runs code in one of four privilege "rings."
On paper, this was fantastic. In practice, it had three problems:
- Segments were still limited to 64 KB.
- DOS programs routinely did arithmetic on segment values (adding 1 to a segment means "16 bytes further"). In protected mode, that produces a random selector and a crash.
- And the biggest one: once you switched to protected mode, you couldn't switch back.
Entering protected mode was as simple as setting one bit:
smsw ax          ; read the Machine Status Word
or   ax, 1       ; set the PE (Protection Enable) bit
lmsw ax          ; ...and there's no instruction to undo this
But DOS and the BIOS only worked in real mode. So how did the PC/AT get back? IBM built a hack into the motherboard: the program wrote a "shutdown code" into the CMOS memory, then asked the keyboard controller to pulse the CPU's reset line. The CPU rebooted, the BIOS noticed the shutdown code, and jumped back into the program, now in real mode. It worked, but it was painfully slow.
Bill Gates famously called the 286 "brain-damaged," mainly because it couldn't run several DOS programs side by side under a protected-mode operating system. Most 286 machines spent their lives running DOS in real mode, as a very fast 8086.
The A20 Gate
The 286 created another, stranger problem. On the 8086, the highest address you can form is FFFF:FFFF, which is 10FFEFh. That needs 21 bits, but the 8086 only has 20 address lines, so the top bit is lost and the address wraps around to the bottom of memory.
Some software depended on that wraparound. DOS's CP/M-style CALL 5 entry point relied on it to reach code at physical address C0h, and programs built with IBM/Microsoft Pascal used it as a space-saving trick. The 286 has 24 address lines, so it does not wrap, and those programs broke.
IBM's fix was to put a logic gate on address line 20 (A20), controlled by... a spare pin on the 8042 keyboard controller. With the gate closed, the PC/AT wraps at 1 MB like an 8086. With it open, real-mode code can reach the High Memory Area: 65,520 bytes just above 1 MB, which is where DOS=HIGH loads DOS.
This hack lived much longer than anyone expected:
A20M# pin to the CPU itself, and according to Intel's manuals, Intel only stopped supporting the A20 gate with the Haswell processors (2013). Source.
                        The 286 also had an undocumented instruction called LOADALL that could load the CPU's hidden segment caches directly, which tools like HIMEM.SYS used to reach extended memory without the slow reset trip. Hidden segment caches will come back very soon.
The 386: Intel Goes Alone
The 80386 was introduced as samples in October 1985, with mass production starting in June 1986. It had 275,000 transistors, and its chief architect was John Crawford (Pat Gelsinger, years later Intel's CEO, also worked on the project).
The 386 fixed the 286's problems one by one:
- 32-bit registers: EAX, EBX, ECX... (the "E" means extended), with AX and AL still living inside them.
- 4 GB segments: set every segment to start at 0 with a 4 GB limit and segmentation effectively disappears. This "flat model" is what DOS extenders like DOS/4GW (used by Doom) gave to C programmers.
- Paging: memory split into 4 KB pages with a two-level page table, which made real virtual memory possible.
- Virtual 8086 mode: a protected-mode task that behaves like an 8086. This is how EMM386 and Windows ran DOS programs safely, each believing it owned the machine.
- A way back: clearing the PE bit in CR0 returns to real mode. No keyboard controller needed!
mov  eax, cr0
and  al, 0FEh    ; clear PE
mov  cr0, eax    ; back in real mode, no reset required
Combining the way back with those hidden segment caches gave demo coders a favorite trick: unreal mode. You enter protected mode, load a segment register with a 4 GB limit, and return to real mode without reloading it. The CPU keeps using the cached 4 GB limit, so your real-mode program (with DOS still working!) can read and write all of memory using 32-bit offsets.
How did 32 bits fit into an instruction set designed for 16? Intel didn't add new opcodes for 32-bit operations. Instead, it added a bit to each code segment that sets the default size, plus two prefix bytes (66h for operand size and 67h for address size) that flip it for a single instruction. That's why a DOS program running in real mode on a 386 can still use EAX: the assembler simply adds a 66h prefix in front of the instruction.
The Business Decision
The 386's biggest story was not technical. Intel decided that the 386 would be single-source. As early as 1984, Intel had decided to stop cooperating with AMD, and it delayed and eventually refused to hand over the 386's technical details. AMD invoked arbitration in 1987, Intel cancelled the 1982 agreement, and the fight went on for years. AMD released its own Am386 in March 1991 (and sold one million of them by October of that year), and in 1994 the Supreme Court of California sided with AMD.
Then something happened that would have been unthinkable a few years before: IBM was not first. The Compaq Deskpro 386 shipped in September 1986, the first time a fundamental part of the IBM PC standard was moved forward by a company other than IBM.
And one more fun detail: some early 386 chips had a bug in 32-bit multiplication. Intel marked the affected chips with "16 BIT S/W ONLY", which was fine at the time because almost all software was still 16-bit anyway!
The 486: Same Instructions, New Engine
The 486 was announced at Spring Comdex on April 10, 1989, and it was the first x86 chip with more than one million transistors (about 1.2 million).
Here's the interesting part: the 486 added almost nothing to the architecture. A few instructions, like BSWAP, XADD, and CMPXCHG, and some control bits. What changed was the engine underneath:
- An 8 KB on-chip cache (16 KB on the later DX4)
- The floating-point unit integrated on the same chip
- A tightly pipelined five-stage design, where simple instructions finally finished in a single clock
Intel kept spinning variants: the 486SX (September 1991) with the FPU disabled, the clock-doubled DX2 (March 1992) that ran the core twice as fast as the motherboard, and the clock-tripled DX4 (March 1994).
For assembly programmers, the pipeline changed the rules of optimization. On the 8086, every instruction ran through microcode, and the "clever" complex instructions were often the fastest way to do things. On the 486, simple instructions became fast, and the old clever ones became the slow ones. The classic example is LOOP:
On an 8086, LOOP was the fast way to write a loop. On a 486, it's almost twice as slow as the "naive" version. If you read Michael Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book, you'll see this shift everywhere: forget the microcoded tricks, use simple instructions, and keep your data inside the cache.
And Then It Got a Name
So why isn't the next chip called the 586? Because in 1991 Intel lost a trademark dispute over the name "386," when a judge ruled that a number was generic and could not be trademarked. AMD could call its chips "386" and "486" too.
Intel hired a branding agency and came up with a name instead of a number. The Pentium (from the Greek word for "five") was introduced on March 22, 1993. A few years later it would get those famous "with MMX technology" stickers, but that's another story.
Conclusion
Hopefully, by now, you can look at an x86 instruction set reference and see it as a geological record. Every layer was laid down by a specific event:
The pattern is always the same. A chip is designed quickly, often as a stopgap, with one very practical goal in mind. Software starts to depend on its exact behavior (including its accidents). And from that moment on, every future chip has to carry that behavior forward, emulate it, or work around it with a hack.
That's the real lesson of x86 history: the architecture wasn't designed, it accumulated. And once you know the story, the quirks stop being things you memorize and start being things you can explain.
If you're curious to dig deeper, Stephen Morse's "Intel Microprocessors: 8008 to 8086" is a great read straight from the architect, and Ken Shirriff's blog has amazing die-level reverse engineering of the 8086.
And that's it for our trip from a calculator chip to the 486. If you have any suggestions for this article, you can yell at me on Twitter. Also, remember to visit the courses page to access my lectures on retro programming.
See you inside!

'Human' Is Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2026
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
14:43:52 GMT
23:43:52 KST

The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026.
The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.
'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’.
In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay.
Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.
"But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”
‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”.
Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs).
Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman.
As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’. Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April.
Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.
“AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."
Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.
“We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?
“All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you."
Lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary said: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.”
Adapted from the Cambridge University Press & Assessment website.

The Verge’s 2026 holiday gift guide for travelers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
14:36:21 UTC
23:36:21 KST

Everyone has that traveler in their life. That person who feels more at home on a 14-hour train ride than a quiet Sunday on the couch. They speak multiple languages, have a gut like a goat, and make friends wherever they go. Whether they’re your kindred spirit or the person you live vicariously through, one thing never changes: They always need new gear.
The Verge’s 2026 holiday gift guide for travelers
Globe-trotting can be a real slog, but with the right tools, hitting the open road (or air) doesn’t have to be a struggle.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
That’s what makes travelers so fun to buy for. But you don’t want to get them just anything. The key is to find that clever gift even they didn’t know they needed, and that’s where we come in. From streaming gadgets for the hotel to portable espresso makers and high-capacity chargers, these are our favorite gifts to help travelers take their next adventure to the next level.
Presented by: Delta
Give Yourself A Gift With Holiday Travel Deals. Make the most of the season with limited-time holiday offers on travel and more. However you choose to celebrate, explore more ways to save and make your next journey even more rewarding. Terms apply. Ends December 15, 2026.
Matic robot vacuum
It’s time for a smarter robovac. Thankfully, there’s the Matic, which looks less like the rambling discs that pervade the space and more like an actual robot that, well, vacuums. It doesn’t get under beds, but it also doesn’t get stuck under them, and it does a great job providing truly no-fuss cleaning thanks to its superb mapping.
One charging port, two phones. That’s not a problem with Anker’s dual-headed USB-C cable, which offers either 4 or 6 feet of length to provide game-changing versatility when you need it most.
Built for jet setters, Anker’s 100W travel adapter features a durable design, a handy LCD display to track charge percentage, and compatibility in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does have four USB inputs for all your portables, including a trio of USB-C ports.
Xreal One Pro AR glasses
Who says you can’t travel with a big screen? The Xreal One Pro feature dual micro-OLED displays to project a virtual 171-inch screen from your device of choice. A 57-degree field of view, max 120Hz refresh rate, and built-in speakers round things out, delivering portable cinematic entertainment for one.
For frequent flyers, a plain suitcase sticker may not be enough. In the age of QR codes, Pebblebee’s Link Bag Tags make a lot more sense. They’re battery-free, scannable by anyone with a phone, and offer built-in privacy with the ability to share or deny personal information.
AirPods Pro 3
Apple’s AirPods Pro are the epitome of wireless earbud refinement, with fantastic noise-canceling and transparency modes, a light and airy fit, and clear sound thanks to ear tips that seal your ears without plugging them up. The latest pair continues the quest for perfection with faster processing, more features, and better ergonomics than ever.
Oura Ring 5
Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness-tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.
Sea to Summit Lightweight Dry Bag (5-liter)
Whether you’re white-water rafting or trekking through a damp jungle, keeping your gear dry is essential. The Sea to Summit dry bag is a slick, affordable solution with clever features, including a reflective interior and a D-ring buckle to secure it to boats and bikes. The solid warranty is just a plus.
SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan
SwitchBot’s powerful, battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. You can also control it via an app, and it even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.
Wacaco Minipresso GR2 portable espresso maker
Espresso in the woods? Yes, please. The GR2’s magical mechanics make it possible, letting you turn 12 ounces of grounds into espresso without power. Its carrying case houses all the accessories needed to get that sweet shot of bean, making real coffee available virtually anywhere.
Aurzen Zip Tri-Fold Portable Mini Projector
You can’t project anything anywhere from your phone or watch (yet), but the Aurzen Zip makes that moment feel closer. Bright and durable, the foldable projector can mirror content from your phone or tablet on most flat surfaces, but fair warning: It doesn’t work with streaming services like Netflix without a $129.99 CastPlay HDMI dongle.
Theragun’s latest therapeutic cure for sore muscles is as packable as it is luxurious. The third-gen Mini includes clever features like a travel lock to keep it off during transport, guided routines, and USB-C charging. There’s even a Y2K edition for the ’90s kid in all of us.
Uniqlo Utility Backpack
Every traveler needs a go-to backpack, and the Uniqlo Utility stands out for all the little things. Its minimalist, water-resistant design hides plenty of pockets on the front and sides, plus a roomy laptop sleeve and extras, including a handy key holder in the front pocket.
For travelers hitting the road when the thermometer is rising, cooling off is essential. Nitecore’s long-lasting izzCool 10 Pro offers heat relief with a powerful fan and fillable reservoir that mists you for a refreshing respite from the sun. It even works with larger containers to double as a nighttime humidifier.
Every traveler needs quality noise-canceling for long flights, but flagship headphones are becoming increasingly spendy. Sony’s former flagship WH-1000XM4 were so good, they’ve been bestsellers through two new generations. Now the company has revamped them in the XM4C, adding minor improvements to a stone-cold classic at a nice price.
Packing light is essential for all travelers, but it’s particularly vital for those who trek long distances. This high-capacity Nitecore charger is a killer addition to any pack, with water resistance, fast charging, and a slim, lightweight design that can power your devices without weighing them down.
The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.
Tessan Surge Protector Power Strip
Every traveler’s been there. You get to the hotel or rental place, go to plug in your gear, and there’s only one outlet available. Fortunately, Tessan’s pack-friendly power strip offers all the ports, with multiple USB-C, USB-A, and AC inputs to charge everything in one place.
If you have an avid road tripper on your list, Ugreen’s four-port car charger blends slick design with serious utility. More importantly, it has a built-in retractable USB-C cable that delivers up to 60W of power and keeps things tidy.
For the fastidious person on your list who can’t stop polishing their camera, tablet, or other delicate piece of equipment, there’s the lightweight Magic Wrap. The foldable, plush fabric sticks to itself, with no zippers, edges, or even magnets to scuff or scratch your most precious gear.
For on-the-go creators, it’s all about capturing the moment in the highest video quality possible. Insta360’s Luna Pro steadycam offers plenty of features to get the job done right, including 4K vertical video, swift file transfers, four hours of battery life, and a detachable touchscreen that doubles as a remote.
Buying your loved one a pair of shoes is tougher than you might think, but a gift card to The Walking Company is a step in the right direction. The store offers a wide variety of ultra-comfortable kicks, boots, sandals, and even orthotics, along with a shoe finder to help them find the right fit.
Retroid Pocket 5 Handheld
Retroid has had its stumbles, but the Pocket 5 is a hit, making it a great gift for the globe-trotting gamer. Chicken and Stuffing Casserole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

If my childhood could be summed up in one dinner, this Chicken and Stuffing Casserole would be it. It was the meal my mom could make for our family of five that guaranteed instant happiness. With a box of stuffing mix and just 15 minutes of prep, you get tender, juicy chicken, a velvety homemade sauce, and a crispy, golden stuffing on top, all for just $1.28 a serving. I’ll happily make this easy, incredibly comforting casserole any time of year, so if I spot a good deal on stuffing mix around Thanksgiving, I always pick up a box to keep in the pantry for later!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
A Creamy Chicken Bake With a Buttery Stuffing Top
My mom is an incredible home chef, and like any smart, busy parent, she relied on shortcuts, such as cream of chicken soup, to make dinners like this casserole easier. However, for my version, I wanted a gravy I could season myself. Making the gravy in the same skillet I use to sear the chicken breasts means the chicken broth picks up all those flavorful browned bits. The butter and flour give the gravy enough body to coat the chicken, milk makes it creamy, and a little onion and garlic powder season it without any extra chopping.
I always make stuffing from scratch for the holidays, but I like to keep a box of chicken-flavored stuffing mix in the cupboard for dinners like this. The bread is already cut and seasoned, and it soaks up the broth right in the baking dish so it stays tender underneath. I still dot the top with pats of butter so the stuffing bakes up golden and crisp (because my mom said you can’t skip this step!). Give me a corner piece with extra-crisp stuffing and plenty of gravy to scoop up with the chicken, and I’m happy. 😋 My mom actually tried my take on her chicken and stuffing casserole while visiting and told me she liked it even better than hers. That’s the highest praise to me because I’m her biggest fan!
Recipe Success Tips
- Let the chicken sit before you flip it. I pat the 1-inch cubes dry, then give them 3 minutes undisturbed over medium-high heat. That uninterrupted contact with the hot skillet helps the underside brown and develop lots of flavor. If the pieces don’t fit in a single layer, I recommend you work in batches so trapped moisture doesn’t steam the chicken.
- Drain the chicken on fresh paper towels. This helps soak up excess oil and juices that could otherwise thin the gravy in the baking dish.
- Let the broth thicken before adding the milk. When you’re making the gravy, turn the heat down to medium and whisk the butter and flour for about 2 minutes so the roux can cook without scorching. Then whisk in the first cup of broth slowly to keep it smooth. I always give it about 3 minutes to thicken before adding the milk. Seeing the broth thicken at this stage is how I know the roux is doing its job.
- Get the broth into the corners. Pour the remaining cup of broth evenly over the dry stuffing so you don’t end up with hard, dry patches around the edges. I also dot the top with some butter for extra flavor and browning. If you want to save a little money, you can skip those pats of butter on top if needed (it’ll still turn out delicious, just a little less browned!)
- Wait before scooping. I recommend letting the casserole cool for at least 10 minutes after it comes out of the oven. If the chicken isn’t drained off well, it’ll release liquid as it cooks, which needs to be absorbed back into the dish. The sauce will also thicken during the rest, but you can still enjoy it right away if you can’t wait. Just know the sauce will be a little thinner.
Short on Time?
Boxed stuffing already gives this casserole a head start, but if I need to get it into the oven a little sooner, I’ll check the fridge and pantry first. Leftover cooked chicken or condensed soup can save me a step and put something I already have to good use:
- Use condensed soup. Replace the gravy with two small cans or one family-size can of condensed soup. My mom uses cream of chicken, and our homemade condensed soup substitutes work here too. Keep the cup of broth that goes over the stuffing.
- Use rotisserie chicken. Pull the cooked meat off the bones and spread it in the baking dish in place of the seared chicken. That saves you the chopping and searing. Any shredded chicken you’ve meal prepped will work here, too.
how to make Chicken and Stuffing Casserole step-by-step photos
Gather all your ingredients: Preheat the oven to 350°F and coat a 9×9-inch casserole dish with nonstick cooking spray. I also like to measure the chicken broth into two 1-cup portions now, so I have one ready for the gravy and one for the stuffing.
Season the chicken: Cut 2 lbs. chicken breasts into 1-inch cubes and pat them dry with paper towels. Sprinkle evenly with ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp black pepper. Drying the surface helps the chicken brown better when it hits the hot skillet.
Sear the chicken: Heat 1 Tbsp vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers, add the chicken in a single layer. You should hear it sizzle as it goes in. Work in batches if needed. Leave the chicken undisturbed for 3 minutes to brown on the underside. Flip the pieces and cook for another 3 minutes, then transfer them to a plate lined with fresh paper towels to catch any excess oil and juices.
Make the roux: Reduce the heat to medium and melt 4 Tbsp butter in the same skillet. Sprinkle in ½ cup flour and whisk constantly for about 2 minutes. The flour and butter should come together into a smooth paste.
Add the broth: Now slowly pour in 1 cup chicken broth, whisking as you go to keep the mixture smooth and loosen the browned bits from the skillet. Keep whisking for about 3 minutes, until the broth has visibly thickened.
Finish the gravy: Whisk in 1 cup milk, the remaining ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp onion powder, and ½ tsp garlic powder.
Keep whisking for about 3 minutes, until the gravy is smooth and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Turn off the heat.
Layer the chicken in the dish: Spread the seared chicken in an even layer across the bottom of the prepared casserole dish so each scoop gets some chicken.
Cover the chicken with gravy: Spoon the gravy over the chicken and use the back of the spoon to spread it all the way to the edges.
Add the stuffing topping: Scatter one 6 oz. box of dry chicken-flavored stuffing mix evenly over the gravy.
Pour over the broth: Slowly pour the remaining 1 cup chicken broth over the entire surface, including the corners, so there are no dry patches.
Add the butter: Cut the remaining 2 Tbsp butter into small cubes and dot them across the top for a buttery finish.
Bake and let it rest: Bake uncovered for about 30 minutes, until the stuffing is golden brown and the center of the casserole and the larger pieces of chicken near the center reach 165°F. Let it rest for 10 minutes before scooping so the gravy has a chance to settle. Serve and enjoy!
What to Serve with Chicken and Stuffing Casserole
I like a little crunch on the side when dinner comes with this much gravy. Our sautéed green beans are crisp and garlicky, and you can make them on the stovetop while the casserole bakes. If you’ve already got a bag of broccoli in the freezer, oven-roasted frozen broccoli is an inexpensive side with no chopping, and a simple side salad with a tangy vinaigrette helps balance the rich gravy. Or if I’m feeding a few extra people, I’ll sometimes add a batch of homemade biscuits to help stretch the meal further. Split one open and use it to mop up the gravy left on your plate!
Storage & Reheating
Divide leftovers into shallow, airtight containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. They’ll keep in the fridge for 3-4 days. Keep in mind the topping can soften, and the sauce will thicken in storage.
Reheating
Warm refrigerated portions in an oven-safe dish at 350°F until the center reaches 165°F. Cover loosely with foil to keep the chicken and gravy from drying out, then uncover for the last few minutes to help crisp up the stuffing. You can also microwave a single portion in short bursts, though the topping will be softer.
Freezing
I prefer to freeze individual portions in airtight, freezer-safe containers (for up to 3 months). Thaw overnight in the fridge, then reheat at 350°F as directed above. The stuffing will soften a little after freezing, so reheating it in the oven is worth the extra time if you like a crisp top.
Try These Easy Chicken Casseroles Next!
- For another creamy chicken bake with a golden topping, I’d make our Chicken Cobbler. The cheddar biscuit topping bakes right over the chicken and vegetables, and dinner’s ready in 50 minutes.
- Our Chicken and Rice Casserole starts the same way, with chicken seared in a skillet and a homemade sauce made in that same pan. Rice, broccoli, and cheddar make it a full meal for $1.27 per serving!
- If the buttery topping is your favorite part, try our Million Dollar Chicken Casserole. It has tender chicken and mushrooms in a creamy homemade sauce, with buttery cracker crumbs on top.

Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
14:03:37 UTC
23:03:37 KST

Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- American Heart Association
- Summary:
- A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.
- Share:
Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.
The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.
Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.
Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health
The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.
Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.
A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).
However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.
Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.
"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."
FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events
To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.
The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.
Several differences stood out in the analysis:
- Cardiac arrest: Reports involving caffeine and stimulant products were approximately 11 times more likely to mention cardiac arrest than reports involving products without these ingredients.
- Heart attacks: Heart attacks appeared about 4.5 times more frequently in reports associated with energy drinks and stimulant supplements.
- Abnormal heart rhythms: Reports involving stimulant products were roughly four times more likely to include ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal rhythm in the heart's lower pumping chambers) or heart palpitations.
- Other cardiovascular symptoms: The researchers also identified higher reporting frequencies for rapid heart rate (nearly 3 times more often), chest pain (2.71 times more often) and fainting (about 2 times more often).
- Young adults: Approximately 45% of cardiovascular event reports involving caffeine and stimulant products concerned adults between ages 18 and 34.
- Men and women: Comparable patterns appeared in reports submitted for both sexes.
These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.
"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.
Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable
One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.
Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.
How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.
These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.
Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?
Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.
"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."
Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.
Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.
How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports
The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.
Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.
Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).
Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.
The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.
Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.
Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.
Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by American Heart Association. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
14:03:07 UTC
23:03:07 KST

Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.
Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a new social simulator powered by AI.
The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.
Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”
I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow. The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency, which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.”
Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.
Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.
Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”
“We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.
“We’re not making slop.”
MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.
“It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?
Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”
Update, November 18th: Added context about Artificial Agency.

Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
13:18:02 UTC
22:18:02 KST

Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy
On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford.
Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine", and the post reached the front page of Hacker News. In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting.
What Quad9 is, and why it matters
A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9.
Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual:
- It is a non-profit. It was founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House, and moved its legal seat to Zürich in 2021, hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises."
- Security filtering is its main purpose. Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims 670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries.
- It keeps no user records. Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point.
Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France Télévisions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield. Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out, when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working."
How France got here
The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport
The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code. It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021, the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom. L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement).
That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026, Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport, which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous."
The cases: from ISPs to everyone
The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened:
The ruling itself
The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter:
- The €580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for €10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is €580,000 a day. The judge set €1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14.
- The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France.
- Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty."
€1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about €24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says: "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases."
Why Quad9 can't just comply
Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work.
1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver.
2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case, Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak: "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia.
3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025, compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, … an existential threat."
That leaves leaving.
Why DNS blocking doesn't work
The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want.
It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing.
It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers. Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert."
It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754, the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering: "Le DNS n'a pas été conçu pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.)
It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it.
Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024. A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers". The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe, which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider.
Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events."
What France loses
Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security.
- French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data. As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web."
- Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix.
- The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver.
- France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain.
It's not just France
Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe.
- Belgium: DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and OpenDNS left Belgium in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court upheld the core of the order, with fines of €100,000 per match day capped at €20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline.
- Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare €14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes."
- Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses.
- Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare.
- The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region."
That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave.
The counter-arguments
The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers.
"Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement.
"Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy.
"Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie.
"The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator.
What you can do
If you use Quad9 in France, check whether you do at on.quad9.net, and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first.
If you're in France or the EU, do what John Todd asked: write something long-form, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage."
If you work on infrastructure, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network.
If you can afford it, Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal.
The canary
Quad9 put it this way: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues.
The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.
