Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline.
- Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare €14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes."
- Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses.
- Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare.
- The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region."
That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave.
The counter-arguments
The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers.
"Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement.
"Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy.
"Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie.
"The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator.
What you can do
If you use Quad9 in France, check whether you do at on.quad9.net, and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first.
If you're in France or the EU, do what John Todd asked: write something long-form, ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage."
If you work on infrastructure, push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network.
If you can afford it, Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal.
The canary
Quad9 put it this way: "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues.
The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first.

Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
13:01:05 UTC
22:01:05 KST

Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.
Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.
“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.
The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t —keep financing neoclouds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it.
And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter, which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter.
But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said.
Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking. She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion.
Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said.
“There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress said to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call.
She pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before.
Kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future.
“The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.”
One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products. Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over.

NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
12:03:36 UTC
21:03:36 KST

After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
It’s taken Voyager 1 almost 50 years to journey farther from Earth than light can travel in 24 hours.
It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 mph.
The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning, and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.
Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.
Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.
Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.
“The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”
Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.
Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.
The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.
Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document.
“In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”
The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.
Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.
Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.
Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.
Currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

I had AI read my entire field, Theoretical Astrophysics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
11:45:02 UTC
20:45:02 KST

I had AI read my entire field.
158,059 papers and 554,670 citations. Every paper with full text screened, 659 of the most important recomputed and checked, and every verified error followed through the papers that cite it. This is the map, and what it says about whether science corrects itself.
Errors that nobody fixed
I spent five years in this field doing my PhD at Caltech, and a few months of that went to errors in the literature that were already known. The equations my code was built on came from Bishop, Gómez, Lehner, Maharaj & Winicour, “High-powered gravitational news” (1997), the paper the subfield's characteristic codes descend from. People knew it had mistakes. The fixes were scattered through some 10,000 lines of intersecting email threads that contradicted each other, and the paper itself was never corrected. The best I could do was correct the record in my own papers: an appendix setting out the full set of equations, made consistent, and a parenthetical “with a sign error in s3 corrected” for anyone reading closely.
That is the limit of human literature review. Mine was not deep: my three thesis papers cite fewer than a hundred papers between them, in a field of tens of thousands. Nobody re-derives every equation they cite, referees check one paper once, and nobody is paid to go back and fix the original. So every student who builds on a broken paper pays the same tax, one at a time, and the correction lives in somebody's inbox. A machine can read the whole field, recompute it, and follow each error to every paper that copied it. So I had one do it. It found errors in my own papers too.
Every dot is a paper
Height is time: the 1960s at the bottom, this year at the top. Each faint line is a citation. The bright dots are the papers everything else leans on, ranked the way Google ranked the early web.
The seed is TAPIR, Caltech's theoretical astrophysics group, where I did my PhD: 4,093 papers by its 326 members since 2004. Add every paper they cite and every paper that cites them and you get 158,059 papers joined by 554,670 citations. The 49,301 drawn here are the ones tied to TAPIR at least three times over.
Watch it grow
The map holds 499 papers from the 1970s, 2,035 from the 1990s and 18,976 from the 2010s. The old layers are the survivors, the papers people working today still cite. Everything else from 1975 has already been forgotten, right or wrong.
Most of what this field knows was written in the last twenty years, by people who are still around to answer email. Hold that thought.
A subfield is a column
Nobody told the layout what numerical relativity is. Papers that cite each other pull together, so a subfield shows up as a column: the same few dozen people writing about the same problem year after year, each layer standing on the last.
There are 32 columns, from fast radio bursts to the Milky Way's halo.
Numerical relativity
Solving Einstein's equations on a computer until two black holes merge. 278 papers in this column, 71 of them TAPIR's, busiest in 2010.
Every subfield has a page: the questions it is organised around and whether each is open, contested or settled, who wrote the central papers and where, how fast it publishes, and which of its errors we traced.
Each open question also carries a flag for what today's AI could do about it. Of 155, a model judged 8 answerable now from data and codes that already exist, 119 ones AI would speed up, and 28 stuck waiting on a telescope or a detector.
Every paper gets screened
Reading a paper carefully costs a few dollars of model time. Screening one costs nothing, so every paper I could get the full text of got screened: 50,269 papers, 421 million words, checked for the fingerprints of the worst kinds of trouble. That covers 76% of the papers drawn here. Nothing before 1991 is on arXiv and journal-only papers aren't open, so the rest got only the checks that run on a database record. (Gold marks TAPIR's own papers.)
- Paper-mill language: none.
- Chatbot residue and hidden instructions to AI reviewers: none.
- Text shared between papers with no author in common: 43 pairs in 34,286 papers, led by successive survey catalogues and data releases. The rest are queued for a human look.
- Retractions: 13 among 184,733 papers with a DOI. None is TAPIR's.
- TODO and FIXME notes shipped to arXiv: 62 papers.
Astrophysics is relatively clean. Whatever is wrong with this literature, it isn't fraud. The one needle that moves is vocabulary: “delve”, “crucial” and friends are 2.5 times as common in 2025 as in 2016.
The 200 that matter get checked line by line
Citations are brutally unequal, and a few hundred papers carry the field. So the 200 most-cited TAPIR papers of 2006–2019 (gold) each got their own AI reviewer with the LaTeX source, tools to run its own calculations, and orders to recompute everything it could: re-derive the equations, test the limits, rebuild the numbers from the paper's own tables. It worked blind, with no access to errata or later papers.
A flag is not a finding. Only what a second reviewer upholds is called an error here.
Thirteen fixed, fifty-six through
About 136 of the 200 were revised between the first preprint and the published paper, so we read those first preprints the same way. 13 verified errors were in the preprint and gone from the journal version, fixed by the referee or by the authors on a second look (purple).
56 went through review and into the journal (gold). On this evidence peer review removes about one error in five. At least two of the thirteen were copied by later papers anyway, from the stale preprint.
A factor of four, 2005–2014
Smith, Kamionkowski & Cooray convert the gravitational waves left over from inflation into an energy density a detector could see. Two factors of one half went missing, so the answer is four times too big: a 6 in the denominator where the textbook has 24. This one was double-checked. The paper's numbers in the paper's formula reproduce its result; the same numbers in the standard formula give a quarter of it.
Watch the years run. Red papers copied the factor of four. The green one said it was wrong, in 2008. The copying carried on until 2014: six copies, one objection.
Five copies for every criticism
Then we cast the net wider. The same recompute-and-verify check, run on 459 more still-cited papers across the map, mostly highly cited ones that a cheaper first read had flagged, upheld 816 more errors. That makes 872 in 433 papers. 159 of them were copied, wrong value and all, into at least one later paper. Counting papers:
367 papers copied an error. 68 criticised one.
Only 47 of the 872 were ever criticised in print, and 21 of those kept being copied afterwards, by 51 more papers. These are floors: we read only the citing papers whose text we hold.
And 872 is a floor for the field too. Only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map got the thorough treatment so far. Scaled up from the papers that did, the likely number of undetected errors in this field's papers cited 100 or more times is about 34,000 (25,000–48,000). How that number is reached →
Half are still being copied 7 years later
How effective is peer review and publishing at detecting and expunging errors from the literature? We can actually measure it.
Share of copied errors still being copied, by years since the paper appeared. Band: 95% interval. 33 errors are old enough to be observed at year 10.
The curve is still at 52% at year 7 and crosses one half at year 8; at year 10 it is at 39%. Counting papers that lean on the affected result without showing which value they used, it crosses at year 9. The errors we traced most thoroughly last longer, crossing at year 10: a shallower search simply finds fewer late copies.
What finally stops an error? Of the 56 errors in the 200 papers read most closely, 52 are still in the latest arXiv version, where a fix is free. Of the 200 papers read most closely, the database records an erratum for 2. And of the 87 errors that did die out, 67 were never criticised by anyone. They faded when the subfield moved on, which retires right answers and wrong ones at the same rate.
4% of the papers that matter, so far
Every paper with open full text was screened and skimmed. The expensive check, the one that recomputes, has reached 659 papers, starting with the most cited. Each bar is the papers on the map with that many citations, filled by how far they have been read.
A field outgrows its errors. It rarely corrects them.
All of this would cost about $2,720 in model time bought at list price, roughly $3 per verified error. In practice it ran within a Claude Max subscription. The whole project, this field and the others, took about 4.9 billion tokens and about 44 hours of my time over 41 days. It is one field, read by a first-generation method, with limits spelled out on the method page. And it is not finished: the deep check has reached only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map, most cited first. The rest of the queue is a budget decision, and so is the next field.
Errors were found by one AI session and re-derived by a second, independent one, and each was confirmed in the version the journal published. Five were also double-checked step by step against the source. No person has checked any of them. As a test, 40 drawn at random went to a third session that saw only the paper and the passage: it found 33 of the 40 wrong, so some named here will not survive scrutiny. If we have your paper wrong, say so and we will fix it and say that we did.

India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed US robotics companies the data they need
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.
The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups, including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI, are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.
Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.
Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.
“Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said.
Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers.
The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.
That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.
Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups, including Human Archive and BuildAI, tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes.
Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.
Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said.

Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18

20:16:53 KST

Suno has introduced image and video generation in its latest effort to expand beyond being an AI music platform. The new feature, called “Visuals,” allows users to turn Suno songs into AI-generated video clips that automatically lipsync to lyrics, or make images via prompt descriptions that can be used as thumbnails and album artwork.
Suno now lets you make AI videos for your AI music
The new Visuals feature generates images and 15-second videos that automatically sync with Suno songs.
Visuals is available on web, iOS, and Android. The exact layout differs across Suno’s desktop and mobile interfaces, but users will find a new Visuals tab under Create mode on each version. Web users can also access Visuals by selecting the three dot menu on a song in their library. From there, users can select which section of the track to use, up to a maximum of 15 seconds, and select a reference image to build the generated video clip.
There are three options available for the starting image reference: selecting one of the original character presets provided by Suno, uploading your own photo or artwork, or generating the image directly on Suno using descriptive prompts. The image generation capabilities also allow users to select specific aspect ratios, optimizing results for landscape or portrait modes and online platforms.
For video generation, users can select whether the reference image is used as the start or end frame, making it easier to edit the 15-second clips together. There’s a toggle to automatically lipsync vocals to the generated video, and tools for adjusting aspect ratio and clip length. Visuals also includes a dedicated video editing timeline for assembling clips into longer videos, and adding customizable song lyric text.
The H3 Move AI model is being used to power Visuals, based on H3 from MiniMax. Suno says the AI has been “optimized for our community including adding additional protections and safeguards,” which include a “suite of new text and visual filters” designed to block people from using or generating the likeness of specific artists, public figures, copyrighted works and IP. Visuals also uses its own “Visuals credits” to generate videos and images, which are distinct from the song credits used to make AI music, meaning Suno users will have additional expenses to pay in order to use this new feature.
The Visuals launch follows Suno introducing a Speech feature in October for generating spoken words and voiceovers. Adding video capabilities is another attempt to diversify the platform after Suno’s music generator attracted a number of high-profile lawsuits, though it seems some users would rather the company focus on improving those song-generating capabilities. In the YouTube video for the Visuals launch, one user says “FIX AUDIO BEFORE ADDING CRAP NOBODY ASKED FOR” — a sentiment that other commenters are echoing.

Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
11:04:20 UTC
20:04:20 KST

How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade.
Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
Thirteen years later, Rockstar has crafted a worthy successor to GTA V and the new standard-bearer for open-world games.
That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen.
Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait.
At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence.
Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction. It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal.
Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two.
What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet.
To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers.
The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play.
There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games.
All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops.
Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson.
But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time.
It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t.
Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive.
Despite spending more than 70 hours in the world, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience
I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out.
You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience.
Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time.
It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine.
Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI.
To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI.
For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it.
Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite.
Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries, is working to break that dominance.
Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market.
“The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology.
Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells.
The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd.
The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage. It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S.
“We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.”
Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements.
The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way.
Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a by-product.
But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high-quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen.
The company says both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further.
The new factory, Boyd said, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.”

Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
Unknown

Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth (space.com) 73
			
		 	
				NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. "Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal -- so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky," reports Space.com. From the report:  But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.
[...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
10:58:33 UTC
19:58:33 KST

Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t just the biggest GTA game to date; it’s also the most romantic. Though the series is well known for its sordid assortment of criminal leads, GTA VI switches things up by starring a pair of thieves who also happen to fall in love after meeting while stealing a car. It’s still an open-world action game full of chaos and mayhem. But many players will also be attempting to nurture the budding relationship in between heists. The sprawling game is designed to support both audiences.
‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet
Producer and head of development Rob Nelson explains the studio’s approach on Grand Theft Auto VI.
“It’s a risk,” explains Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North. “It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”
Despite the couple — named Jason and Lucia — being so central to the GTA VI experience, the development of the game didn’t start with characters or story. It began with a place. Nelson says that “pretty quickly” the team settled on placing the game in Leonida, the GTA universe’s version of Florida and the setting of one of the series’ most iconic games, Vice City on the PS2. In 2015, a small group of developers from Rockstar headed to Florida to get a sense of the place and set the groundwork for what would go on to become GTA VI.
“We just went around to feel it out,” explains Nelson. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate. And then the map team starts building our version of that and talking very loosely and very broadly about what types of people we want to include and what types of places.”
The team realized they wanted to tell a story that would pull players through the various locations they were creating. And the best way to do that was to have characters who were relatively small-time criminals. They would start near the bottom of the criminal underworld and work their way up, traversing Leonida’s various locations, culminating in the splashy Vice City.
At the same time, the developers also wanted to do something different with the character-switching mechanic from GTA V, which let players swap between three unique criminals, each with very different stories and motivations. For GTA VI, a couple working together to steal enough money to escape the outlaw life fit both of these ideas perfectly. But it also presented some new challenges.
“Could we make a relationship work?” Nelson remembers thinking. “It’d be very different from three characters living separate lives that come together for narrative purposes and then split. These two are going to need to be together all the time and that’s going to be a challenge. It felt really wrong to have these people that are supposedly together only be together when we’re giving you scripted content.”
While GTA V is the obvious reference point, the new GTA also builds off of Rockstar’s 2018 Western Red Dead Redemption 2. That game was notable in particular for giving players more ways to interact with the world: You could talk to any NPC, sit around a campfire while drinking coffee or playing cards, or grow out your beard for a new look.
GTA VI expands this in ways that are designed to reinforce the relationship aspect of the experience. For instance, not only can you drink coffee, but you can also make a cup and hand it to your partner. The two can spend time together sitting on the couch watching TV, or go out to a club and dance. There’s even a button dedicated exclusively to making Jason and Lucia hold hands when they’re together.
“If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”
Nelson notes that when the team implemented the hand-holding feature, it was a revelatory moment for showing how the story and gameplay could connect. “When we got that mechanic in — and it’s not just a toggle, it’s an active thing that you have to commit to and hold — it was a really profound thing,” he says.
But it’s also a careful balancing act. While RDR2 was a widely praised game, it also received criticism for its slow pace, which was due in large part to all of the small mechanical details. These added animations and button prompts that gave texture to the world but could also lead to a plodding pace. That would be a much bigger problem in a game like GTA, which is built around action. Nelson says that he can be “freakishly obsessive” about these kinds of details, but he and the team had to learn to let go when realism got in the way of the game itself.
“Maybe you don’t have to carry around antifreeze in your trunk so that if your engine starts smoking you can top it up,” he says. “Certain things fall by the wayside in developing the game, where it’s like, we don’t need this. But other things, like eating food, it was important for us. You want to feel like you are this person existing in this world to a degree. That felt like it was additive. I love walking down the street with a beer and a cigarette and switching between the two, feeling like a dude. If it’s additive, and it makes you laugh, we include it.”
This also led the team down some unexpected paths. For instance, GTA VI is the first game in the series with functioning bedsheets. In past titles, and in basically every other video game, characters simply lay on top of a bed to go to sleep. That’s because it’s a lot of effort to both animate a character going under the covers as well as rig the sheets so that characters can interact with them in a way that looks and feels natural. The payoff isn’t worth it. But in the context of GTA VI, where the characters hide out together in everything from dingy motel rooms to fancy hotels, it made sense to actually build it.
“Because you’re sharing a living space, and you come in and see your partner sleeping at 3AM, it’s weird to see them laying on the top of the bed all the time,” Nelson says. “Nobody does that. It’s a lot of work to rig the covers on all of the different beds and have them both be able to get in and out of it and be able to be under the covers together.”
Bedsheets, holding hands, cups of coffee — they’re seemingly small details in a world as large as Grand Theft Auto VI, one that encourages players to run wild. But they’re also indicative of the approach Rockstar took with this latest GTA and how the studio attempted to make every element work in concert, even if it required a lot of extra work, like the bed covers. “That’s an example of something that was a lot of work, but it was worth it.”

Voyager 1 hits one light day from Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
10:38:30 UTC
19:38:30 KST

On Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 2:16:07 a.m. PST, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will be 16.094 billion miles (25.902 billion kilometers) away from Earth — or, the distance light travels in 24 hours, also known as one light-day.
Voyager 1 will be the first human-made object to reach this distance from Earth, adding to a long list of historic firsts for the mission. Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to ever operate outside the heliosphere, or the protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields generated by the Sun.
Use their cosmic odometers below to follow the progress of Voyager 1 and 2.
‘Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day’
Help celebrate Voyager 1's epic milestone — NASA invites everyone in the world to create a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset on Tuesday, Nov. 17, by flashing a message to the spacecraft with phones, flashlights, and even entire buildings. See how to join in!
What Is a Light-Day?
The milestone Voyager 1 will reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, is about distance, not time. And it's very, very far — more than 16 billion miles, during a journey that's taken 49+ years, from our cosmic neighborhood out to interstellar space. Learn all about it.
If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response.
Use Eyes on the Solar System, NASA's 3D interactive visualization tool, to see where Voyager 1 is at this moment. Or, use the controls to see where it's going, or anywhere that it's already been since 1977, on its journey from Earth, past Jupiter and Saturn, to interstellar space.
NASA/JPL-Caltech
Voyager 2 — Current Position Visualization
Use Eyes on the Solar System, NASA's 3D interactive visualization tool, to see where Voyager 2 is — right now. Or, use the controls to see where it's going, or anywhere that it's already been since it launched in 1977, left Earth for its Grand Tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, then headed for interstellar space.

Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
09:29:32 UTC
18:29:32 KST

TL;DR – We introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), reasoning models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. Its value scores candidate predictions without requiring an external verifier, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a natural signal for stopping. With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs achieve 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model. On N-Queens and Graph Coloring, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy.
Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.
Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection.
Score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state and the initial board . Lower means better compatibility.
Refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction.
Stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion.
Select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy.
Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from.
Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going.
EBR acts like stochastic gradient descent and can capture many different solutions. Coverage captures the share of each input's distinct valid solutions that 20 samples find.
@misc{chen2026energybasedreasoners,
  title         = {Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model},
  author        = {Chen, William Xingxu and Gladstone, Alexi and Li, Zeyu Michael and Ji, Heng and Du, Yilun},
  year          = {2026},
  eprint        = {2611.08977},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  primaryClass  = {cs.LG},
  url           = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08977}
}

Australia's full national topographic library at your fingertips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
07:10:46 UTC
16:10:46 KST

News
Australia’s full national topographic library at your fingertips
Published:31 March 2026
Geoscience Australia has completed the nationwide release of its AUSTopo 1:250,000 digital topographic map series, putting authoritative, up‑to‑date topographic coverage of the entire country just a click away. Free to download, easy to print, and ready to use offline on mobile devices.
Available through Geoscience Australia’s online map application, the series provides comprehensive national coverage at a scale where 1 centimetre on the map equals 2.5 kilometres on the ground.
Branch Head of Geoscience Australia’s National Location Information Branch, Lisa Bush, said
‘This is Australia’s national topographic library, modernised and in your pocket. Users can browse the full catalogue, download the latest and previous editions, print when needed, or add maps to a tablet or phone for offline use - all at no cost.’
What’s new
- Latest data, nationwide: Since 2023, over 500 maps in the series have been updated, with ongoing improvements to keep data current.
- Open and accessible: Maps are free to download via the dashboard and licensed for reuse under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0.
- Previous editions preserved: Users can access both the latest releases and historical editions for comparison, teaching, and research.
Why it matters
As Australia’s national mapping agency, Geoscience Australia is committed to delivering reliable, authoritative topographic information that is easy to access and use. The AUSTopo series builds on over a century of mapping expertise, now delivered through a contemporary digital experience that supports:
- Policy, planning and engineering decisions that require consistent, nationwide context.
- Emergency management planning, exercises and briefings.
- Environmental assessment and land management.
- Transport, logistics and regional infrastructure planning.
- Teaching, research and fieldwork across schools and universities.
- Recreation and travel, including offline use on mobile devices for planning and navigation support.
Want to add maps to your device for offline use?
Whether you’re planning a regional project or heading into the field, it’s easy to take AUSTopo with you:
- Open the dashboard and select a map sheet.
- Download the PDF (latest edition or a previous release).
- On iPad/iPhone: open the file and Save to Files or Open in Books for offline viewing.
- On Android: save to your device and open with your preferred PDF or mapping app.
- Printing: PDFs are print‑ready for home, office supply stores, or commercial print shops.

Hacker Pleads Guilty to Leak of Grand Theft Auto VI Footage (therecord.media) 39
			
		 	
				Artion Kurtaj, the British hacker responsible for leaking early footage of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022, pleaded guilty Monday to six offenses stemming from cyberattacks against Rockstar Games, Uber and Revolut. The 21-year-old, who was previously deemed unfit to stand trial due to severe autism, carried out the hacking spree "using a mobile phone and an Amazon Fire Stick connected to a hotel room television," reports The Record, "despite bail restrictions limiting his access to the internet." From the report:  Now 21, he admitted six offenses at Woolwich Crown Court on Monday, four under the Computer Misuse Act, one of fraud and one of possession of a mobile phone in prison, and is due to be sentenced next week. Kurtaj "used sophisticated hacking techniques to carry out a sustained campaign of cyberattacks, causing serious disruption to major international business and putting sensitive information at risk," said specialist prosecutor Robert Hutchinson.
"The defendant was involved in a hacking group responsible for attacks which caused millions of dollars in losses. His offending was calculated and, even after being charged with serious offenses, he continued to target organizations, demonstrating a persistent disregard for the harm he was causing and the law. This was an exceptionally complex and challenging case, but despite his efforts to conceal his identity online, our specialist prosecutors were able to work closely with the City of London Police and international law enforcement partners to build a strong case that exposed his actions and resulted in his guilty pleas," said Hutchinson.

AI is killing All About Berlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
06:47:26 UTC
15:47:26 KST

AI is killing All About Berlin
Posted on
Psst! There is an update to this post.
This is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews.
When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic.
It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future.
It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities.
If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went.
This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it.
It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads.
I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.
This was also discussed on Mastodon, Hacker News, LinkedIn and Twitter. If you are affected, reach out. Let me know how you are doing. You are not going through this alone.
Mentions:
Similar stories:
- StackOverflow’s traffic down 99% from its peak
- How Google and AI are Killing Travel Blogs Like Mine
- What’s happening with Liliputing?

Why Fibonacci?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
05:35:02 UTC
14:35:02 KST

I was inspired to create my first Fibonacci LED piece after seeing this video by Jim Bumgardner in 2015. I credit him for starting my Fibonacci obsession.
Fast forward to 2026. I’ve made dozens of Fibonacci designs. Recently, I saw this brilliant post by Nick Pisarro explaining the use of the golden angle in creating his beautiful Halo Pixel. It got me thinking about how to explain the techniques I use.
Every Fibonacci board I make, from the tiny One Inch Fibonacci64 to the Fibonacci1024, puts its LEDs on a Fermat spiral, the same pattern as the seeds in a sunflower. It’s different from the “Fibonacci spiral” drawn from squares, which is a single curve. The Fibonacci section shows where the name comes from.
The rules
Start at the center. Then repeat:
- Step out a little.
- Add an LED.
- Turn 137.508°.
Every LED on every¹ Fibonacci board is placed by those rules. LED n sits n × 137.508° around from the first, and about √n out from the center. The next two sections explain those two numbers.
¹ There are exceptions to the √n rule, of course, like Fibonacci64 Flower and Fibonacci256 Expanding.
The golden angle
Any simple fraction of a turn makes spokes. At 90° (a quarter turn), every 4th LED lands on the same line. 120° makes 3 spokes, and 135° (3/8 of a turn) makes 8.
At 137° the LEDs still bunch into arms with gaps between them. 137.5° is exactly 55/144 of a turn, so the edge starts to crowd. It takes about 400 LEDs for that to show, though. With 256, 137.5° scores the same as the golden angle.
The golden angle, 360° ÷ φ² ≈ 137.508°, can’t be written as a fraction at all, so the LEDs never line up. The animation measures how close the two nearest of 600 LEDs get, as a percentage of the spacing in a perfect honeycomb.
The golden angle’s digits never end, but a board only needs a few of them. Each extra digit buys a lot more LEDs before arms start to show:
Two digits are plenty for the Fibonacci1024.
² The seventh digit actually makes things worse: 137.5077641° is just as far from the golden angle as 137.507764°, but on the other side.
The golden angle isn’t the only angle that scores well, though. Other “noble” angles, like 99.5°, come close. The golden angle is the one that’s furthest from every fraction.
Angles past 180° just mirror these: 222.492° (360° − 137.508°) makes the same spiral, flipped. That’s why you’ll sometimes see the golden angle given as about 222.5°.
The √n radius
With the angle set, the next question is the radius: how far from the center each LED sits. Each cell in the animation is the part of the board that’s closer to its LED than to any other.
If every step out is the same size, the edge has far more room than the middle but gets no more LEDs, so the LEDs end up crowded together in the middle and far apart at the edge. The biggest cell is about 150 times the size of the smallest.
A disc’s area grows with the square of its radius, so the steps out have to shrink as you go. Putting LED n at a distance of √n from the center gives every LED the same share of the board, and neighboring LEDs end up evenly spaced. The biggest cell is then only 1.3 times the smallest. If the steps shrink faster than that, it flips, with the LEDs far apart in the middle and crowded at the edge.
With equal area for every LED, the pixel density is the same all the way across the board.
You can always add one more
A square grid only looks tidy at square numbers, rings only when every ring is full, and a hex grid only at 7, 19, 37, 61… The faint outlines in the animation show the spots each layout still needs to fill before it looks right again.
The spiral is an even, round disc at every count, and adding an LED never moves any of the others. The Fibonacci32, Fibonacci64, Fibonacci128, Fibonacci256, Fibonacci512 and Fibonacci1024 all use the same layout, with differently sized LEDs and different spacings, each stopped at a different count.
Where the Fibonacci numbers come from
Look closely at any of the boards and you’ll see spiral arms. Connect every 3rd LED and you get 3 arms, because the golden angle is close to 1/3 of a turn. Every 5th LED makes 5 arms curving the other way, every 8th makes 8, and so on. Each of those fractions (2/5, 3/8, 5/13, 8/21…) is a little closer to the golden angle than the last, so each set of arms is a little straighter.
Any other count, like 4 or 30, zigzags or wobbles across the board instead.
The arm counts are 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 and 34. Put 1, 1 and 2 in front and each number is the sum of the two before it. They’re the Fibonacci numbers, which is where the boards get their name. Count the spirals in a sunflower head and you’ll find Fibonacci numbers there too.
Real boards
The video shows a real Fibonacci256, then the One Inch Fibonacci64, One Inch Fibonacci128, Fibonacci512 and Fibonacci1024. All of them follow the same rules.
More on Wikipedia: Fermat’s spiral, the golden angle, and phyllotaxis, the way plants arrange their leaves and seeds.
The animations and videos in this post are © Evil Genius Labs LLC, licensed CC BY-NC 4.0. You’re welcome to share and adapt them with credit, but not commercially.
