I had AI read my field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
05:26:41 UTC
14:26:41 KST

I had AI read my entire field.
158,059 papers and 554,670 citations. Every paper with full text screened, 659 of the most important recomputed and checked, and every verified error followed through the papers that cite it. This is the map, and what it says about whether science corrects itself.
Errors that nobody fixed
I spent five years in this field doing my PhD at Caltech, and a few months of that went to errors in the literature that were already known. The equations my code was built on came from Bishop, Gómez, Lehner, Maharaj & Winicour, “High-powered gravitational news” (1997), the paper the subfield's characteristic codes descend from. People knew it had mistakes. The fixes were scattered through some 10,000 lines of intersecting email threads that contradicted each other, and the paper itself was never corrected. The best I could do was correct the record in my own papers: an appendix setting out the full set of equations, made consistent, and a parenthetical “with a sign error in s3 corrected” for anyone reading closely.
That is the limit of human literature review. Mine was not deep: my three thesis papers cite fewer than a hundred papers between them, in a field of tens of thousands. Nobody re-derives every equation they cite, referees check one paper once, and nobody is paid to go back and fix the original. So every student who builds on a broken paper pays the same tax, one at a time, and the correction lives in somebody's inbox. A machine can read the whole field, recompute it, and follow each error to every paper that copied it. So I had one do it. It found errors in my own papers too.
Every dot is a paper
Height is time: the 1960s at the bottom, this year at the top. Each faint line is a citation. The bright dots are the papers everything else leans on, ranked the way Google ranked the early web.
The seed is TAPIR, Caltech's theoretical astrophysics group, where I did my PhD: 4,093 papers by its 326 members since 2004. Add every paper they cite and every paper that cites them and you get 158,059 papers joined by 554,670 citations. The 49,301 drawn here are the ones tied to TAPIR at least three times over.
Watch it grow
The map holds 499 papers from the 1970s, 2,035 from the 1990s and 18,976 from the 2010s. The old layers are the survivors, the papers people working today still cite. Everything else from 1975 has already been forgotten, right or wrong.
Most of what this field knows was written in the last twenty years, by people who are still around to answer email. Hold that thought.
A subfield is a column
Nobody told the layout what numerical relativity is. Papers that cite each other pull together, so a subfield shows up as a column: the same few dozen people writing about the same problem year after year, each layer standing on the last.
There are 32 columns, from fast radio bursts to the Milky Way's halo.
Numerical relativity
Solving Einstein's equations on a computer until two black holes merge. 278 papers in this column, 71 of them TAPIR's, busiest in 2010.
Every subfield has a page: the questions it is organised around and whether each is open, contested or settled, who wrote the central papers and where, how fast it publishes, and which of its errors we traced.
Each open question also carries a flag for what today's AI could do about it. Of 155, a model judged 8 answerable now from data and codes that already exist, 119 ones AI would speed up, and 28 stuck waiting on a telescope or a detector.
Every paper gets screened
Reading a paper carefully costs a few dollars of model time. Screening one costs nothing, so every paper I could get the full text of got screened: 50,269 papers, 421 million words, checked for the fingerprints of the worst kinds of trouble. That covers 76% of the papers drawn here. Nothing before 1991 is on arXiv and journal-only papers aren't open, so the rest got only the checks that run on a database record. (Gold marks TAPIR's own papers.)
- Paper-mill language: none.
- Chatbot residue and hidden instructions to AI reviewers: none.
- Text shared between papers with no author in common: 43 pairs in 34,286 papers, led by successive survey catalogues and data releases. The rest are queued for a human look.
- Retractions: 13 among 184,733 papers with a DOI. None is TAPIR's.
- TODO and FIXME notes shipped to arXiv: 62 papers.
Astrophysics is relatively clean. Whatever is wrong with this literature, it isn't fraud. The one needle that moves is vocabulary: “delve”, “crucial” and friends are 2.5 times as common in 2025 as in 2016.
The 200 that matter get checked line by line
Citations are brutally unequal, and a few hundred papers carry the field. So the 200 most-cited TAPIR papers of 2006–2019 (gold) each got their own AI reviewer with the LaTeX source, tools to run its own calculations, and orders to recompute everything it could: re-derive the equations, test the limits, rebuild the numbers from the paper's own tables. It worked blind, with no access to errata or later papers.
A flag is not a finding. Only what a second reviewer upholds is called an error here.
Thirteen fixed, fifty-six through
About 136 of the 200 were revised between the first preprint and the published paper, so we read those first preprints the same way. 13 verified errors were in the preprint and gone from the journal version, fixed by the referee or by the authors on a second look (purple).
56 went through review and into the journal (gold). On this evidence peer review removes about one error in five. At least two of the thirteen were copied by later papers anyway, from the stale preprint.
A factor of four, 2005–2014
Smith, Kamionkowski & Cooray convert the gravitational waves left over from inflation into an energy density a detector could see. Two factors of one half went missing, so the answer is four times too big: a 6 in the denominator where the textbook has 24. This one was double-checked. The paper's numbers in the paper's formula reproduce its result; the same numbers in the standard formula give a quarter of it.
Watch the years run. Red papers copied the factor of four. The green one said it was wrong, in 2008. The copying carried on until 2014: six copies, one objection.
Five copies for every criticism
Then we cast the net wider. The same recompute-and-verify check, run on 459 more still-cited papers across the map, mostly highly cited ones that a cheaper first read had flagged, upheld 816 more errors. That makes 872 in 433 papers. 159 of them were copied, wrong value and all, into at least one later paper. Counting papers:
367 papers copied an error. 68 criticised one.
Only 47 of the 872 were ever criticised in print, and 21 of those kept being copied afterwards, by 51 more papers. These are floors: we read only the citing papers whose text we hold.
And 872 is a floor for the field too. Only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map got the thorough treatment so far. Scaled up from the papers that did, the likely number of undetected errors in this field's papers cited 100 or more times is about 34,000 (25,000–48,000). How that number is reached →
Half are still being copied 7 years later
How effective is peer review and publishing at detecting and expunging errors from the literature? We can actually measure it.
Share of copied errors still being copied, by years since the paper appeared. Band: 95% interval. 33 errors are old enough to be observed at year 10.
The curve is still at 52% at year 7 and crosses one half at year 8; at year 10 it is at 39%. Counting papers that lean on the affected result without showing which value they used, it crosses at year 9. The errors we traced most thoroughly last longer, crossing at year 10: a shallower search simply finds fewer late copies.
What finally stops an error? Of the 56 errors in the 200 papers read most closely, 52 are still in the latest arXiv version, where a fix is free. Of the 200 papers read most closely, the database records an erratum for 2. And of the 87 errors that did die out, 67 were never criticised by anyone. They faded when the subfield moved on, which retires right answers and wrong ones at the same rate.
4% of the papers that matter, so far
Every paper with open full text was screened and skimmed. The expensive check, the one that recomputes, has reached 659 papers, starting with the most cited. Each bar is the papers on the map with that many citations, filled by how far they have been read.
A field outgrows its errors. It rarely corrects them.
All of this would cost about $2,720 in model time bought at list price, roughly $3 per verified error. In practice it ran within a Claude Max subscription. The whole project, this field and the others, took about 4.9 billion tokens and about 44 hours of my time over 41 days. It is one field, read by a first-generation method, with limits spelled out on the method page. And it is not finished: the deep check has reached only 4% of the highly cited papers on the map, most cited first. The rest of the queue is a budget decision, and so is the next field.
Errors were found by one AI session and re-derived by a second, independent one, and each was confirmed in the version the journal published. Five were also double-checked step by step against the source. No person has checked any of them. As a test, 40 drawn at random went to a third session that saw only the paper and the passage: it found 33 of the 40 wrong, so some named here will not survive scrutiny. If we have your paper wrong, say so and we will fix it and say that we did.

Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
04:14:04 UTC
13:14:04 KST

Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
Discussion on Hacker News▲ 238 points125 comments
While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes:
Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this.
I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage.
Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s
Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s
i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things
dude why is carbon so fucking slow
carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it
To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness.
The Task
In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes.
Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop.
Slow inference, or more work?
The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes:
Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show:
Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input.
Ruling out the obvious
Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations.
- The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference.
- Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix.
Reading the traces
We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work:
Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for:
- Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch.
- Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported.
In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes.
Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?"
With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows.
Carbon's necessary work is also slower
Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen.
Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime.
Conclusion
On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources:
- Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus.
- Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out.
- Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter.

Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?

Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
Discussion on Hacker News▲ 238 points125 comments
While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes:
Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this.
I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage.
Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s
Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s
i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things
dude why is carbon so fucking slow
carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it
To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness.
The Task
In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes.
Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop.
Slow inference, or more work?
The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes:
Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show:
Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input.
Ruling out the obvious
Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations.
- The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference.
- Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix.
Reading the traces
We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work:
Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for:
- Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch.
- Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported.

To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?"
With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows.
Carbon's necessary work is also slower
Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen.
Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime.

Claude was trained on protein sequences at scale
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
11:47:43 CST
12:47:43 KST

A next-amino-acid test on little-studied proteins finds that the latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences at scale. Other frontier models show no sign of it.
The latest Claude models were trained on protein sequences, at scale. Give Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Opus 5.5 the start of a little-studied bacterial protein and they predict the next amino acid. Shuffle the protein and they can’t. No other model we tested can do this. Like a protein language model, they do better on bigger protein families, and they do it even in families with no papers at all. Fable 5.2 beats every open protein language model we ran, and Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B, the largest of them.
Update, 18 November 2026. Since the first version:
Frontier LLMs have started to look good at protein tasks. Atharv Jayprakash showed GPT-6 Astra ranking SOD1 variants as well as ESM-2, and PG-LLM found the same across many proteins. Did these models learn from protein sequence databases such as UniProt, or from what is written about proteins?
Famous proteins can’t tell the two apart: GFP is printed in countless papers, and most frontier models recite it. So we tested proteins that almost nobody writes about.
We give a model the start of a protein and ask for the next amino acids. Then we ask again on a shuffled copy of the same protein. Shuffling keeps the letters and destroys their order, so the difference in accuracy measures what the model knows about the sequence itself.
The test set is 668 bacterial and archaeal proteins from 167 Pfam families of unknown function. No family has a solved structure or more than three papers, and no protein has a close relative in UniProt. Each protein is cut at five points. At each cut the model writes the next 10 amino acids, and we score the first. Thinking is at its lowest setting. Appendix E has the details.
Fable 5.2 gets the next amino acid right 54% of the time on real proteins and 9% on shuffled ones. The gap is there in nearly every family, not just a few easy ones. It appears in Opus 4.7, jumps in Opus 5.5, and jumps again in Fable 5.2. GPT, Gemini and the seven open-weight models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen 3.8, Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron 3 Ultra) stay near zero, even when they simply continue raw FASTA text, the way they were trained. The latest Claude models also write runs of correct residues that other models rarely manage (Appendix B).
Protein language models learn only from sequences, so they are the natural yardstick. The closest to an LLM are the ones that read a protein left to right and predict the next residue: ProtGPT3, whose 10-billion-parameter version is the largest open one, and ProGen3, whose largest public version has 3 billion. On the same input, Fable 5.2 beats both by a wide margin. Opus 5.5 is level with ProtGPT3-10B and below ProGen3-3B.
ESM models are trained to see both sides of a residue, so continuing from the left is harder for them. Appendix C has all nine models.
If the models learned from sequences, families with more sequences should be easier. To test this over a wide range, we added 90 smaller families, down to 20 proteins each, for 257 families in all.
They are. Opus 5.5 rises with the two protein language models, ProtGPT3-10B and ProGen3-3B, which are trained on nothing but sequences. Fable 5.2 rises fastest and levels off at about 300 proteins per family. Earlier Claude models rise at a lower level, and GPT and Gemini stay near zero. The knowledge also carries over to proteins published after the training cutoff, with no close relative before it (Appendix G).
Two other explanations don’t fit:
Famous proteins are a different story. Many models do well on them, and several recite hundreds of residues letter for letter (Appendix B), because these sequences are all over papers and the web. In a first round with famous and obscure proteins side by side, Gemini 4 Carbon was strong on the famous ones and dropped to almost nothing on the obscure ones. The latest Claude models and ProtGPT3-10B held up, and Fable 5.2 was the strongest on both.
This also explains the SOD1 and PG-LLM results. Ranking variants of a well-known protein can lean on what is written about it: which residues are buried, which substitutions break a helix, which mutations cause ALS. In PG-LLM, accuracy doesn’t depend on alignment depth and improves with more thinking, both signs of that route. Our test shuts it out. GPT-6 is good at the first kind of task and weak at the second; the latest Claude models are good at both.
The latest Claude models know protein families that almost nobody has studied. That takes a lot of sequence data, not a few examples: protein sequences were a sizeable part of their training. Opus 5.5 behaves like a protein language model, and Fable 5.2 goes beyond the best one we could run. GPT and Gemini show none of this. Whatever protein sequence they saw in training, it was not enough to learn these families.
DNA is different. Opus 5.5 predicts human and mouse coding sequence but not the rest of the genome, and barely the bacterial genes behind the proteins it knows (Appendix A). It learned proteins, not genomes.
We are curious what else this knowledge supports. Fable 5.2 predicts little-studied proteins better than any open protein language model we ran, and protein language models carry more than next-residue statistics: ESM-2’s internal representations hold enough structure that a small folding module on top predicts 3D structures (ESMFold), and their probabilities rank the effects of mutations. Could Claude fold a protein, or rank its variants, the same way?
All code, test sets, model outputs and figures are in llm-bioseq-probe.

220-nucleotide windows, 200 shown and 20 to predict, from hg38, mm39 and the bacterial genes behind the test proteins, 500 per region. Non-coding windows contain no repeats, and the control shuffles each window keeping its dinucleotide counts. Opus 5.5 wrote all 20 nucleotides right 25 times in 500 human coding windows; a blind guess does that about once in a trillion. Gemini 4 Carbon blocks most DNA prompts before answering, so it is not shown.
All 10 residues right. Each question asks for the next 10 residues. On the 668 little-studied proteins, Claude Fable 5.2 gets all 10 right at 88 real cuts and Opus 5.5 at 12, and neither at any shuffled one. If their residues were independent guesses at their own per-residue accuracy, they would get 15.8 and 0.57 by chance.
Runs in a row. On shuffled proteins neither Fable 5.2 nor Opus 5.5 gets more than 3 residues in a row. Once on track they get surer: after one right residue, Opus 5.5 gets the next right 47% of the time, after four in a row 68%.
Reciting well-known proteins. At 158 points in well-studied proteins, each model was asked for the next 200 residues at once.
GPT-6.1 Sol never reaches 100 residues, and GPT-5.5 never gets past 2.
ProtGPT3-10B gets more answers right than Opus 5.5 (38.4% vs 34.9%) but also more on shuffled proteins (10.7% vs 7.5%), because it knows amino acid composition better; the gap between the two, which is what each model knows about order, comes out the same. Prot-xLSTM is trained to read a protein after a set of its homologs; on the protein alone, as here, it is near zero, though one homolog in context lifts it from 14% to 81% on hemoglobin β. The last row is fill-in-the-blank rather than continuation: ESM-2 also sees the residues after the cut, which the LLMs never get. Every model first passed a sanity check on well-known proteins. Continuing ubiquitin and hemoglobin β from the left, ProGen3-3B gets 98% and 87% of residues right and ProtGPT3-10B 100% and 84%; with the whole protein and one residue masked, ESM-2 gets 80% of ubiquitin, ESM C and ESM3-open 100%. Masks are set on token ids, because the ESM SDK’s “_” character is not ESM C’s mask token. ProtGPT2 uses multi-residue tokens, so a residue’s probability is the sum over the tokens that start with it; ProGen3 and ProtGPT3 use one token per residue.
Choosing the proteins. We started from every Pfam family whose name says “domain of unknown function” (DUF) or “protein of unknown function”, and kept those with no structure in the PDB, at most 3 Europe PMC hits for the family’s accession, and at least 300 member proteins. We binned them by size (300 to 1,000 proteins, 1,000 to 3,000, 3,000 to 10,000, over 10,000) and drew 50 families per bin at random; only 17 families qualify above 10,000, so the set has 167. From each family we took 4 proteins from UniProt that are unreviewed (TrEMBL), come from Bacteria or Archaea, are 120 to 800 residues long, use only the 20 standard amino acids, are not low-complexity (Shannon entropy above 3.9 bits per residue), and are alone in their UniRef90 cluster, so no other UniProt protein is 90% or more identical to them. That gives 668 proteins.
Smaller families. For the family-size test we drew 30 more families in each of three smaller bins (20 to 60, 60 to 150 and 150 to 300 proteins) with the same criteria and 4 proteins per family, 360 proteins in all. Every model gets the same prompt and scoring as on the main set.
Cutting. Each protein is cut at 5 positions drawn at random inside its Pfam domain (the longest domain span, at least 40 residues), at least 10 residues from either end of the domain and with at least 30 residues before the cut: 3,340 cuts. Everything before the cut is the prefix; the residue right after it is the answer.
Asking. The model gets this message, with the prefix in 60-character lines (an example from one of the test proteins):
Below is the beginning of a protein sequence in one-letter amino acid codes.
Predict how it continues. Reply with exactly the next 10 amino acids as
one-letter codes on one line, and nothing else.
>sequence
MRSGGQPLHPQPAHRFHYRTAARPRAAWILGCVLHLADAEEGARFWWQYAAGAGDDAAAY
CLYLHCLVLGDSYAAALWREQTSLDTPPHDFDDTSVPTVLRILSRLTPA
Each model runs through its own API with temperature 0 where it is accepted, thinking off or at its lowest setting (for Opus 5.5 and the Fable models, low effort, at which the model still decides whether to think), no tools, and one sample per question. The Claude Fable models run through OpenRouter, since Anthropic’s API serves them only to workspaces that retain data. Models that declined to guess (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, gpt-oss) also got a version that adds “Give your best guess even if you are uncertain. Do not explain or refuse.”; those runs are marked separately.
Thinking. A reply counts as thought about when the API reports thinking tokens for it: thinking_tokens in Anthropic’s usage report, reasoning_tokens in OpenRouter’s. The thinking text itself is not kept; only the visible reply is scored. Fable 5.2 thought on 9% of questions, Opus 5.5 on 36%, Fable 5.1 never. Without thinking, Fable 5.2 is right 54.7% of the time on real proteins and 8.8% on shuffled ones (48.2% and 10.6% with thinking), and Opus 5.5 35.3% and 6.9% (34.1% and 8.6%).
Scoring. We read the last sequence the reply states: a run of capital amino-acid letters on its own line or after a label such as “Answer:”, skipping words, lists and anything inside thinking tags. If it starts by restating the end of the prefix, the restatement is dropped. Its first letter is the predicted next amino acid. A reply cut off at the length limit counts only if it opens with a sequence. Replies that state no sequence are excluded and counted (0.1% for Opus 5.5). Only the first residue is scored; the full 10 are used for exact continuations and runs. The same reader is used for every model and for real and shuffled proteins.
The shuffled control. Each protein’s residues are shuffled once, with a random seed fixed by its accession, and the same 5 cut positions are asked on the shuffled sequence. The shuffle keeps the composition of the whole protein and destroys the order, so a model that knows only which amino acids are common scores the same on both.
Statistics. For each family we compute the share of correct first residues on real and on shuffled cuts, and take the difference, in percentage points. The result for a model is the mean of that gap over the 167 families. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over families (10,000 resamples), the main test is a one-sided sign-flip permutation test over families, and the family-size trend is the Spearman correlation between a family’s gap and the logarithm of its size.
Raw continuation. For models that allow it, the same prefix is sent without any instruction, as the text “>sequence” followed by the FASTA lines, through a plain completion endpoint (open-weight models on Fireworks) or as the start of the model’s own reply (Gemini 2.5 Pro). The first letter the model writes is scored as above.
Protein language models. They get the same prefix and no prompt. ProGen3, ProtGPT3, ProtGPT2 and Prot-xLSTM read it left to right and give a probability for the next token; the ESM models see the prefix, a mask in place of the next residue, and the end of the sequence. In every case the prediction is the most likely of the 20 standard amino acids.
Total API cost was about $730, plus a few dollars of GPU time for the protein language models.
Gemini 4 Carbon blocked about 75% of DNA prompts outright. OpenAI rejected 23 GPT-6 requests in the first round and 17 GPT-6.1 Sol requests in the main run as possible biological misuse, and 6.6% of GPT-6.2 Astra’s main-set questions (GPT-6.2 Sol: 0.6%). Claude Sonnet 4.5 refused 97% of requests that started its reply with a protein sequence, and Anthropic’s filter blocked 44% of Claude Fable 5’s questions as cyber content.
Leo Tianlai Chen built a set of 56 proteins from 31 of the families that were first made public in August 2026, after the assumed 1 July training cutoff, and have no earlier relative at 50% identity or more. The models cannot have seen them or anything close. Both Claude models still predict them, Fable 5.2 ahead of both protein language models, while GPT-6.2 Sol stays at zero. Every model scores about half of what it scores on the same families in the main set, as expected for proteins this distant. What the latest Claude models learned carries over to new members of a family.
The proteins were dated at their source, and none matches an earlier UniRef50 cluster at 50% identity or more. Cuts follow the main set’s rules. With 56 proteins only gaps of about 14 points or more are reliably detected, and the 1 July cutoff is an assumption.

Choosing the proteins. We started from every Pfam family whose name says “domain of unknown function” (DUF) or “protein of unknown function”, and kept those with no structure in the PDB, at most 3 Europe PMC hits for the family’s accession, and at least 300 member proteins. We binned them by size (300 to 1,000 proteins, 1,000 to 3,000, 3,000 to 10,000, over 10,000) and drew 50 families per bin at random; only 17 families qualify above 10,000, so the set has 167. From each family we took 4 proteins from UniProt that are unreviewed (TrEMBL), come from Bacteria or Archaea, are 120 to 800 residues long, use only the 20 standard amino acids, are not low-complexity (Shannon entropy above 3.9 bits per residue), and are alone in their UniRef90 cluster, so no other UniProt protein is 90% or more identical to them. That gives 668 proteins.
Smaller families. For the family-size test we drew 30 more families in each of three smaller bins (20 to 60, 60 to 150 and 150 to 300 proteins) with the same criteria and 4 proteins per family, 360 proteins in all. Every model gets the same prompt and scoring as on the main set.
Cutting. Each protein is cut at 5 positions drawn at random inside its Pfam domain (the longest domain span, at least 40 residues), at least 10 residues from either end of the domain and with at least 30 residues before the cut: 3,340 cuts. Everything before the cut is the prefix; the residue right after it is the answer.
Asking. The model gets this message, with the prefix in 60-character lines (an example from one of the test proteins):
Below is the beginning of a protein sequence in one-letter amino acid codes.
Predict how it continues. Reply with exactly the next 10 amino acids as
one-letter codes on one line, and nothing else.
>sequence
MRSGGQPLHPQPAHRFHYRTAARPRAAWILGCVLHLADAEEGARFWWQYAAGAGDDAAAY
CLYLHCLVLGDSYAAALWREQTSLDTPPHDFDDTSVPTVLRILSRLTPA
Each model runs through its own API with temperature 0 where it is accepted, thinking off or at its lowest setting (for Opus 5.5 and the Fable models, low effort, at which the model still decides whether to think), no tools, and one sample per question. The Claude Fable models run through OpenRouter, since Anthropic’s API serves them only to workspaces that retain data. Models that declined to guess (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, gpt-oss) also got a version that adds “Give your best guess even if you are uncertain. Do not explain or refuse.”; those runs are marked separately.
Thinking. A reply counts as thought about when the API reports thinking tokens for it: thinking_tokens in Anthropic’s usage report, reasoning_tokens in OpenRouter’s. The thinking text itself is not kept; only the visible reply is scored. Fable 5.2 thought on 9% of questions, Opus 5.5 on 36%, Fable 5.1 never. Without thinking, Fable 5.2 is right 54.7% of the time on real proteins and 8.8% on shuffled ones (48.2% and 10.6% with thinking), and Opus 5.5 35.3% and 6.9% (34.1% and 8.6%).
Scoring. We read the last sequence the reply states: a run of capital amino-acid letters on its own line or after a label such as “Answer:”, skipping words, lists and anything inside thinking tags. If it starts by restating the end of the prefix, the restatement is dropped. Its first letter is the predicted next amino acid. A reply cut off at the length limit counts only if it opens with a sequence. Replies that state no sequence are excluded and counted (0.1% for Opus 5.5). Only the first residue is scored; the full 10 are used for exact continuations and runs. The same reader is used for every model and for real and shuffled proteins.
The shuffled control. Each protein’s residues are shuffled once, with a random seed fixed by its accession, and the same 5 cut positions are asked on the shuffled sequence. The shuffle keeps the composition of the whole protein and destroys the order, so a model that knows only which amino acids are common scores the same on both.
Statistics. For each family we compute the share of correct first residues on real and on shuffled cuts, and take the difference, in percentage points. The result for a model is the mean of that gap over the 167 families. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over families (10,000 resamples), the main test is a one-sided sign-flip permutation test over families, and the family-size trend is the Spearman correlation between a family’s gap and the logarithm of its size.
Raw continuation. For models that allow it, the same prefix is sent without any instruction, as the text “>sequence” followed by the FASTA lines, through a plain completion endpoint (open-weight models on Fireworks) or as the start of the model’s own reply (Gemini 2.5 Pro). The first letter the model writes is scored as above.
Protein language models. They get the same prefix and no prompt. ProGen3, ProtGPT3, ProtGPT2 and Prot-xLSTM read it left to right and give a probability for the next token; the ESM models see the prefix, a mask in place of the next residue, and the end of the sequence. In every case the prediction is the most likely of the 20 standard amino acids.
Total API cost was about $730, plus a few dollars of GPU time for the protein language models.
Gemini 4 Carbon blocked about 75% of DNA prompts outright. OpenAI rejected 23 GPT-6 requests in the first round and 17 GPT-6.1 Sol requests in the main run as possible biological misuse, and 6.6% of GPT-6.2 Astra’s main-set questions (GPT-6.2 Sol: 0.6%). Claude Sonnet 4.5 refused 97% of requests that started its reply with a protein sequence, and Anthropic’s filter blocked 44% of Claude Fable 5’s questions as cyber content.
Leo Tianlai Chen built a set of 56 proteins from 31 of the families that were first made public in August 2026, after the assumed 1 July training cutoff, and have no earlier relative at 50% identity or more. The models cannot have seen them or anything close. Both Claude models still predict them, Fable 5.2 ahead of both protein language models, while GPT-6.2 Sol stays at zero. Every model scores about half of what it scores on the same families in the main set, as expected for proteins this distant. What the latest Claude models learned carries over to new members of a family.
The proteins were dated at their source, and none matches an earlier UniRef50 cluster at 50% identity or more. Cuts follow the main set’s rules. With 56 proteins only gaps of about 14 points or more are reliably detected, and the 1 July cutoff is an assumption.

Engineering Vitals in the Age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
03:36:12 UTC
12:36:12 KST

Every engineering organization is being asked the same question right now: is AI actually making us better at building software?
It’s a fair question. We’re spending real money on tokens and tooling, and we’re reshaping how our teams work. We should be able to say what we’re getting for it.
The answers I see tend to fall into two camps. The first counts activity: lines of code generated, tokens consumed, the percentage of code written by agents. The second skips straight to the destination, and declares that the only thing worth measuring is value.
LaunchDarkly’s recent Release Autopilot announcement is a good example of the second camp. It describes the goal they set for their AI software factory: maximize the valuable software reaching customers for each hour of human attention it takes to get it there.
That isn’t a goal. It’s an aspiration.
How do you count valuable software? Value shows up weeks or months after changes ship, and it’s the product of many decisions made across product, design, engineering, and sales. Value is a team sport. How do you count an hour of human attention? I won’t be the person who introduces timesheets for attention.
It’s worth looking at the evidence the same post offers. With roughly the same number of engineers, monthly merged pull requests more than doubled, and time spent in major and critical incidents fell by about 70%. Those are throughput and stability measures. They’re good evidence, and they sit a lot closer to a pull request count than they do to value.
This post is about what we’ve chosen to measure at Octopus, and why. None of it is revolutionary. But some of it is counter to the current product development zeitgeist.
Outcomes are made of outputs
Outcomes over outputs is one of the most repeated phrases in product development. It’s true that the outcome is ultimately the thing that matters. But the phrase obscures how we get to one.
Outcomes are realized through the continuous delivery of outputs. We make a decision, ship something, watch what happens, and decide again. It’s the OODA loop. The first thing we ship is almost never the most valuable thing. It helps us learn, pivot or persevere, and eventually reach a point where we’ve realized a lot of value.
You can’t ship just one thing and win. You also could ship infinite things and not win. You’ve got to produce outputs and go through the loop.
This is the value discovery loop. The faster we complete it, the more value we accumulate over time.
Velocity: the speed with which we complete the value discovery loop.
Outputs are a proxy to value.
Engineering vitals
Who is the primary driver of the value discovery loop? Engineering.
“But Besty, our product managers and designers are all shipping changes to our product these days thanks to Claude!” you might say. Congratulations to them - they are now also engineers, and their efforts will be reflected in engineering’s vitals.
One of the jobs of engineering leaders is to unblock and enable their organization’s teams to ship as effectively and efficiently as they can. Once you go past a handful of engineers, you can’t put your hand on your heart and say you are fulfilling this responsibility without having some sort of data to back it up.
At Octopus there have been multiple times when we have paused to measure something in our delivery pipeline, and discovered some healthy optimizations we could make.
Your vitals should give you insight into how effectively your engineering organization is producing outputs and maintaining its service level objectives. They will help you move beyond vibes, and to a more concrete view of how well you are delivering and contributing to your organization’s outcomes.
Why we rebooted our vitals
AI is a disruptive force, and at Octopus leaning into this disruption matters. AI is a lever - it can help us achieve more, and provide an increasingly better customer experience, without significantly increasing our costs. But even more importantly - our customers are undergoing the same disruption. Our customers are engineers - they ship software day in, day out, and most are somewhere along the same AI adoption journey we are on at Octopus. To truly empathize with our customers’ pain on this journey, we need to live it ourselves.
Our hypothesis about where software engineering is heading is simple: an overwhelming volume of change. We’re already seeing two-engineer teams become normal thanks to the leverage AI gives them, and the time it takes to build and ship is compressing.
We are rebooting our engineering vitals because our AI transformation is changing the shape of our work. I don’t use the word “transformation” hyperbolically here - the changes are actually transformational. We need to know whether the shifts we’re making in our AI-driven development lifecycle are helping us get through the value discovery loop faster, while maintaining our SLOs.
If the hypothesis holds, these are the questions we need to be able to answer:
- How frequently are we shipping changes and progressively releasing them to customers?
- Are our engineering feedback loops meeting our standards for speed and reliability?
- Is the volume of change increasing as we lean into agentic workflows, while headcount stays stable?
- Is work starting that previously wouldn’t have been done regularly, or at all?
- Is our operational burden shrinking? Fewer people, less time, less toil.
- Is quality improving at the same time?
- Are people still finding joy and satisfaction in their work, as the nature of that work changes?
These questions help us understand the effectiveness of our engineering organization, and help to identify which levers we might be able to pull if we spot things that are slowing us down.
AI adoption has its own set of measures that sit alongside our vitals - we will talk to these in a separate blog post.
The measures
We’ve divided our vitals into three areas.
Delivery objectives measure the effectiveness of our delivery pipeline and feedback loops. They’re measured per system, and the team that owns the system sets the service level objective (SLO).
Quality objectives measure the quality of what we ship, and the quality of our developer experience. They’re measured across the whole organization, and I as CTO own the SLOs.
Trends are measured across the whole organization, and deliberately have no SLO. We capture them because they give us insight, particularly when read alongside the objectives.
If you know the DORA metrics, most of this looks familiar. However there is one particular fight I’ll pick with DORA’s metrics - change failure rate does nothing to help you understand customer impact.
Do not obscure the customer impact of failure
We don’t measure change failure rate.
For a long time our change failure rate sat below 2%, which is healthy by any benchmark. Yet sometimes the failures that did occur still had significant customer impact. The signal said everything was fine. Our customers’ lived experience said otherwise.
AI makes this problem worse. A rate has a denominator, and the denominator is the thing we expect to explode. If we double the changes we merge and hold our failure rate steady, we’ve doubled the defects reaching customers, and the dashboard hasn’t moved.
Customers don’t experience a percentage. They experience the defect.
So we count. Every month we look at the number of Sev 0-2 defects that reached customers, and as leaders we dig into the specific issues behind the number. We can still derive a rate if we want one.
This only works if all work is tracked. If a defect has been merged to main and deployed, it’s logged with a severity, whether a customer found it or we did. We’re our own customer zero, so any issue that affects us affects a customer.
Trends without targets
We care about velocity, and need to reason about it in aggregate over time. In this, we take heed of Goodhart’s law for trends: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. So we don’t set goals for it.
Pull request volume is our proxy for velocity, and our window into the value discovery loop.
We care how quickly we are getting through the value discovery loop. We want to see a trend up and to the right as we lean further into agentic development.
We set other measurable goals that seek to impact velocity. An example might be the % of PRs that are shipped without human intervention.
Trends are particularly useful in combination with service level objectives. Pull request volume rising while Sev 0-2 counts hold flat and lead time stays steady tells a richer story than just understanding velocity is improving.
We’re in good company
While counter to some popular product development ideologies, none of this is particularly esoteric.
I’m a big fan and a regular reader of Gergely Orosz’s Pragmatic Engineer newsletter. In one publication, Laura Tacho and Gergely looked at how 18 tech companies measure the impact of AI, including Google, GitHub, Microsoft, Dropbox, and Monzo. Two findings stood out to me:
- Most of the types of measures look the same as they did before AI. The companies getting clear answers are the ones that had already invested in understanding their engineering performance.
- Almost every company pairs a measure of speed with a measure of quality, so each keeps the other in check.
More recent data tells the same story with bigger numbers. Atlassian’s write-up of DX data from more than 500 companies reports that median pull request throughput has doubled. It also reports that pull request size grew 122% in four quarters, engineers’ confidence in their changes dropped, and the share of capacity going to new customer value moved by a single percentage point.
That’s the overwhelming volume of change arriving, without the value arriving with it. It’s also why pull request volume is a trend for us and not a goal.
The same write-up describes Dropbox pointing its unlocked capacity at long-deferred maintenance, like language migrations and dependency upgrades. That’s one of our own questions being answered: work is starting that previously wouldn’t have been done.
There’s one place we’re out of step. Nearly all of these companies track change failure rate as their quality measure, and we’ve chosen counts. I’ve explained why above.
And to be fair to LaunchDarkly, their numbers fit this pattern too. Merged pull requests up, incident time down, headcount flat. Speed and quality, measured side by side. It’s good evidence that their machine is working. Whether the software was valuable is a different question, answered somewhere else.
Speaking of LaunchDarkly, did you know Octopus now has Feature Flags? Octopus feature flags are available in all license tiers at no additional cost, are built on OpenFeature, and are a natural fit for organizations deploying with a high frequency, who want more control over the release of changes to their customers and users.
Conclusion
AI hasn’t changed what makes an engineering organization effective. It has changed how much flows through one, and how quickly a weakness gets exposed.
Measuring value per hour of human attention is a fine thing to want. But value is a lagging signal with many owners, and you can’t steer your organization by it week to week.
So start with the measuring what you can steer. Know how long it takes to get a change into customers’ hands, how quickly you recover when a change is wrong, how many serious defects reached customers this month, and whether the volume of change is growing while those numbers hold.
When you can answer those questions on demand, you can then raise your gaze: if your measures are healthy and the needle still isn’t moving, you know where to look next.
Measure the efficiency of your engineering machine. Then set your sights on value.
Sources
- AI changed how we write software. We must change how we release it., LaunchDarkly, November 2026
- State of AI-assisted Software Development, DORA, 2025
- Balancing AI tensions: Moving from AI adoption to effective SDLC use, DORA, March 2026
- How tech companies measure the impact of AI on software development, The Pragmatic Engineer, September 2025
- Measuring and orchestrating AI across the full engineering lifecycle, Atlassian, November 2026

US Officially a Measles Endemic Country 139
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years.
Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response.
"We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."

Bank CEOs, NSA Tell Congress That AI-Driven Patches Are Behind Outages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
01:45:11 UTC
10:45:11 KST

Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week’s widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations.
Over the last few days, the country has faced a series of startling tech failures, leading to a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down.
While it does not appear that these disruptions were caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials have told lawmakers that they stem from attempts to fix gaps in cyber defenses identified by AI models, the sources said. The fixes, however, temporarily overwhelmed the systems.
“These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away,” said one congressional official briefed on the matter. “They’re trying to push through a lot of patches all at once — more than the system was designed for.”
Trending
On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that “scheduled routine maintenance” was responsible for the “temporary degradation” of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that “they’re pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We’re going to see more of this as new technology rolls out.”
Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves, seeking to identify the vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them. Once these gaps are identified, they are under immense pressure to patch them as soon as possible, knowing that malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools — or will soon.
This urgency is what has driven a wide range of public- and private-sector actors to rush fixes to their systems faster than they normally would, the sources said. But even entities with large resources, such as the nation’s top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.
The outages rippled across the country this week. The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal. Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook.
Microsoft blamed a technical defect for the disruption. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down.
“There’s some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there’s not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems,” said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. “Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won’t be a one and done thing — we’ll continue to find more vulnerabilities.”
The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.
The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.
But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.
Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.” Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.
It’s also become a big financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.
The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.
Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.
“We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

Cerebras Disaggregated Inference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
00:56:23 UTC
09:56:23 KST

We’ve deployed Cerebras Wafer Scale Engines with GPUs to deliver lightning-fast tokens at scale
The world is hungry for ultrafast tokens. In 2026, Cerebras saw an insatiable demand for fast inference, both on our inference cloud and via our partners. To meet demand, we began developing disaggregated inference: GPUs handle prompt processing (prefill) and Cerebras systems handle output generation (decode).
This solution is now in production and delivers five times more tokens per megawatt at the same ultrafast Cerebras speeds.
We can now serve more ultrafast tokens via Cerebras Inference Cloud to meet market demand. Infrastructure partners can also leverage the Cerebras disaggregated solution to achieve more ultrafast tokens in their own datacenters.
Alongside our recently announced CS-4, our dramatically scaled manufacturing, and our planned 700MW of data center capacity, disaggregated inference will enable Cerebras and partners to serve many more ultrafast tokens in 2027 and beyond.
In this blog we cover:
- The need for more ultrafast inference capacity
- Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode
- Cerebras disaggregated inference production results
- Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners
The need for more fast inference capacity
Agentic applications like Muse, Copilot, and Codex are scaling rapidly and require highly interactive inference to keep users engaged. To meet the growing demand of these applications in a power-constrained environment, our industry must deliver significantly more inference capacity per megawatt, at response speeds that make these applications useful.
Sources: Goldman Sachs Research, “AI Agents Forecast to Boost Tech Cash Flow as Usage Soars,” May 20, 2026; Goldman Sachs data center capacity estimates, as reported by Investing.com, November 6, 2026.
That is why Cerebras invested in disaggregation. Pairing a prefill accelerator for prompt processing with the Cerebras System for response generation increases token throughput per megawatt while preserving Cerebras’ ultrafast generation speeds. For inference providers, that means more capacity to serve customers and greater revenue potential from the same power budget.
Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode
An inference request has two main stages. Prompt processing, known as prefill, processes the input and produces intermediate model state. Response generation, known as decode, uses that state to generate output tokens. There are many ways to split the inference workload, including draft–target and attention–FFN among others, but separating prefill from decode is uniquely advantageous when the goal is highly interactive inference.
Decode is autoregressive. That means the model generates one token at a time, using each generated token as an input to generate the next. Each step means reading model data from memory again, so memory bandwidth matters a lot. In the ultrafast inference domain, SRAM-centric chips have an advantage because they can keep that data on-chip and read it much more quickly. Cerebras takes this to wafer scale, with tens of gigabytes of SRAM and tens of petabytes per second of memory bandwidth on a single chip—350× the SRAM capacity and 5,400× the memory bandwidth of a typical GB300 GPU. This allows the Cerebras System to fit more concurrent requests and model layers directly on the chip, enabling the CS-3, CS-4, and CS-5 to achieve ultrafast speeds at an attractive throughput.
Cerebras disaggregated inference production results
Pairing Cerebras systems, which are optimized for ultrafast decode, with accelerators well-suited to the compute needs of prefill, such as AMD Instinct GPUs, allows the delivery of an immense amount of ultrafast inference at scale. In a production deployment on the Cerebras Inference Cloud, AMD Instinct GPUs process prompts, and Cerebras CS-3 systems generate responses. Moving prompt processing to GPUs allows Cerebras systems to devote their serving capacity to response generation. In our measured production deployment, this combination delivered 5X the throughput per megawatt of a CS-3-only configuration, with no loss in token generation speed.
Source: November 14th shared GPT-OSS-120B endpoint via the Cerebras Inference Cloud throughput per megawatt before and after enabling disaggregated inference, normalized to the aggregated inference baseline (1×).
We plan to deploy disaggregated inference broadly across hundreds of megawatts in the Cerebras Inference Cloud and in partner deployments by the end of 2027. Our aim is to increase the ultrafast inference capacity available for our customers.
Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners
The Cerebras disaggregated inference solution was also built for our partners to adopt. Infrastructure partners can deploy disaggregated inference clusters based on Cerebras-provided reference architecture, co-locating their chosen prefill accelerators and Cerebras systems within a unified network. For software integration, partners can either integrate with the Cerebras end-to-end disaggregated software stack or a decode-only SDK.
The end-to-end disaggregated software stack is best suited for partners optimizing time-to-market. It consists of:
- A disaggregated inference framework to route requests between prefill and decode pools and manage replica capacity and health.
- A prefill engine to process prompts using open-source inference engines like vLLM or SGLang.
- A Cerebras decode engine for response generation on Cerebras systems.
- KV Portal software, an interface to transfer intermediate model state, including key-value caches, between prefill and decode engines over RDMA.
The decode-only SDK is best suited for partners optimizing for control. With the decode-only SDK, partners can bring their own inference framework and prefill engine to the Cerebras decode engine and KV Portal software. In addition, the decode-only SDK provides development aids such as a mock Cerebras decode replica and a reference integration to an open-source disaggregated inference framework and prefill engine.
Early-access partners, including Amazon Web Services, Fireworks AI, Gimlet Labs, and General Compute, already have access to the Cerebras disaggregation solution for their deployments. We are now expanding access to additional partners looking to bring ultrafast inference to their customers at scale.
To discuss the results, solutions, or deployment opportunities in more detail, contact us here.

Cerebras Disaggregated Inference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-18
00:56:23 UTC
09:56:23 KST

We’ve deployed Cerebras Wafer Scale Engines with GPUs to deliver lightning-fast tokens at scale
The world is hungry for ultrafast tokens. In 2026, Cerebras saw an insatiable demand for fast inference, both on our inference cloud and via our partners. To meet demand, we began developing disaggregated inference: GPUs handle prompt processing (prefill) and Cerebras systems handle output generation (decode).
This solution is now in production and delivers five times more tokens per megawatt at the same ultrafast Cerebras speeds.
We can now serve more ultrafast tokens via Cerebras Inference Cloud to meet market demand. Infrastructure partners can also leverage the Cerebras disaggregated solution to achieve more ultrafast tokens in their own datacenters.
Alongside our recently announced CS-4, our dramatically scaled manufacturing, and our planned 700MW of data center capacity, disaggregated inference will enable Cerebras and partners to serve many more ultrafast tokens in 2027 and beyond.
In this blog we cover:
- The need for more ultrafast inference capacity
- Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode
- Cerebras disaggregated inference production results
- Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners
The need for more fast inference capacity
Agentic applications like Muse, Copilot, and Codex are scaling rapidly and require highly interactive inference to keep users engaged. To meet the growing demand of these applications in a power-constrained environment, our industry must deliver significantly more inference capacity per megawatt, at response speeds that make these applications useful.
Sources: Goldman Sachs Research, “AI Agents Forecast to Boost Tech Cash Flow as Usage Soars,” May 20, 2026; Goldman Sachs data center capacity estimates, as reported by Investing.com, November 6, 2026.
That is why Cerebras invested in disaggregation. Pairing a prefill accelerator for prompt processing with the Cerebras System for response generation increases token throughput per megawatt while preserving Cerebras’ ultrafast generation speeds. For inference providers, that means more capacity to serve customers and greater revenue potential from the same power budget.
Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode
An inference request has two main stages. Prompt processing, known as prefill, processes the input and produces intermediate model state. Response generation, known as decode, uses that state to generate output tokens. There are many ways to split the inference workload, including draft–target and attention–FFN among others, but separating prefill from decode is uniquely advantageous when the goal is highly interactive inference.
Decode is autoregressive. That means the model generates one token at a time, using each generated token as an input to generate the next. Each step means reading model data from memory again, so memory bandwidth matters a lot. In the ultrafast inference domain, SRAM-centric chips have an advantage because they can keep that data on-chip and read it much more quickly. Cerebras takes this to wafer scale, with tens of gigabytes of SRAM and tens of petabytes per second of memory bandwidth on a single chip—350× the SRAM capacity and 5,400× the memory bandwidth of a typical GB300 GPU. This allows the Cerebras System to fit more concurrent requests and model layers directly on the chip, enabling the CS-3, CS-4, and CS-5 to achieve ultrafast speeds at an attractive throughput.
Cerebras disaggregated inference production results
Pairing Cerebras systems, which are optimized for ultrafast decode, with accelerators well-suited to the compute needs of prefill, such as AMD Instinct GPUs, allows the delivery of an immense amount of ultrafast inference at scale. In a production deployment on the Cerebras Inference Cloud, AMD Instinct GPUs process prompts, and Cerebras CS-3 systems generate responses. Moving prompt processing to GPUs allows Cerebras systems to devote their serving capacity to response generation. In our measured production deployment, this combination delivered 5X the throughput per megawatt of a CS-3-only configuration, with no loss in token generation speed.
Source: November 14th shared GPT-OSS-120B endpoint via the Cerebras Inference Cloud throughput per megawatt before and after enabling disaggregated inference, normalized to the aggregated inference baseline (1×).
We plan to deploy disaggregated inference broadly across hundreds of megawatts in the Cerebras Inference Cloud and in partner deployments by the end of 2027. Our aim is to increase the ultrafast inference capacity available for our customers.
Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners
The Cerebras disaggregated inference solution was also built for our partners to adopt. Infrastructure partners can deploy disaggregated inference clusters based on Cerebras-provided reference architecture, co-locating their chosen prefill accelerators and Cerebras systems within a unified network. For software integration, partners can either integrate with the Cerebras end-to-end disaggregated software stack or a decode-only SDK.
The end-to-end disaggregated software stack is best suited for partners optimizing time-to-market. It consists of:
- A disaggregated inference framework to route requests between prefill and decode pools and manage replica capacity and health.
- A prefill engine to process prompts using open-source inference engines like vLLM or SGLang.
- A Cerebras decode engine for response generation on Cerebras systems.
- KV Portal software, an interface to transfer intermediate model state, including key-value caches, between prefill and decode engines over RDMA.
The decode-only SDK is best suited for partners optimizing for control. With the decode-only SDK, partners can bring their own inference framework and prefill engine to the Cerebras decode engine and KV Portal software. In addition, the decode-only SDK provides development aids such as a mock Cerebras decode replica and a reference integration to an open-source disaggregated inference framework and prefill engine.
Early-access partners, including Amazon Web Services, Fireworks AI, Gimlet Labs, and General Compute, already have access to the Cerebras disaggregation solution for their deployments. We are now expanding access to additional partners looking to bring ultrafast inference to their customers at scale.
To discuss the results, solutions, or deployment opportunities in more detail, contact us here.
